311.body:
graphersal store create <DIR> [--from <SOURCE>] [--chunk-size <BYTES>] [--single-file] [--on-damage maintenance|continue] Creates a store in the new (missing or empty) DIR, at commit 0 with one snapshot. The chunk size, the damage policy and the backend are fixed for the store's life . Option --from <SOURCE> the initial graph: the --graph sources modern, empty, large, tree, a GraphSON/GraphML file, or a packed snapshot (.gsnap, copied as is). Default: an empty graph --chunk-size <BYTES> the snapshot chunk size (default 1 MiB), fixed for the store's life --single-file a single-file store whatever the name (a DIR ending in .gstore is one anyway) --on-damage <POLICY> what the store does when damage is found on disk while it is open: maintenance (default: it turns read-only) or continue (it keeps committing and reports the damage); fixed for the store's life $ graphersal store create data/ --from modern
Created the store data/: graph 01a11a54-8209-7661-92e2-147ae6d8bbd3, commit 0, 1 snapshot(s); damage policy maintenance (fixed for its life).
Use it: graphersal --graph data/ (or --server)
$ graphersal store create graph.gstore --from modern --on-damage continue
Created the single-file store graph.gstore: graph 01a11a54-8ca5-7fd3-8ed5-fcd7729f0e80, commit 0, 1 snapshot(s); damage policy continue (fixed for its life). Exit 2 when the source cannot be loaded or --on-damage names no policy; 1 when DIR is a directory that is not empty (cannot create a store in data/: the directory is not empty, with the help to choose an empty or new directory, or to look at it with graphersal store info data/ if it is a store) or a store already (it is a store already). graphersal --graph <DIR> --create-store [--on-damage <POLICY>] creates a store on first use instead (--on-damage without --create-store is a usage error; for an existing store with another policy it is refused: the policy never changes).

graphersal store checkpoint <DIR> [--name <NAME>] Writes a snapshot of the current state of the CLOSED store, merged from the last snapshot and the WAL after it without loading the graph ( how ): Snapshot at commit 3 (8 vertices, 6 edges).

317.body: graphersal store verify <DIR> Reads every checksum (snapshots, WAL, GRAPH, marks). Exit 0 with ok: no damage found; exit 1 with every problem and the damage report (the donor of each damaged item). See Verify . Files of a newer format version are never listed as damage: verify exits 1 with the "written by a newer Graphersal" refusal shown under info (no DAMAGE lines, no repair advice), and store repair refuses such a store the same way.

318.body:
graphersal store fork <DIR> <NEW_DIR> [TARGET] A new store in NEW_DIR (it must not exist, or be empty) from the state at TARGET (default: the latest), with a new lineage that records DIR as its parent. DIR is not changed. $ graphersal store fork data/ branch/ --at-mark before-import
Forked into branch/ at commit 1: graph 01a11a54-87d2-7995-b2cb-e450e4319735 (parent 01a11a54-8209-7661-92e2-147ae6d8bbd3).
Marks not carried (1; they stay targets of data/ only): before-import @ commit 1
Open it: graphersal --graph branch/ --server (or the REPL: graphersal --graph branch/).
data/ is unchanged; to undo the fork, delete the directory branch/. A fork starts without marks: the Marks not carried lines (printed only when there are any) name the source's marks at or before the fork's position. Exit 1 when the target is not reached (Recovery target mark "nosuch" not reached).

319.body:
graphersal store rollback <DIR> TARGET [--delete] Rolls the store back in place to TARGET: everything after it moves to the attic (with --delete: deleted, no undo), and the store continues as a new lineage. Prints the attic id and the commands that undo it. Exit 2 without a target; exit 1 when there is nothing after the target or the store is in use. See Rollback and the Attic . $ graphersal store rollback data/ --at-commit 1 --delete
Rolled back from commit 4 to commit 1: new lineage 01a11a54-8b90-7dba-b74a-cadc851e226f.
The history after it (commits 2..=4, 1 snapshot(s), 2 WAL file(s)) was deleted: this cannot be undone.

321.body:
graphersal store backup <DIR> <BACKUP_DIR> [--full]
graphersal store backup <DIR> <FILE.zip> --zip A consistent copy up to the last durable commit; works while a server has the store open. Into an empty or new BACKUP_DIR: a full backup. Into an existing backup of DIR: an incremental one. --full forces a full backup (the directory must be empty or new). --zip writes one ZIP archive (always full; the file must not exist; feature persist-zip, on in the CLI). $ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Full backup into backup/: snapshot 3, the WAL up to commit 3 (1 segment(s)); 8 file(s), 9605 bytes.
The backup is read-only (graphersal --graph backup/ opens it so); `graphersal store restore backup/` makes it the live store.
$ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Incremental backup into backup/: nothing new since commit 4; the backup is current.
The backup is read-only (graphersal --graph backup/ opens it so); `graphersal store restore backup/` makes it the live store.
$ graphersal store backup data/ data.zip --zip
Full backup of snapshot 3 and the WAL up to commit 4: 8 file(s), 9688 bytes, in data.zip; every checksum read back. Every checksum of what is copied is read in DIR first and again in the copy (a ZIP archive is read back). Damage stops the backup (exit 1): nothing of it is kept (a new directory or archive is removed, an increment rolled back), and the report names the damaged files and recommends repairing the STORE (store repair DIR --to NEW_DIR), never the backup. Damage of a redundant copy (one GRAPH copy, one manifest copy, the marks file) is a warning: on stderr; the backup is intact. $ graphersal store backup data/ backup/
Error: The backup stopped: the store data/ is damaged: wal/00000000000000000001.wal at byte 64: record of commit 1: checksum mismatch; nothing of the backup into backup/ was kept
Help: Repair the MAIN store, never the backup: graphersal store repair data/ --to <new_dir> ... Refused (exit 1, the backup unchanged): a backup of another graph, a directory holding a store that is not a backup, a non-empty directory without a backup, --full into a non-empty directory, a rollback of the store behind the backup, a pruned gap, a fork, repair or conversion of the backed-up store (another store id). --zip --full is a usage error (exit 2: "--zip backups are always full: drop --full"). --from-memory is a usage error here (exit 2) that says where it works: a backup from memory writes the graph of a store open in this process (whose files are damaged), and this command runs in a new process. Use the dev server's Store menu (Back up from memory), POST /api/store/backup {"from_memory": true}, or Python store.backup(path, from_memory=True). See Backup and Restore .

322.body:
graphersal store restore <BACKUP_DIR>
graphersal store restore <FILE.zip> <DIR> With one argument: makes the backup in BACKUP_DIR the live store, in place, with the original's graph id (a backup directory of an older Graphersal: upgrade it first). With two: unpacks a ZIP backup into the new directory DIR as the live store; a ZIP of an older Graphersal's store is upgraded to the current format as it is unpacked (verified). To keep a backup as it is, fork it instead (store fork BACKUP_DIR NEW_DIR). $ graphersal store restore backup/
Restored: backup/ is now the live store (the backup up to commit 4, taken 2026-10-08T07:05:09Z; the same graph id). Use it: graphersal --graph backup/
$ graphersal store restore data.zip restored/
Restored into restored/ (the live store). Use it: graphersal --graph restored/

323.body: graphersal store export <DIR> <FILE.gsnap> [--commit <N>] Writes the latest stored snapshot (or the one at commit N, which must be a snapshot's commit: store list) as one packed file (Exported the snapshot at commit 3 to data.gsnap.). Load it with --graph FILE.gsnap, store create --from FILE.gsnap, or the playground.

324.body:
graphersal store prune <DIR> --up-to <COMMIT> [--drop-marks] Removes snapshots and WAL only needed for targets before COMMIT; the last two snapshots and the attic's bases always stay (Kept from commit 0; removed 0 snapshot(s) [] and 0 WAL segment(s).). Without --up-to it is a usage error (exit 2: nothing is pruned implicitly). On a backup directory it prunes the backup. A prune never makes a mark unreachable unless told to: when it would remove the history a mark needs, it names those marks, changes nothing and exits 1: $ graphersal store prune data --up-to 4
Error: `store prune` would make the mark(s) "m0", "m1" unreachable: it removes the history they need, so they cannot be opened, forked or rolled back to afterwards (only from a backup that holds older snapshots). Nothing was changed.
Help: run it again with --drop-marks to prune anyway, or back the store up first (`graphersal store backup data <BACKUP_DIR>`). With --drop-marks it prunes and names them on a second line ("No longer reachable (their history was pruned): the mark(s) ..."); store marks no longer lists them. Without affected marks the flag changes nothing. See Prune, Compact and Retention .
324.breadcrumbs: Keeping a Graph on Disk » The graphersal store Command » prune

325.body:
graphersal store compact <DIR> [--drop-marks] Prunes up to the current commit, then, for a single-file store, rewrites the file without its free space (the disk needs room for the live data meanwhile). On a directory the prune is all. Like prune, it refuses (exit 1, nothing changed) when the prune would make marks unreachable, naming them, unless --drop-marks is given; compact-advice lists them beforehand (marks lost m0, m1 (...)). $ graphersal store compact graph.gstore
Pruned: kept from commit 0; removed 0 snapshot(s) and 0 WAL segment(s).
Compacted the file: 23.7 KiB -> 22.8 KiB (930 B given back).

326.body:
graphersal store compact-advice <DIR> [--min-ratio <R>] [--min-reclaimable <BYTES>] [--min-size <BYTES>] Whether compact is worth it now, and the numbers; cheap (reads only names, sizes and small metadata files, no element data) and works while a server has the store open. The rule: at least --min-ratio of the store (0.0..1.0, default 0.5) and --min-reclaimable bytes (default 64 MiB) to gain, in a store of at least --min-size bytes (default 64 MiB), and enough free disk space. Always exit 0 (the answer is in the text: compact now: ... with a Run: graphersal store compact <DIR> line, or no compaction needed: ...). $ graphersal store compact-advice data/
no compaction needed: the store is smaller than the minimum of 64.0 MiB
store 9.6 KiB (directory: compact = prune)
prune 0 B
reclaimable 0 B (0 % of the store)
decided by total_bytes

327.body:
graphersal store convert <DIR> <NEW> [--single-file] Copies the whole closed store (snapshots, WAL, marks, attic) into NEW, byte for byte: a directory into a single file (NEW ending in .gstore, or --single-file) or back. NEW must not exist (or be an empty directory); the copy is verified; DIR is not changed. The copy is a new store with its own store id ( creation parameters ): it does not continue the backups of DIR (its first backup is a full one into a new directory). $ graphersal store convert data/ graph.gstore
Copied the store data/ into the single file graph.gstore: 9 file(s), 9.6 KiB; verified.
Use it: graphersal --graph graph.gstore. data/ is unchanged.

328.body:
graphersal store upgrade <DIR> <NEW> [--single-file]
graphersal store upgrade <DIR> --in-place Converts a store written by an older Graphersal (store format version 2: Graphersal 0.1.x) to the current format, without the older binary . DIR is a store directory, a single-file store or a backup directory (it stays a backup). With NEW: a new store in NEW (a new or empty directory, or a single file: NEW ending in .gstore, or --single-file); DIR is not changed. With --in-place: DIR itself; back it up first (a copy of the closed directory or file will do): afterwards the older Graphersal refuses it as newer. Everything is carried: the graph, its schema and catalog, the history (snapshots and WAL), the marks, the lineage, the attic entries and the store's identity and creation parameters ; only GRAPH and GRAPH.copy are rewritten, every other file stays byte for byte. DIR is verified first. Exit 1 when it is damaged (nothing is written; store repair DIR --to NEW writes a repaired store of the current format), in use (a server or another writer has it open), of a newer or a pre-release version, or a copy of a store that is already current; exit 2 without NEW or --in-place, or with a NEW that exists. An upgrade in place of a current store prints nothing to do (exit 0). An interrupted upgrade leaves no store in NEW (run it again: it clears what was left), and in place leaves the store either older or upgraded (run it again). A ZIP backup of an older store is upgraded by store restore FILE.zip DIR. See Format Versions . Which versions are upgraded, and how, is decided by one table (the same in Format Versions and the format specification 15.1 ); a version without a supported row is refused before anything is written, a row "into a copy only" refuses --in-place (StoreFailure::UpgradeNeedsCopy), and a store with any file of a newer version is refused like every other command does (below): From store format version Written by To Upgrade 1 never released (no store id) 3 unsupported (packed snapshot) 2 Graphersal 0.1.x 3 in place or into a copy (version word) 3 Graphersal 0.2.x 3 nothing to do $ graphersal store upgrade old/ new/
Verified the store old/ (store format version 2): 2 snapshot(s), 2 WAL segment(s), 10 record(s).
Upgraded into new/ (store format version 3): 15 file(s), 21.2 KiB; verified. old/ is unchanged (keep using new/: it is the same store, with the same identity).
Use it: graphersal --graph new/
$ graphersal store upgrade old/ --in-place
Verified the store old/ (store format version 2): 2 snapshot(s), 2 WAL segment(s), 10 record(s).
Upgraded old/ in place to store format version 3: GRAPH rewritten, every other file kept. The older Graphersal no longer opens it.
Use it: graphersal --graph old/
328.breadcrumbs: Keeping a Graph on Disk » The graphersal store Command » upgrade
328.title: upgrade

329.body: graphersal store repair <DIR> --to <NEW_DIR> Builds a repaired copy of a damaged store in NEW_DIR (never in place; the damaged files are not changed) and reports what was repaired, lost and diverged. A store of an older released format (Graphersal 0.1.x) is read as it is; the repaired store has the current format. Exit 0 with ok: nothing lost, exit 1 when data is lost or diverged (the repaired store is written anyway: read the lists), exit 2 without --to. The repaired store starts without marks: one mark not carried: name @ commit N line per mark of the damaged store at or before the repaired position. When both GRAPH copies are damaged, repair and verify print the note lineage before commit N is approximate (both GRAPH copies damaged) (verify then exits 1 with the damage report instead of "not a store"). See Damage, Maintenance and Repair .
329.breadcrumbs: Keeping a Graph on Disk » The graphersal store Command » repair
329.title: repair

33.body: An embedding is a list of numbers that a machine-learning model computes for a piece of data: a sentence, a document, an image, a product. The model places similar things close together, so "how do I feed my cat?" and "Feeding your cat" get vectors that point in almost the same direction, while "Rust for beginners" points elsewhere. Searching by embedding finds what is meant , not only what is spelled the same. Graphersal stores embeddings as a vector value, searches them exactly with nearest() and similarity(), and combines the hits with everything a graph does well: filters, edges, paths. Graphersal never calls a model on its own. A semantic model runs in your host program (Python, a server, an MCP tool), which writes the result as an ordinary property value, or registers the model as an embedder that the embed step calls. Built in is one small embedder, hash-ngram/1: no model, lexical similarity only (typos and word forms, not meaning), enough for fuzzy lookup and for trying the steps; the reference page has the details and the reasoning. The graphersal command line registers a real semantic model for you: a downloaded Model2Vec model, run locally. This page is the practical tour. Every detail (element kinds, metrics, schema rules, formats) is on the reference page Vectors .
33.breadcrumbs: Embeddings and Vector Search » Embeddings and Vector Search
33.title: Embeddings and Vector Search

330.body: The web playground runs the engine in the browser (WebAssembly), where there is no disk to write to. It still gives every graph the full Store: a MemDir store, with the same byte format as on disk. Every graph you load (a sample, the empty graph, a file) is kept as a Store in memory: the loaded state is commit 0 (its first snapshot), every run that changes the graph adds a commit to the store's write-ahead log, and the Store menu in the top bar works on it exactly as the dev server's does on a store directory: the position (commit, time of the last commit) and the sizes: the store's bytes in memory next to the graph's own footprint; Checkpoint (a snapshot of the current state; one is also written automatically after 4 MiB of log since the last one) and Mark (a name for the current position); the marks and the snapshots (each with a .gsnap download), the newest five of each; Calendar… (or See all… when there are more) opens the history calendar ; on every snapshot and mark, and through Go to commit / Go to time : Open read-only here (queries read that past state, writes are refused, a banner offers Back to the live graph ), Fork into a new database and Roll back here (what comes after moves to the attic ); the attic: Show changes (100 commits per page with Previous/Next, the totals over all of them; the dialog scrolls in both directions and has a full-screen toggle, Esc restores its size), Restore , Fork , Remove ; Databases : the store you loaded and every fork made from it ("fork of Modern (TinkerPop) @ commit 12"), each a store in memory with its own history, with Switch to (the tabs' results may be stale afterwards) and Close (frees its memory); Disk space with Compact : in memory a compaction is a prune up to the current commit (the last two snapshots stay), which frees the memory old snapshots and WAL hold; the button is always enabled (not while another store action runs); when the compaction advice does not recommend it, it asks first, showing what it would free and why it is not recommended; Verify the store checks every checksum, and Download current state (.gsnap) saves the state on screen. The menu after a few commits, three marks and three snapshots (the buttons View , Fork… and Roll back… are the three actions above): The Store menu of the playground: position, checkpoint and mark, databases, marks, snapshots, any point in time, disk space Calendar… shows every mark and snapshot by day, with the same actions: The history calendar: a month with the days that have marks and snapshots, and the entries of the selected day A running store action is shown in three places (the same on the dev server): its button switches to the running text in bold accent colour with a spinner and the elapsed time ("Verifying the store… 0:42"); the Store button in the top bar shows it while the menu is closed ("Store · verifying… 0:42"); and a toast gives the result at the end (a problem found, such as Verify's damage, has a Details button that opens the menu, where the last Verify's result is listed under its item). Meanwhile every other store action is disabled, its tooltip saying which one to wait for; screen readers hear the start and the end through a polite live region. The engine reports no progress for these actions and none of them can be cancelled: the elapsed time is all there is. In memory: everything is lost on page reload. Download a .gsnap to keep a state (load it back from the start page). The browser has no disk the playground writes to: syncs are no-ops, and the byte format is the same as on disk, so a downloaded snapshot opens anywhere. Stop (next to Run) restarts the engine: the graph is restored as it was last loaded or saved, and the store in memory starts over from that state (its history is lost). To keep a history across reloads, run the same UI on a store on disk with the dev server : graphersal --graph data/ --server.

import graphersal graph = graphersal.Graph.tinkerpop_modern()
graph.save("g.gsnap") # {"commit_seq", "vertex_count", "edge_count"}; name= optional

graph.execute('g.addV("person").property("name", "ann").next()')
graph.mark("after-ann") # {"name", "commit_seq", "time"} graph, report = graphersal.Graph.recover("g.gsnap", ["g.wal"]) # to the end
graph, report = graphersal.Graph.recover("g.gsnap", ["g.wal"], mark="after-ann") # or commit_seq=, time= Graph.recover takes one target: commit_seq=, time= (microseconds since the Unix epoch) or mark=; without one it replays to the end. An interrupted last write is ignored (report["torn_tail"]); damage raises GraphersalError with its location. 335.body: Snapshot, journal or Store? A .gsnap when the application decides when to save (a script, the browser, a download). A journal when you need durability over streams you manage yourself. The Store for everything else: it is a snapshot plus a journal plus recovery, retention, backups and repair. See Persistence . Directory or single file? A directory for a server (parts can live on other disks, the files are easy to inspect); a .gstore file when the store travels as one document. Both have the same guarantees, and graphersal store convert switches between them. Is GraphSON or GraphML not enough? They are exchange formats: they do not carry the schema, the commit position or the auto-id sequences, and GraphML loses value types without a schema. A snapshot is lossless.

337.body: A refused operation reads Cannot <operation>: <reason>. Its cause is one of a closed set (graphersal::persist::StoreFailure, #[non_exhaustive]), so a program or a server can react to it with a match; StoreFailure::name() is the stable name, which the Python exception carries as err.cause (None for every other error). Each cause has its own help: Cause (name()) When What to do Closed (closed) the store was closed (close, shutdown) open it again LockPoisoned (lock_poisoned) a thread panicked while it held a lock of the open store end the process and reopen the store NameTaken (name_taken) a snapshot name in use, or a mark name used before (also by a mark a prune made unreachable) choose another name; store list, store marks NameTooLong (name_too_long) a snapshot name over 255 bytes a shorter name SnapshotExists (snapshot_exists) a named checkpoint at a commit that already has a snapshot under another name commit something first, or checkpoint without a name NoSnapshot (no_snapshot) an export of a commit without a snapshot, a backup of a store without one store list, store checkpoint BackupRunning (backup_running) a prune while a backup copies the files prune again afterwards PruneRunning (prune_running) a backup while a prune deletes files back up again afterwards NothingAfterTarget (nothing_after_target) a rollback to the current commit or later an earlier target UnknownAtticEntry (unknown_attic_entry) no attic entry with that id store attic <dir> lists them AtticLineageChanged (attic_lineage_changed) a later rollback or restore came after the entry's rollback restore the newer entry first, or fork the entry ChangedSinceRollback (changed_since_rollback) commits or marks since the entry's rollback fork the entry (store attic <dir> fork <id> <new_dir>) AtticBaseMissing (attic_base_missing) the snapshot an attic entry continues is gone store verify; take the entry from a backup or remove it NotABackup (not_a_backup) a backup-only operation (prune_backup) on a live store open and prune it as a store KeptSnapshotDamaged (kept_snapshot_damaged) a snapshot a prune would keep fails verification; nothing was removed store verify, then store repair <dir> --to <new_dir> CopyDoesNotVerify (copy_does_not_verify) a converted or repaired copy does not read back intact check the target disk, repeat into a new directory ChangedConcurrently (changed_concurrently) a store file changed or vanished while the operation read it never edit a store's files; repeat, then store verify JournalSyncFailed (journal_sync_failed) writing or syncing the journal failed fix the disk, reopen the store MissingCapability (missing_capability) the graph's storage does not claim atomic and change_capture, so no journal can be attached (never for TraversalGraph) keep the graph in a storage that claims both ReloadFailed (reload_failed) the files of a rollback or attic restore changed, but loading the new state into the open graph failed: the graph in memory was emptied and the store stopped close the store and open it again (restart the server): the open completes the change Stopped (stopped) an earlier rollback or attic restore failed part-way, so the store writes nothing more (Store::stopped_reason) close the store and open it again AlreadyCurrent (already_current) store upgrade <dir> <new> of a store that already has the current format open it as it is; for a copy use store convert or a backup DamagedSource (damaged_source) the store to upgrade does not verify (the message lists the first problems); nothing was written graphersal store repair <dir> --to <new_dir> reads the older store and writes a repaired one in the current format; or upgrade a backup instead UpgradeNeedsCopy (upgrade_needs_copy) store upgrade <dir> --in-place of a store whose version the upgrade table upgrades only into a copy; nothing was written graphersal store upgrade <dir> <new_dir> (the older store stays as it is)

338.body: Can I change the damage policy (or the chunk size) of a store? No. Both are fixed at creation and carried by every fork, repair, conversion and backup. To get another policy, create a new store with it and load the data (for example graphersal store export old/ graph.gsnap, then graphersal store create new/ --from graph.gsnap --on-damage continue). Does a backup check what it copies? Yes, every checksum, in the store before anything is written and again in the copy. A backup never copies damage silently; see Every checksum, twice . Is a commit really on disk when the query returns? Yes, with the default Durability::EveryCommit: the WAL record is written and fsynced first; a failed sync rolls the commit back. With Interval or Os a machine crash may lose the last commits (never one in the middle). See Commits and Durability . The dev server (or my program) was killed. Is the store damaged? No. The next open replays the WAL and cuts an interrupted last write; stderr notes that the store was not closed cleanly, which is harmless. Ctrl+C closes it cleanly in the first place. Why does the store keep growing? Nothing is deleted implicitly: every commit is in the WAL and every checkpoint adds a snapshot until you prune . store compact-advice tells you what a prune and a compaction would give back. How do I see the graph as it was yesterday? Store::open_read_only(dir, RecoveryTarget::Time(..)), the dev server's Go to time... , or graphersal store fork data/ yesterday/ --at-time 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z and open the fork. See Point in Time . I rolled back by mistake. graphersal store attic data/ lists the rolled-back history; store attic data/ restore <ID> undoes the rollback as long as nothing was committed or marked since, otherwise store attic data/ fork <ID> <NEW_DIR> keeps it as a new store. A rollback with --delete cannot be undone (restore a backup). Can I copy a store with cp or rsync? While no process has it open, yes: no file records a path. While it is open, use graphersal store backup (it copies up to the durable end and pins the files against a concurrent prune); a plain copy of a live store may catch a half-written file. Can two processes use one store? One writer at a time (an operating-system lock). Any number of readers (info, verify, fork, backup, Store::open_read_only) at the same time as the writer. Does a backup include the attic? No. It holds the snapshots and the WAL up to the durable end, and the marks. Where is the time zone? Everything is stored and printed in UTC. --at-time takes any offset, but refuses a time without one. Does it work in the browser? Snapshots, journals and recovery work over any stream in WebAssembly; the Store works there over a MemDir (the playground does that). There is no disk: download a .gsnap to keep a state. Can another program read the WAL (change data capture)? Yes. The byte format is public ( specification ); a reader tails the WAL segments, reads complete records only, and treats records after the writer's durable end as possibly not final. In Rust, store.changes_since(commit) yields the ChangeSets. Is the format stable? Store format version 3 (with file format version 2) is specified on the specification page; a newer version is refused, never guessed at, and a store of an older released version is upgraded by graphersal store upgrade without the older build (every build keeps the readers of every released format; Format Versions ).

339.body: Graphersal's reference storage is TraversalGraph, an in-memory graph. A host (a server, an application) can bring its own in-memory storage instead: any type that implements the GraphStorage trait. The engine, the Rhai DSL, saved queries, the session of the playground and the dev server (graphersal-session) and the persist Store then work over it. EXPERIMENTAL in 0.2.x. GraphStorage, PersistentStorage, AnyGraph and the conformance crate graphersal-storage-tests may change in any 0.2.x release. Pin the exact versions (graphersal = "=0.2.0", graphersal-storage-tests = "=0.2.0"). graphersal-session is internal and has no stability guarantees at all.

340.body: The engine (GraphTraversalSource<'g, S>) is generic over the storage and statically dispatched: a traversal over a host storage is compiled for that storage, with no virtual call per element. Everything above the engine holds one object-safe type per layer instead, and makes one virtual call per operation (a terminal, a schema method, a catalog call, a view): Layer Holds Implemented for Rhai DSL, saved queries (graphersal::script) Arc<dyn AnyGraph> every Graph<S> (sealed blanket implementation) Session (graphersal-session) Arc<dyn SessionGraph>, Arc<dyn SessionStore>, Arc<dyn GraphFactory> every Graph<S>, every Store<S>, StorageKind<S> Store (graphersal::persist) Store<S>, internally a non-generic core every S: PersistentStorage Graph<S> (in graphersal::storage, also in the prelude) is the shared form of a storage: S behind a read-write lock, with read()/write() guards that dereference to S. Graph without a parameter means Graph<TraversalGraph>.

340.title: How it fits together

341.body: GraphStorage (required). Only the read methods, the element-inserting and element-removing methods and the property writes are required; everything else has a default that is correct for a simple, non-transactional storage. The trait's rustdoc ("A guide for storage implementers") is the reference: handles that never alias, the write checks and their public helpers, units of atomicity, capabilities, change capture, statistics, schema and the catalog. The schema's defaults on create come for free: you implement the primitive insert_vertex/insert_edge (store exactly this; imports, change sets, replay and copies call it), and the queries create through the provided add_vertex/add_edge (add_vertex_with/add_edge_with with a pinned time), which fill the defaults in from get_schema() and then call your insert_vertex/insert_edge (override add_vertex_with/add_edge_with only to avoid that schema copy). Default (required by the DSL and the session). A whole script runs as one unit by moving the storage out of the shared lock while the write lock is held (std::mem::take), which leaves an empty instance behind. The session also builds every new graph (a sample, a file load) by reading it into a TraversalGraph and copying it into an S::default() (through the load sink of a PersistentStorage, through the write methods otherwise). Send + Sync + 'static , so the graph can be shared between threads. Change capture (optional; needed for commit hooks, dry runs and the Store). A storage that claims change_capture (and therefore atomic) in capabilities() builds the ChangeSet of every committed unit itself with the public constructors (ChangeSet::builder, one Mutation constructor per kind). There is no reusable undo log or capture component: the storage derives what a unit changed from its own bookkeeping. It embeds a CommitHooks (graphersal::storage) and calls it at its commit point, so the order of the hooks (user hooks in registration order, then the journal) is implemented once; the rustdoc of CommitHooks says when to call each event. PersistentStorage (optional, feature persist; needed for snapshots and the Store): the lineage id, the commit position, a load sink outside units, clear, the journal slot and replay. See Your Own Storage . Units and transactions come for free: the Transactional extension trait (transaction, transaction_with, dry_run) is implemented for every GraphStorage on top of the trait's unit methods. dry_run needs change_capture.

342.body: Front end Entry point Engine GraphTraversalSource::new(&storage) (reads), GraphTraversalSource::new(&mut storage) (writes) Shared graph Graph::new(storage); Graph::new_persistent(storage) for a PersistentStorage (adds g.export_snapshot(path) in the DSL) Rhai DSL graph_scope(graph), graph_scope_with_options(..), every eval_* function: they take impl IntoAnyGraph, i.e. an Arc<Graph<S>> or an Arc<dyn AnyGraph> Session Session::with_storage(Arc::new(StorageKind::<S>::persistent())) for a PersistentStorage (graphs, .gsnap loads, stores in memory), StorageKind::<S>::new() for any other storage (graphs only); session.load_shared(graph, name, kind) serves a graph the host already holds, session.attach_store(Arc::new(store), label) a Store Store Store::create_in(dir, storage, options), Store::open_in(dir, options, S::default), open_backup_in, open_read_only_in, create_from_packed_in; the Store page has the table Snapshots persist::write_snapshot(&storage, writer, &options), persist::read_snapshot_into(reader, &options, S::default()) A Store requires the capabilities atomic and change_capture and fails with StoreFailure::MissingCapability without them. The files a Store<S> writes do not depend on S: a store written by a host storage opens as Store<TraversalGraph> (in graphersal store, the dev server, Python) and the other way round.

344.body: Scratch graphs. Graphs a script creates itself are always TraversalGraphs, whatever the host's storage: GraphSource::*, __, _g, the results of subgraph()/cap()/toGraph() and schema.toGraph(). A host-chosen scratch storage is not planned. withSideEffect(name, graph) into a host graph. A subgraph() writes only into a TraversalGraph; a foreign target fails with GraphError::Unsupported. Let the subgraph land in a scratch graph and copy what is needed. Compressed properties. A foreign storage keeps compression rules in its catalog like any definition (defined, listed, persisted, dropped), but nothing applies them: recompress fails with GraphError::Unsupported and the compression statistics are absent. The session's compression manager lists and edits the rules and says "not supported by this storage" for the rest. The undo log and its change-capture derivation. A foreign storage brings its own (see "Change capture" above). The Store's internal working graphs. The merge checkpoint's delta graph, salvage (maintenance mode) and repair work on internal TraversalGraphs and write files; they never touch the host's graph. The shipped front ends. The CLI (REPL, one-shot runner), the dev server and its MCP endpoint, the Python binding and the WebAssembly playground serve TraversalGraph. A host that serves its own storage builds on graphersal-session instead. Sample graphs and TraversalGraph::with_execution_policy. The sample constructors (TraversalGraph::tinkerpop_modern(), ...) build TraversalGraphs (the session copies them into the host storage); the trait method execution_policy() gives a host storage the same policy hook. Operations a storage does not implement fail with GraphError::Unsupported, which names the operation; its help points to the storage's documentation and capabilities.
344.title: What stays TraversalGraph-only

346.body: Add graphersal-storage-tests as a dev-dependency (with its persist feature to test the PersistentStorage side) and invoke the macro in one test of the implementing crate: graphersal_storage_tests::conformance!(my_storage, base = MyStorage::default() => base); Each contract item becomes its own test; the capability-conditional items (rollback, savepoints, hooks, change sets, dry runs) run for what capabilities() claims. See Storage Conformance .
346.title: The conformance suite

347.body: graphersal_storage_tests::forwarding::Forwarding forwards every GraphStorage (and, with persist, PersistentStorage) method to a wrapped TraversalGraph, but has its own element handle types. Graphersal uses it to prove that the front ends are storage-independent: crates/graphersal/tests/all/foreign_storage_tests.rs runs every documented DSL example and a curated set of mutating, whole-script, dry-run and saved-query scripts on both storages and requires the same results; crates/graphersal/tests/all/foreign_store_tests.rs runs the Store on Forwarding over every backend (commits, reopen, checkpoints, rollback, backups, ZIP, marks, damage) and opens the files with the other storage type; crates/graphersal-session/src/storage/tests.rs requires the same JSON from a session over either storage; GRAPHERSAL_TEST_STORAGE=forwarding runs the whole TinkerPop suite on it, gated against the same baseline; the first three run in every cargo test of the workspace; the TinkerPop run on Forwarding is a check before every release. A host can follow the same pattern for its own storage: run the same scripts on a Graph<TraversalGraph> and on a Graph<MyStorage> loaded with the same data and compare the rendered results. Differences are either bugs of the storage or behaviour the host chose (and documents).
347.title: The Forwarding pattern

348.body: A storage behind Graph<S> runs within 1-4 % of TraversalGraph itself on the measured traversals (measured with the Forwarding test storage), because the engine is monomorphised for it. The price is build time: one engine instantiation per storage type a host uses.
348.title: Cost

349.body: GraphStorage is experimental in 0.2.x : its methods and associated types may change in any 0.2.x release (a layered storage with snapshot reads is planned). The trait's own rustdoc is the implementer's guide: handles, units, capabilities, change capture and statistics. The crate graphersal-storage-tests (on crates.io, EXPERIMENTAL like the trait: it may break in any minor release before 1.0, so pin the exact version) runs one contract against any GraphStorage implementation. Add it as a dev-dependency (graphersal-storage-tests = "=0.2.0") and, in a test of the implementing crate: graphersal_storage_tests::conformance!(my_storage, base = MyStorage::new() => base); The suite uses only graphersal's public API. Each contract item is a separate test (ids, label sets, edge endpoints, property kinds, JSONPath writes and removals, cascading drops, counts and *_by_label equal to scans after every mutation, schema application, read-only wrappers, stale handles that never alias another element) plus a smoke layer that loads the modern graph through the trait and compares eight traversals with TraversalGraph. Schema support is optional: the schema items check enforcement only when set_schema does not return GraphError::Unsupported (the trait default); otherwise they pass without checking anything. Schema enforcement is not reusable outside graphersal yet, so a storage in another crate keeps that default and still passes conformance!. conformance_core! leaves the schema items out entirely, for a storage that accepts schemas but deliberately does not enforce them. Some items depend on what the storage claims in capabilities() (see Transactions ): capabilities_are_consistent always runs (change_capture requires atomic); the rollback, savepoint and unit_changes items run for an atomic storage; the commit-hook and apply_change_set items run for a storage with change_capture (and check that a storage without it refuses hook registration). Where the trait documentation is silent the reference implementation decides; those points are listed in the crate README. The suite is run against TraversalGraph, &mut TraversalGraph, Box<TraversalGraph>, Arc<TraversalGraph>, (read-only items) &TraversalGraph and the blanket &G view of that wrapper, the crate's Forwarding test storage (own handle types, every method forwarded to a TraversalGraph) and a wrapper in the suite's own tests that keeps the trait's schema defaults. It found two contract violations in TraversalGraph (a panic in add_edge for a dropped endpoint, stale edge-id entries after drop_vertex); both are fixed and the suite runs with no ignored test.

352.title: What gql() is

353.body:
Gremlin steps may follow gql(). They see the row maps and reach a column by its name, so whatever GQL cannot do yet, a Gremlin step after it can: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p ORDER BY p.name").select("p").out("created").values("name").order().to_list() // "lop", "lop", "lop", "ripple"
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows]->(b) RETURN *").select("a", "b").by("name").to_list() // #{"a": "marko", "b": "josh"}, #{"a": "marko", "b": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age").select("age").sum().next() // 123
g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name").select("name").dedup().order().to_list() // "josh", "marko", "peter" An element column (RETURN p) holds the live vertex or edge, so select("p").out(..) continues the walk from it.

355.body: The Supported Subset : clauses, patterns, label expressions, expressions, functions, parameters, and what is not supported yet. Semantics : trail matching, quantified edges and path patterns and their limits, OPTIONAL MATCH, NULL and three-valued logic, subqueries (EXISTS, COUNT, COLLECT, CALL), UNION and NEXT, aggregation, DISTINCT equality, comparisons, ordering, the rules of the functions (strict CAST, lenient toInteger, rounding, where they differ from Neo4j), ids. Result Shape : row maps, column names and their order, path values. Writing with GQL : INSERT (Cypher CREATE), what a row sees, units, schema, permissions, and the write clauses that come later. Writing GQL in Rhai Strings : quotes, multi-line queries, comments, parameters, and when the MCP tool is easier. Cypher Aliases : every accepted Cypher spelling and its GQL form. Refused Constructs : what gql() will not do, and why. Errors : GQLSTATUS codes and diagnostics. Plans and Performance : what a query becomes in profile(). GQL Conformance : the GQL features supported, partially supported and not supported. The generated step page gql .
355.title: In this chapter

356.body: This page lists what gql() accepts in this version, construct by construct, each with a runnable example and, where it is natural, its Gremlin twin. Everything not listed here is an error that says so ( Not supported yet at the end, Refused Constructs for what will never be supported).
356.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » The Supported Subset » The Supported Subset
356.title: The Supported Subset

357.body:
[ clauses, in any order and number: [OPTIONAL] MATCH <pattern> [, <pattern> ...] [WHERE <condition>] LET <name> = <expr> [, ...] FILTER [WHERE] <condition> FOR <name> IN <list> [WITH ORDINALITY <name> | WITH OFFSET <name>] UNWIND <list> AS <name> -- Cypher spelling of FOR WITH [DISTINCT] <item> [AS <name>], ... -- or WITH *; Cypher [ORDER BY ...] [OFFSET <n>] [LIMIT <n>] [WHERE <condition>] [OPTIONAL] CALL [(<name>, ...) | (*)] { <query> } -- a subquery run for each row [OPTIONAL] CALL <folder>.<name>(<arg>, ...) -- a saved query run for each row [YIELD <column> [AS <name>], ... [WHERE <condition>]] INSERT <pattern> [, <pattern> ...] -- Cypher spelling: CREATE; creates per row SET <item> [, ...] / REMOVE <item> [, ...] -- change properties and labels per row [DETACH | NODETACH] DELETE <expr> [, ...] -- removes per row; NODETACH is the default MERGE [<name> =] <pattern> -- Cypher; finds or creates one pattern per row { ON CREATE SET <item> [, ...] | ON MATCH SET <item> [, ...] } -- any number, any order ]
RETURN [DISTINCT] <item> [AS <name>], ... -- or RETURN *; items may aggregate -- (mandatory unless the last clause writes; -- FINISH ends a query without a result)
[ORDER BY <expr> [ASC | DESC], ...]
[OFFSET <n>] -- Cypher alias: SKIP
[LIMIT <n>]
[ UNION [ALL | DISTINCT] <clauses> RETURN ... [ORDER BY ...] [OFFSET ..] [LIMIT ..] ] -- any number
[ NEXT <the same again: clauses, RETURN, UNION ...> ] -- any number
[;] -- or a standalone call of a saved query, the whole query:
CALL <folder>.<name>[(<arg>, ...)] [YIELD * | YIELD <column> [AS <name>], ... [WHERE <condition>]] A pattern is a path of node and edge patterns, optionally named (p = (a)-->(b)); an edge may carry a quantifier (-[:knows]->{1,3}), and so may a parenthesized part of the path (((x)-[:knows]->(y)){1,3}, a quantified path pattern). A query usually starts with MATCH, but it may start with any clause, or with RETURN alone ( Queries without MATCH ). Queries ending in RETURN combine with UNION and continue with NEXT ( UNION and NEXT ); NEXT binds looser than UNION. A CALL runs a whole query of that shape for each row ( CALL subqueries ), and CALL folder.name(..) a saved query of the graph's catalog ( Calling saved queries ). INSERT creates nodes and edges once per row, SET / REMOVE change them, DELETE removes them and Cypher's MERGE finds or creates them; a query whose last clause writes may end there and returns no rows ( Writing with GQL ). Keywords are case-insensitive (match, Match, MATCH); variables, labels and property keys are case-sensitive. The words ISO GQL lists as non-reserved (FIRST, LAST, LABELED, SHORTEST) keep their meaning where the grammar expects them (NULLS FIRST, IS LABELED) and are names everywhere a variable can stand: WITH [1, 2] AS first RETURN first. Line breaks are whitespace, so a query may span lines. Comments are // ..., /* ... */ and the GQL -- ... ( the -- rule ). g.gql("match (n:person) where n.age > 30 return n.name as name order by name desc").to_list() // #{"name": "peter"}, #{"name": "josh"}

357.title: The shape of a query

358.body:
MATCH takes one or more patterns separated by commas. A variable written twice is the same element: that is how patterns join. Several MATCH clauses in a row combine the same way. g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows]->(b), (b)-[:created]->(s) RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s ORDER BY s").to_list() // #{"a": "marko", "s": "lop"}, #{"a": "marko", "s": "ripple"}
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows]->(b) MATCH (b)-[:created]->(s) RETURN b.name AS b, s.name AS s ORDER BY b, s").to_list() // #{"b": "josh", "s": "lop"}, #{"b": "josh", "s": "ripple"} Patterns that share no variable form a Cartesian product: every combination of their matches. g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (s:software) WHERE a.age > 32 RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s ORDER BY a, s").to_list() // #{"a": "peter", "s": "lop"}, #{"a": "peter", "s": "ripple"}

365.body:
WHERE after a MATCH clause (or inside a node or edge pattern) keeps the rows for which the condition is TRUE; FALSE and NULL drop the row ( three-valued logic ). It may read every variable of its MATCH clause and of the clauses before it. g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (b:person) WHERE a.age < b.age AND a.name STARTS WITH 'm' RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()
// #{"a": "marko", "b": "josh"}, #{"a": "marko", "b": "peter"}

367.body:
COUNT { } counts and COLLECT { } collects what a subquery finds for each row. They are not GQL: like the list predicates they are openCypher compatibility forms, accepted with their Neo4j Cypher 25 meaning ( Cypher Aliases ). Their bodies are those of EXISTS, and they stand anywhere an expression does: COUNT { <pattern> [WHERE <condition>] } -- the number of matches
COUNT { MATCH ... } -- the same
COUNT { <query ending in RETURN> } -- the number of rows the query returns
COLLECT { <query ending in RETURN <one item>> } -- the list of that item, one entry per row COUNT { } is an integer, 0 when nothing matches, never NULL; COUNT { .. } > 0 keeps the rows EXISTS keeps. COLLECT { } is a list in the order the body returns its rows (its own ORDER BY decides it), [] when there are none, with NULL items kept. Each row runs the body once, like the Gremlin twins project(..).by(__.out("created").count()) and by(__.out("created").values("name").fold()): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list() // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0
g.v().has_label("person").order().by("name").project("name", "n").by("name").by(__.out("created").count()).to_list() // the same rows
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name ORDER BY s.name } AS sw ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh [lop, ripple], marko [lop], peter [lop], vadas []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.lang } AS l").to_list() // #{"l": [(), ()]}: NULLs kept
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } > 1 RETURN p.name AS name").to_list() // #{"name": "josh"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.lang AS l UNION MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name AS l } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh 1 (java once), marko 3, peter 1, vadas 0 COLLECT { } needs a body ending in a RETURN of exactly one item. When a COUNT { } body is one query whose final RETURN only projects (no aggregate, DISTINCT, ORDER BY or UNION), its rows are counted without evaluating the RETURN items, so an expression there that would fail raises no error ( Semantics ). g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name, f.age } AS l") // error: COLLECT { } needs a body that ends in a RETURN of exactly one column
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN 1 / 0 AS x } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list() // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0: 1 / 0 never runs

375.title: ORDER BY, OFFSET, LIMIT

376.body:
UNION combines the rows of queries that each end in RETURN. Every operand returns the same column names, in any order; the result has the column order of the first operand. UNION (also written UNION DISTINCT) removes duplicate rows with GQL's equality (1 and 1.0 are one value), UNION ALL keeps them; one chain uses one kind. Each operand is a query of its own: its own variables, and its own ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT, which apply to that operand only. Gremlin's twin is union(), followed by dedup() for UNION: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name").to_list() // josh, peter, lop, ripple (in any order)
g.union(__.V().has("person", "age", P.gt(30)), __.V().has_label("software")).values("name").to_list() // "josh", "peter", "lop", "ripple"
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION ALL MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name").count().next() // 8: duplicates kept
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS a, 2 AS b UNION RETURN 2 AS b, 1 AS a").to_list() // #{"a": 1, "b": 2}: one row, the first operand's order
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name ORDER BY p.age DESC LIMIT 1 UNION ALL MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name ORDER BY name LIMIT 1").to_list() // peter, lop: per operand
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS y") // error: the operands of UNION must return the same column names
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 3 AS x") // error: UNION ALL is mixed with UNION in one query NEXT continues after a RETURN: the rows that RETURN builds are the input of the next statement, which sees only its columns, by name (RETURN * passes every variable on). It may start with any clause: NEXT RETURN, NEXT FILTER, NEXT MATCH continuing from an element column. NEXT binds looser than UNION, so a NEXT after a union sorts, filters, pages or aggregates the whole union, which no operand's ORDER BY can: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name NEXT RETURN name ORDER BY name LIMIT 3").to_list() // josh, lop, marko
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age NEXT FILTER age > 30 RETURN name ORDER BY name").to_list() // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "peter"}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p NEXT MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS who, s.name AS sw ORDER BY who, sw").to_list() // josh lop, josh ripple, marko lop, peter lop
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age NEXT RETURN count(*) AS n, avg(age) AS mean").to_list() // #{"mean": 30.75, "n": 4}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name NEXT RETURN p.age") // error: the variable `p` is not in scope: the RETURN before NEXT does not return it A NEXT after a plain query is the Cypher WITH of the same items: q1 RETURN a, b NEXT q2 gives the rows of q1 WITH a, b q2 ( Cypher Aliases ). NEXT YIELD is not supported yet.
376.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » The Supported Subset » UNION and NEXT
376.title: UNION and NEXT

377.body:
CALL { } runs a whole query (any clauses, UNION, NEXT, ending in RETURN) once for each incoming row , and joins the row with each row the body returns: the columns of the body's RETURN become new variables of the query. Three things make it more than a MATCH: the body's aggregates, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT apply to each row's records: a count per row, the top k per group; a row whose body returns no row is dropped, OPTIONAL CALL keeps it with the new variables NULL (an aggregating body returns one row anyway: count is 0 there); a UNION or NEXT inside the body works per row too. CALL (a, b) { <query> } -- imports a and b (GQL and Cypher 25)
CALL (*) { <query> } -- imports every variable in scope
CALL () { <query> } -- imports nothing
CALL { <query> } -- imports nothing, unless it starts with WITH a, b (Cypher's importing WITH)
OPTIONAL CALL ... -- keeps a row without results, with NULL columns g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[e:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS top ORDER BY e.weight DESC LIMIT 1 } RETURN p.name AS who, top ORDER BY who").to_list()
// #{"top": "ripple", "who": "josh"}, #{"top": "lop", "who": "marko"}, #{"top": "lop", "who": "peter"}: vadas has no row
g.v().has_label("person").as("p").flat_map(__.out_e("created").order().by("weight", Order.desc).limit(1).in_v()).project("who", "top").by(__.select("p").values("name")).by("name").to_list() // the same three rows
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw ORDER BY sw LIMIT 1 } RETURN p.name AS who, sw ORDER BY who").to_list()
// josh lop, marko lop, peter lop, vadas ()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN count(f) AS friends } RETURN p.name AS who, friends ORDER BY who").to_list() // josh 0, marko 2, peter 0, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name AS other UNION MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS other } RETURN p.name AS who, other ORDER BY who, other").to_list()
// josh lop, josh ripple, marko josh, marko lop, marko vadas, peter lop
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN p.name AS who, sw ORDER BY who, sw").to_list() // Cypher's importing WITH: josh lop, josh ripple, marko lop, peter lop The body reads only the variables it imports: in CALL { MATCH (p)-->(s) .. } without a scope clause, p is a new variable of the body, not the outer one. A body that imports nothing still runs once per row ( Semantics ). The returned names must be new, and a body without RETURN (a unit subquery) must end in a write ( Inside CALL ): a body that only reads must return something; IN TRANSACTIONS is refused . A later clause continues from a returned element as from a WITH column: g.gql("CALL { MATCH (s:software) RETURN s } MATCH (s)<-[:created]-(p) RETURN s.name AS sw, count(p) AS n ORDER BY sw").to_list() // lop 3, ripple 1
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f AS p } RETURN p") // error: the CALL body returns `p`, which is already defined outside it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN p") // error: a CALL { } body without RETURN only makes sense for writes

379.body:
INSERT <pattern>, ... (Cypher CREATE) creates the pattern's new nodes and edges once for each row that reaches it; a variable bound before connects an existing node. Edges need a direction and one label, node labels are a conjunction (:A&B, Cypher :A:B). The full rules are on Writing with GQL . g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'}) RETURN f.name AS fruit").to_list() // #{"fruit": "apple"}
g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'bob'] CREATE (:person {name: n})").to_list() // no rows

379.title: INSERT

38.breadcrumbs: Embeddings and Vector Search » GraphRAG: a vector hit, then the graph
38.title: GraphRAG: a vector hit, then the graph

380.body:
SET <item>, ... changes the elements of each row that reaches it, items left to right: a property (SET n.k = expr), all properties (SET n = {..}; Cypher's merge SET n += {..}) or labels of a node (SET n:A, SET n IS A). REMOVE <item>, ... removes a property (REMOVE n.k) or labels (REMOVE n:A). A NULL value removes the property, a NULL target is skipped. The full rules are on Writing with GQL . g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = p.age + 1, p:admin RETURN p.age AS age, labels(p) AS labels").to_list() // #{"age": 30, "labels": ["person", "admin"]}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) REMOVE p.age RETURN keys(p) AS keys").to_list() // #{"keys": ["name"]}
380.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » The Supported Subset » SET and REMOVE
380.title: SET and REMOVE

381.body:
[DETACH | NODETACH] DELETE <expr>, ... removes the nodes, edges, paths and lists of them its expressions give, for each row. DETACH DELETE removes a node with its edges; a plain DELETE (the default, also written NODETACH DELETE) fails the query (G1001) for a node that still has edges the same clause does not delete. A NULL target is skipped; reading or returning a deleted element later in the query is an error. The full rules are on Writing with GQL . g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) WITH p, p.name AS name DETACH DELETE p RETURN name").to_list() // #{"name": "vadas"}
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[e:knows]->() DELETE e RETURN count(e) AS deleted").to_list() // #{"deleted": 2}
381.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » The Supported Subset » DELETE
381.title: DELETE

382.body:
MERGE [p =] <pattern> [ON CREATE SET <items>] [ON MATCH SET <items>] (Cypher, a compatibility form ) looks for its one pattern on each row: every match is a row, and when nothing matches, the whole pattern is created, reusing the nodes bound before. Each row sees what the rows before it created. ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET hold SET items for the created or the found elements. A NULL property value in the pattern fails the query (22004). The full rules are on Writing with GQL . g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'ann'] MERGE (p:person {name: n}) ON CREATE SET p.new = true RETURN count(DISTINCT p) AS people").to_list() // #{"people": 1}
g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}), (b:person {name: 'josh'}) MERGE (a)-[e:knows]->(b) RETURN e.weight AS weight").to_list() // #{"weight": 1.0}: found

386.body:
Cypher's all(x IN l WHERE c), any(..), none(..), single(..) and reduce(acc = init, x IN l | expr) are openCypher compatibility forms ( Cypher Aliases has their NULL rules). The predicates are three-valued: a NULL list or, when no item decides the answer, a NULL condition gives NULL. A list comprehension counted with size() gives the same answer when no condition is NULL; over a pattern comprehension they are the Gremlin where(__..) / not(__..) of a pattern. reduce folds a list per row, where FOR and an aggregate fold the rows of a query. g.gql("RETURN all(x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x > 0) AS a, any(x IN [1, NULL] WHERE x > 1) AS b, single(x IN [1, 2] WHERE x > 1) AS c").to_list() // #{"a": true, "b": (), "c": true}
g.gql("RETURN size([x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x > 0]) = size([1, 2, 3]) AS a").to_list() // #{"a": true}, the count form of all()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE all(w IN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s] WHERE w.lang = 'java') AND any(a IN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.age] WHERE a > 30) RETURN p.name AS name").to_list() // #{"name": "marko"}
g.V().hasLabel("person").not(__.out("created").has("lang", P.neq("java"))).where(__.out("knows").has("age", P.gt(30))).values("name").to_list() // "marko"
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, reduce(s = 0, a IN [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.age] | s + a) AS ages ORDER BY name").to_list() // josh 0, marko 59, peter 0, vadas 0
g.gql("FOR x IN [1, 2, 3] RETURN sum(x) AS s").to_list() // #{"s": 6}, one fold over the rows
g.gql("RETURN reduce(s = 0, x IN [1, 2, 3] | s + x) AS s").to_list() // #{"s": 6}, one fold per row
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN all(p IN [1] WHERE p > 0) AS a") // error: the variable `p` of all() shadows the variable `p` in scope
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN any(x IN [1] WHERE x > count(*)) AS a") // error: count() cannot be used inside the WHERE part of all(), any(), none() or single()

397.body:
A quantified edge (-[:knows]->{1,3}, The Supported Subset ) is part of its MATCH clause like any edge: within one match every edge is different , across the repetitions and from the other edges of the clause (trail). Vertices may repeat, so a quantified edge may walk around a cycle, but never over the same edge twice. The zero-length match of a lower bound 0 ({0,n}, *) binds the far node to the near one; the group variable is then []. {0} matches only that. Cypher's empty interval ([*2..1], [*..0]: the lower bound above the upper one) matches nothing, as in Neo4j: no row, and an OPTIONAL MATCH part gets its NULL row. The GQL form {2,1} is a syntax error (ISO). An upper bound larger than any trail can be (beyond about four billion) means "no bound"; such a quantifier behaves like {m,}. Unbounded quantifiers ({m,}, *, +, Cypher [*]) have no limit of their own: trail ends every walk once it has used every edge it can reach, which on a finite graph always happens. Two general limits still apply: repeat.max_loops (10 000 repetitions) and traversal.max_traversers (live rows between two steps). Reaching either is an error, never a shortened result ; its help names the quantifier and how to bound it or raise the limit with g.with(..).gql(..). g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->*(b) RETURN b.name AS b") // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations
g.with("repeat.max_loops", 5).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->*(b) RETURN b.name AS b ORDER BY b").to_list()
// josh, lop, lop, marko, ripple, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[e]->{0}(b) RETURN b.name AS b, e").to_list() // #{"b": "marko", "e": []} The help of the first error reads (shortened): Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{0,} of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ...
Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{0,5}, ... Or raise the limit for the query, g.with("repeat.max_loops", 2).gql(..), ... Each match of a quantified edge is a row of its own (the edges it used keep the rows apart), so the number of rows can grow fast on a densely connected graph: bound the quantifier where the question allows it.

399.body:
A row that reaches an OPTIONAL MATCH whose pattern does not match continues once, with every variable the optional part introduces set to NULL: a property of it is NULL, a group variable is NULL (not []), a path variable is NULL. The variables bound before keep their values. The trail rule is checked per clause, so an optional part may bind an edge the MATCH before it bound. g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(b) OPTIONAL MATCH (b)-[:created]->(s) RETURN b.name AS b, s.name AS s ORDER BY b, s").to_list()
// #{"b": "josh", "s": "lop"}, #{"b": "josh", "s": "ripple"}, #{"b": "vadas", "s": ()}

403.body:
An aggregating answer for every row. COUNT { } and COLLECT { } run their body once per row, like EXISTS, but read it to the end: COUNT { } is the number of rows the body returns (0, never NULL, when there are none) and COLLECT { } the list of its one RETURN item ([] when there are none). An imported NULL variable matches nothing, as in EXISTS, so both give 0 and []. COLLECT { } keeps NULL items, unlike collect_list(), and keeps the body's row order, so an ORDER BY inside it orders the list; without one the order is unspecified, as for a pattern comprehension. g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s {name: 'ripple'}) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { (s)<-[:created]-() } AS n, COLLECT { MATCH (s)<-[:created]-(c) RETURN c.name } AS l ORDER BY name").to_list()
// josh 1 ["josh"]; marko, peter, vadas (s is NULL): 0 []
g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.lang } AS l, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.lang] AS c").to_list() // #{"c": [(), ()], "l": [(), ()]} A deviation: the RETURN of a counted body is not evaluated. When a COUNT { } body is one query whose final RETURN only projects (no aggregate, DISTINCT, ORDER BY or UNION, which need the values), gql() counts the body's rows without evaluating the RETURN items, nor the values a projecting WITH names only for them: the count is the same, but an expression there that would fail on a row (a division by zero, a value of the wrong kind) raises no error, while the same body run as a query (or in CALL) raises it. EXISTS and COLLECT { } evaluate theirs. g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN 1 / 0 AS x } AS n ORDER BY name").to_list() // josh 2, marko 1, peter 1, vadas 0
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN DISTINCT 1 / 0 AS x } AS n") // error: division by zero: DISTINCT needs the value
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN 1 / 0 AS x } RETURN p.name AS name") // error: division by zero: EXISTS evaluates its RETURN

404.body:
Columns by name. The operands of a UNION are matched by column name, not by position: an operand may list the same names in another order, and the result takes the first operand's order. (Whether the standard also allows another order is still to be checked; gql() takes the permissive reading.) UNION removes duplicate rows with GQL's equality, as DISTINCT does (1 and 1.0 are one value, DISTINCT ); which of two equal rows is kept is unspecified. g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 1.0 AS x").to_list() // #{"x": 1}: one row
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 1.0 AS x").to_list() // #{"x": 1}, #{"x": 1.0} Per operand. Each operand is a query of its own: its variables are its own, and its ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT apply to it before the union. The rows of a union come in no defined order: the operands' rows are not interleaved in any documented way, so an order within an operand is not an order of the result. Sort or page the whole union after NEXT. NEXT passes on the columns, not the variables. After NEXT the next statement sees the RETURN columns of the statement before it as its variables and nothing else; an element column is the live element, so a MATCH after NEXT continues from it. NEXT after one plain query is that query with a WITH of the same items, so it gives the same rows and the same plan; after a UNION the union's rows are the input. The order a RETURN .. ORDER BY makes before NEXT is not kept by later clauses ( Ordering ): sort in the last RETURN.

407.body:
What a row sees. Each clause sees every write of the clauses before it, for all rows; within one clause the rows are processed in order and each row sees the writes of the rows before it. This is Neo4j's behaviour for every case the openCypher tests check. It follows from the executor, which runs a plan step at a time : a write step starts only after the read steps before it consumed their whole input. So a query never matches what it is creating (the "Halloween problem"): MATCH (n) INSERT (:X) creates exactly one node per node that existed before, MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) INSERT (a)-[:copy]->(b) exactly one edge per existing edge, and FOR i IN range(1, 3) MATCH (n) INSERT (:Y) three per node, because each row's MATCH ran before any INSERT. No barrier step is added to the plan for this. g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) INSERT (a)-[:copy]->(b)").iterate();
g.e().has_label("copy").count().next() // 6 One element per row. A plan that writes never merges traversers into one with a higher bulk, and a write step treats a traverser of bulk n as n rows: each row creates its own elements. Values are read before the write. A value a row carries (WITH n.age AS a, LET, a RETURN column, an aggregate) is computed when the row is built; elements stay live, so RETURN n.k after a write reads the new state, as in Neo4j. NULL is never stored. INSERT ({k: NULL}) stores no k, and SET n.k = NULL removes k; reading it gives NULL again. A null stored by Gremlin (property("k", ())) also reads as NULL in GQL. Permissions. INSERT asks Create on the labels it creates, exactly like add_v(labels) / add_e(label), and nothing for the properties of the new element. Gremlin's add_v(..).property(..) asks Create and Update (the check runs on the plan as written, before the optimizer folds the property into the creation), so a policy that denies only Update allows the INSERT and refuses its Gremlin twin ( Writing with GQL ). SET and REMOVE ask exactly what their Gremlin twins property(), remove_property(), add_label() and drop_label() ask: Update on Data(vertex) for a node target, whatever labels its pattern names (a node's label set can hold more labels than the pattern tests, and a label item changes it), Update on Data(edge "label") for an edge whose pattern names its labels, and Update on any element when the kind is known only at run time (an item of a FOR list, a WITH column of a list). Where writes differ from Neo4j: Neo4j gql() Why a property value must be a scalar or a list of scalars of one kind; a map, a list of mixed kinds, a nested list or a NULL inside a list is a type error stored as given: maps, mixed and nested lists (a NULL inside a list stays in the list) Graphersal's data model stores JSON-like values ( jpath keys ); a schema restricts a property's type where wanted CREATE requires WITH between a write and a following MATCH (Cypher 5) MATCH may follow INSERT directly GQL's linear statements allow it, as Neo4j's Cypher 25 does SET n = NULL / SET n += NULL an error (22004) whose help names SET n = {} and coalesce($map, {}) a NULL map is more often a missing parameter than a wish to remove every property; an error can be relaxed later without changing a query that works, the opposite would silently start removing properties. GQL's own item takes a braced map only: standard GQL has no SET n = NULL form, so the error is our choice for the compatibility form SET of a list of maps, a map, or a list of mixed kinds is a type error stored as given, as for INSERT as above RETURN n of a node deleted earlier in the query returns it an error whose help shows WITH n, properties(n) AS p DETACH DELETE n RETURN p ( DELETE ) a deliberate deviation (user decision): a returned deleted node would carry no id, labels or properties Graphersal could give, and a silent empty value hides the mistake a plain DELETE of a node that still has edges is checked when the transaction commits: MATCH (n)-[r]-() DELETE n DELETE r works checked per clause, before the clause removes anything (G1001): delete the edges in the same clause (DELETE r, n) or use DETACH DELETE a query is one unit, but each clause states its own result; a per-clause check fails at the clause that is wrong, never later
407.title: Writes

408.body:
Items run left to right. The items of one SET or REMOVE clause run in the order written, for each row in turn, and each item sees the changes of the items before it: SET n.c = 1, n.c = n.c + 1 leaves 2. The same item may be written twice; the last one wins. The value of an item is computed when the item runs, from the row and the current state of the graph. g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.n = 1, p.n = p.n + 1 RETURN p.n AS n").to_list() // #{"n": 2} NULL removes. A property item whose value is NULL removes the property (it is never stored as NULL), and so does a NULL value in the map of SET n = {..} and SET n += {..}. = replaces, += merges. SET n = {..} evaluates the whole map and checks every value before it writes: then it removes every property the map does not name and sets the others. SET n += {..} sets the keys of the map and keeps the rest. A node or an edge on the right stands for its properties, read before the first write (so SET n = n changes nothing); another value that is not a map is an error (22G03), and a NULL map is an error (22004). The target. A target that is NULL (a variable an OPTIONAL MATCH left NULL) makes the item a no-op for that row, whatever its right side: the right side is not evaluated. A target that holds a value which is not a node or an edge is an error (22G03); a target removed before the item runs fails the query, as the element no longer exists. g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (p:person {name: 'nobody'}) SET p.k = 1 / 0 RETURN p").to_list() // #{"p": ()}
g.gql("FOR x IN [1] SET x.k = 1") // error: the target holds a value, not a node or an edge Labels. A label item adds or removes each name in order. Adding a label the node has and removing one it lacks change nothing; the last label may be removed (the node then has none). An edge has exactly one label: a label item on it is an error before the run (42002) when the pattern declares the variable as an edge, and at run time (22G03) when only the row knows it, like add_label() on an edge. g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'ripple'}) REMOVE s:software RETURN labels(s) AS labels").to_list() // #{"labels": []} What a row sees is as for INSERT ( Writes ): a value a row carried before the clause (WITH n.age AS old) keeps its value, while the element itself is live, so RETURN n.k reads the new state. A clause before the SET has found all its rows before the SET runs, so a SET never changes which rows an earlier MATCH matched; a LIMIT 0 after the SET still lets it run for every row.
