410.body: MERGE is a compatibility form with Neo4j Cypher 25's meaning, checked against the openCypher TCK's clauses/merge scenarios ( TCK Compliance ). One pattern. A clause holds one path pattern; a second after , is a syntax error (42001). Node labels are conjunctions only (:A:B, :A&B, IS A & B); an edge has exactly one label, no quantifier, no inline WHERE, and no $parameter stands for a whole property map. A path variable (MERGE p = ..) is a new variable holding the found or the created path. Match or create, per row. For each row the clause searches the whole pattern, with GQL = on the properties (so 1 finds 1.0), label-set containment (a node with more labels than the pattern names is found) and trail semantics (each edge at most once per match). Every match is a row: two matching nodes give two rows. When nothing matches, the whole pattern is created, the variables bound before reused and every other element new; the row continues with exactly one record. NULL is an error. A pattern property whose value is NULL on a row fails the query with 22004 when that row runs, before the search: MERGE can neither find nor store a NULL value. The check is at run time, also for a literal NULL, as the TCK expects. Either direction. MERGE (a)-[:T]-(b) finds an edge in either direction (a found edge in each direction is a row of its own) and creates one from left to right, a to b. Directed edges are found and created as written. Rows see earlier rows. The rows run in order, one at a time, and each row's search sees what the rows before it created: FOR x IN [1, 1] MERGE (:N {x: x}) creates one node, and a second row matching the first row's creation runs ON MATCH. Within a clause this is the only uniqueness MERGE gives (there is no constraint); it is race-free because one query is one unit under the write lock. The search runs inside the write step, row by row, so unlike a MATCH before a write ( Writes ) it sees the clause's own earlier creations. g.gql("FOR x IN [1, 1, 2] MERGE (n:N {x: x}) RETURN count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT n) AS nodes").to_list() // #{"nodes": 2, "rows": 3} ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET. Any number of each, in any order; they apply in the order written, each in its case, with the rules of SET (items left to right, NULL removes). They read the pattern's variables and every variable bound before. They run after the creation, as a second write in the same unit: the schema checks the created element before them ( Writing with GQL ). Bound variables. A node variable bound before is a reference only, (a): new labels or properties on it, a bound edge variable, and a pattern that is only a bound node are refused before the run (42002). After WITH a AS x, a is a new name and finds any node. Schema defaults. A created element gets the schema's create-time defaults and its write-time coercion, exactly as an INSERT of the pattern. Where MERGE differs from Neo4j: Neo4j gql() Why a property existence constraint is checked when the transaction commits, so ON CREATE SET n.k = .. satisfies it a required property of the schema is checked when the element is created, before the ON CREATE SET items: give it in the pattern's map the schema checks each write; a later item is a second write in the same unit ( Writing with GQL ) two concurrent MERGEs of the same pattern may both create, unless a uniqueness constraint holds never: a query writes under the write lock, and each row sees the rows before it one query is one unit; Graphersal has no concurrent writers no permission model on the clause asks Create per label it can create and Update for its ON items before it runs, also when every row would only find; then the Reads of its search the check sees the plan before anything runs ( Writing with GQL )
410.title: MERGE

411.body:
When the kind of an operand is certain from the query text and its place never takes that kind, gql() refuses the query before it runs, with error 22G03, also on an empty graph and behind a short-circuit AND / OR, as Neo4j does (stage 3f, the openCypher TCK). The kind is certain for a literal (and a list or map of literals), a node, edge or path variable of a pattern (or a WITH column holding one), a LET / WITH value computed from those, a comprehension variable over such a list (its items' kind), and the results of operators and of functions with a fixed result kind (size() is an integer, labels() a list of strings, nodes() a list of nodes). The checked places: a condition (WHERE, FILTER, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, a comprehension's WHERE, a WHEN of a searched CASE) takes a boolean: false AND 123, NOT 'x', WHERE (n); IN takes a list on its right: 1 IN true; arithmetic (- * / % ^, a sign) takes numbers: 'a' % 2 (a NULL operand makes it NULL first); a property is read from a node, an edge or a map: p.name of a path, x.num of WITH 123 AS x; type() takes an edge, labels() / element_id() a node or an edge, length() a path, size() a string or a list, keys() / properties() a node, an edge or a map, upper() / lower() / char_length() a string; a label test a node or an edge; a map projection a node, an edge or a map. A $parameter is never looked at: its kind counts as unknown, so a query is accepted or refused whatever the parameter values are (a wrong one fails when a row reaches it). A NULL literal is never refused (NULL AND TRUE is NULL). g.gql("RETURN false AND 123 AS x").to_list() // error: AND takes booleans, not an integer (22G03), before the run
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN type(n) AS t").to_list() // error: type() takes an edge, not a node, also on the empty graph
g.gql("MATCH p = (a)-->(b) RETURN size(p) AS s").to_list() // error: size() takes a string or a list, not a path; length(p) counts its edges
g.gql("WITH 123 AS x RETURN x.num AS y").to_list() // error: cannot read the property `num` of an integer
g.gql("RETURN none(x IN ['a'] WHERE x % 2 = 0) AS r").to_list() // error: arithmetic needs numbers, not a string
g.gql("RETURN 1 IN [1, 2] AS a, NULL AND TRUE AS b").to_list() // #{"a": true, "b": ()}
411.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Semantics » Static kind checks
411.title: Static kind checks

412.body: Where the kind of an operand is not certain from the query text (a property value, a $parameter, an item of a list of mixed kinds, a FOR item), an operand of the wrong kind is a type error (22G03) when a row reaches the expression, and a query whose rows never reach it raises nothing. IN with a right operand that is not a list (nor NULL) is such an error too (1 IN $p with $p = 3): g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN n.k AND true AS x").to_list() // [] on the empty graph: no row reaches the expression g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AND true AS x").to_list() // error: AND takes booleans, not a string (22G03), when the first row reaches it A deliberate deviation from Neo4j: Neo4j may reject more queries at compile time with a SyntaxError or TypeError (InvalidArgumentType), from the static types of its own type system. Graphersal checks only the kinds that are certain from the query text ( Static kind checks ), which covers every such case of the openCypher TCK; any other wrong kind fails when a row reaches it. Errors that do not depend on a row (syntax, unknown variables, misplaced aggregates, the static kind checks) are raised before the run, as always ( Errors ).
412.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Semantics » Type errors surface at evaluation time
412.title: Type errors surface at evaluation time

413.body:
The parameters of gql_with() are bound when the query is compiled into its traversal, before any row exists. So a $parameter of OFFSET / SKIP / LIMIT whose value is negative (22G02) or not an integer (22G03) is refused before the run, also on a graph whose query would return no row: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name LIMIT $n", #{n: -1}).to_list() // error: LIMIT must be a non-negative integer, but $n is negative (22G02)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name LIMIT $n", #{n: 2}).to_list() // #{"name": "josh"}, #{"name": "marko"} A deliberate deviation from Neo4j: the openCypher TCK expects this SyntaxError at runtime. The user sees the same thing, an error before any row; the six TCK cases are excluded from the measured scope with this reason ( TCK Compliance ). A constant expression in their place (LIMIT 1 + 1) is evaluated at the same time ( ORDER BY, OFFSET, LIMIT ).

420.body: The sub-clauses of a WITH run in this order: the items (and their aggregation), DISTINCT, ORDER BY, OFFSET / SKIP, LIMIT, and last the WHERE. So WITH p ORDER BY p.age LIMIT 3 WHERE p.age > 28 takes the three youngest and then filters them (Cypher's order; to be checked against the ISO text). The WHERE sees the variables before the WITH too, as in Neo4j: their elements are still on the row (a projecting WITH keeps it, ORDER BY / OFFSET / LIMIT keep its elements); with DISTINCT it filters before the rows are folded, since one folded row stands for many; after an aggregation only the keys and aggregates remain. A WITH that only passes values on (no DISTINCT, aggregate, ORDER BY, OFFSET or LIMIT) changes nothing in how the query runs; it only limits the names in scope.

428.body: The compatibility functions keep Neo4j's meaning, and the GQL functions follow GQL. These are the places where a query gives a different answer than in Neo4j, each deliberate: Neo4j gql() Why toInteger(1.0e19) saturates to the largest integer; toInteger(NaN) is 0 error 22003 a silent wrong value is worse than an error; toIntegerOrNull gives NULL toFloat('1e400') is Infinity error 22003 (toFloatOrNull: NULL) the same rule for both targets toString(n) of a node, relationship or path gives vendor text ('(:A:B)') error 22G03 naming element_id(x), properties(x) or RETURN p Neo4j's element text is vendor-specific CAST does not exist (toInteger and friends are the alternatives) GQL's strict CAST; it reads decimal text only, no Cypher literals ('0x1F') GQL is normative; the Cypher literals are toInteger's trim(s), ltrim(s), rtrim(s) remove any whitespace spaces only GQL's TRIM removes spaces (to be checked against the ISO text) floor(3), ceil(3) are floats integers (they compare equal) GQL keeps the argument's type round(x, p) takes a float p; range() takes floats error 22G03 an integer argument must be an integer a rounding mode outside Java's names fails with 22000; 'UNNECESSARY' is a mode error 22023; 'UNNECESSARY' refused the code is ours; 'UNNECESSARY' fails whenever rounding is needed round() of a number beyond the integer range the number itself, never saturated left('a', null) raises an error (per the manual) NULL GQL's NULL rule sqrt(-1) is NaN, ln(0) is -Infinity, exp(1000) is Infinity errors 2201F, 2201E, 22003 no NaN or infinity from finite numbers (GQL requires the logarithm error too) split(s, '') splits UTF-16 code units splits characters an emoji stays one item range step 0, negative round precision: 22N38 / 22N03 22023 the ISO / SQL-heritage code log(2, x) and log(10, x) are exact for powers of the base, and keys(map) keeps keys whose value is NULL, both as in Neo4j.

43.body:
The graphersal command line (and the dev server it starts) can run a real, semantic text model itself: a Model2Vec static embedding model. Such a model keeps one vector per token and averages them for a text, so it needs no GPU and no neural network at run time: a small model like minishlab/potion-base-8M (256 dimensions, about 30 MB) embeds thousands of sentences per second on a laptop CPU, and it captures meaning, not only spelling ("car" and "automobile" come out close). It is less precise than a large transformer model, and much faster. 1. Download a model once. This is the only step that uses the network: graphersal embed-model download minishlab/potion-base-8M It fetches config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors from Hugging Face into the models directory ($GRAPHERSAL_EMBED_MODELS, else ~/.cache/graphersal/embed-models, on Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\graphersal\embed-models; --dir overrides it), checks the SHA-256 Hugging Face states for the large file and the git blob id of the small ones, and writes a manifest graphersal-embed-model.json (repository, revision, the commit it resolved to, the files with their sizes and SHA-256). A failed or interrupted download leaves no model behind. --revision <branch|tag|commit> pins a version; HF_TOKEN is sent for gated or private repositories. graphersal embed-model list shows what is there: REPO SIZE IDENTITY
minishlab/potion-base-8M 29.5 MiB model2vec/minishlab/potion-base-8M@fac4fa854e68 2. Register it under a name. --embedder NAME=REPO (a downloaded repository) or --embedder NAME=PATH (any directory holding a Model2Vec model) works with every mode: a one-shot query, the REPL, --server and its MCP tools, a Store. --default-embedder NAME makes it the embedder embed() uses without #{embedder: ..}: graphersal --embedder potion=minishlab/potion-base-8M \ -e 'g.add_v("doc").property("text", "a graph database stores vertices and edges") .add_v("doc").property("text", "banana bread recipe with walnuts") .add_v("doc").property("text", "traversal queries over a network of nodes").iterate(); g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open); g.embed_property(#{label: "doc", from: "text", to: "emb", embedder: "potion"}); g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", "how do I query connected data?", 2) .values("text").to_list()' embedder: "potion" names the embedder registered by --embedder potion=..; without it the default runs (--default-embedder NAME, else hash-ngram/1). The text query needs no embedder: it uses the model the schema recorded for doc.emb. "traversal queries over a network of nodes"
"a graph database stores vertices and edges" The model loads once when the command starts (a model that does not load stops it with exit code 2 and the reason); the built-in hash-ngram/1 stays registered beside it. g.embedders() lists both, GET /api/info of the dev server too. What leaves the machine. Only the explicit embed-model download: it connects to https://huggingface.co (or the mirror in $GRAPHERSAL_HF_ENDPOINT). Loading and running a model is local: no text is sent anywhere. Model identity. Each embedder reports a model identity (g.embedders(), field model): model2vec/<repo>@<12 hex digits>, the start of a SHA-256 over the model's three files (without a manifest model2vec@<12 hex digits>). It names the model, never a path: a copied or moved model directory keeps it, a changed file gets another one. Vectors are comparable only between embedders of the same identity, so embed documents and questions with the same model. embed_property() writes the identity into the schema itself. To declare a vector property by hand, copy the full identity, hash included, from graphersal embed-model list or g.embedders(): a schema naming a model without its hash matches no embedder (the error shows the full identity of the one you tried), so a changed model file can never quietly mix its vectors with the old ones. Licences. A model's licence is the model's own, set by whoever published it (see its Hugging Face page); Graphersal downloads and runs it but does not license it. potion-base-8M is MIT licensed. The Rust library has the same embedder as graphersal::vector::Model2Vec (feature model2vec, native targets; it loads from a local directory only), see Vectors .

433.body: gql() accepts Neo4j's Cypher spellings as compatibility forms with Neo4j's meaning, measured by the openCypher TCK ( TCK Compliance : no supported construct behaves differently from the kit, except where a case is excluded below). Each of these differences is a deliberate decision, described in its section: Neo4j gql() Where a negative or non-integer $parameter of SKIP / LIMIT is a SyntaxError at runtime refused when the query is compiled (22G02 / 22G03), before any row: parameters are bound then (TCK cases excluded) Parameters are bound when the query is compiled more type errors at compile time, from its static type system refused before the run only where the kind is certain from the query text; any other wrong kind fails when a row reaches it Static kind checks , Type errors surface at evaluation time a property value is a scalar or a list of scalars of one kind maps, mixed and nested lists are stored as given (a TCK case excluded) Writes SET n = NULL removes every property an error (22004), also for SET n += NULL Writes a plain DELETE of a node with edges is checked when the transaction commits checked per clause (G1001) Writes , DELETE RETURN n of a node deleted earlier in the query returns it an error naming properties(n) DELETE a required (existence-constrained) property may come from ON CREATE SET checked when MERGE creates the element MERGE the RETURN of a COUNT { } body is evaluated not evaluated when it only projects COUNT and COLLECT a comprehension variable may reuse any name that is not in scope not a name that a LET / WITH value in scope still reads Map projections and comprehensions 'a' + 1 is 'a1' an error (22G03): convert explicitly Comparisons across types some functions saturate, give NaN / infinity or take floats errors or GQL's types Where functions differ from Neo4j id(x) is an integer; rand() ids are strings (element_id(x)); id() and rand() are refused Ids are strings , Refused Constructs a datetime keeps a zone name; values hold nanoseconds; years up to ±999 999 999; zoned time() a datetime keeps the offset (the zone name's TCK cases excluded); microseconds, finer is 0A000; years -9999 to 9999 (TCK cases excluded); time() not yet Where dates and times differ from Neo4j X.realtime() refused; one clock per query Dates and times a procedure argument may read the row; procedures are vendor or user code (db.*, apoc.*, Java) CALL folder.name(..) calls a saved GQL query with constant or $parameter arguments only, positional in the order its body first reads them; a saved query in Rhai, or a call inside EXISTS / COUNT / COLLECT, is 0A000; db, dbms, apoc, gds are refused Calls of saved queries procedure names are qualified, one per namespace saved-query names are unique across all folders: a name in another folder is a "did you mean" error Calls of saved queries a NUMBER argument keeps an integer (42) coerced by the parameter's schema: a number parameter gets 42.0 Calls of saved queries a procedure call is a commit of its own in some drivers the call is part of the calling query's one unit, whose commit names no saved query (unlike g.query(..)) Calls of saved queries Where ISO GQL and Neo4j disagree, gql() follows Neo4j in a few places (comparisons across kinds, list ordering, float division by zero, NaN): Differences from the standard .

441.body: gql() writes too. This version supports INSERT (Cypher CREATE is its alias ), which creates nodes and edges, and SET and REMOVE , which change the properties and labels of existing ones, and DELETE / DETACH DELETE , which remove them; each runs once for each row that reaches it. Cypher's MERGE , which finds a pattern or creates it when it is missing, is accepted as a compatibility form ( MERGE ). A writing query is one unit, like every traversal: it commits when it succeeds, and a query that fails, on any row, changes nothing ( Units ).

446.body:
MERGE is Cypher's "find or create": for each row it looks for its one pattern , and every match becomes a row; when nothing matches, it creates the whole pattern and the row goes on with the new elements. ISO GQL has no MERGE statement; gql() accepts it as a compatibility form with Cypher's meaning, so a query written for Neo4j runs as it is. The second MERGE of the first block finds the city the first one created: g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list(); // #{"name": "Berlin"}: created
g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list(); // #{"name": "Berlin"}: found
g.v().has_label("city").count().next() // 1 g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'marko'}) RETURN p.age AS age").to_list() // #{"age": 29}: found, nothing created
g.gql("MERGE p = (:person {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->(f:person) RETURN f.name AS friend, path_length(p) AS hops ORDER BY friend").to_list() // josh and vadas: two matches, two rows The pattern. One path pattern (a second one after , is a syntax error: write one MERGE per pattern). Its nodes have the labels written (:A:B or :A&B; a found node carries all of them and may have more) and a property map compared with GQL =; its edges have exactly one label and no quantifier, and the pattern has no WHERE. A path variable (MERGE p = ..) gives the found or the created path. A variable bound before stands for its element: write it alone, as (a), and MERGE reuses it in both cases, so an edge between matched nodes is created only when it is missing. Labels or properties on a bound node (MERGE (a:admin)), a bound edge variable, and a pattern that is only a bound node (MATCH (a) MERGE (a)) are refused before the run (42002); change a bound node with SET. An unbound variable is new: the MERGE finds or creates its element. g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}), (b:person {name: 'peter'}) MERGE (a)-[e:knows]->(b) RETURN b.name AS to").to_list(); // #{"to": "peter"}: created
g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}), (b:person {name: 'peter'}) MERGE (a)-[e:knows]->(b) RETURN b.name AS to").to_list(); // found
g.e().has_label("knows").count().next() // 3: marko's two edges and the new one g.gql("MATCH (a:person) MERGE (a)") // error: a bound variable alone has nothing to find or create
g.gql("MATCH (a:person) MERGE (a:admin)") // error: a bound node carries no new labels in MERGE; SET a:admin does
g.gql("MERGE (a:person {name: 'x'}), (b:person {name: 'y'})") // error: MERGE takes exactly one pattern Either direction. An edge without a direction, -[:T]-, matches an edge in either direction; when it is created, it points from left to right, from the node written first: g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'josh'}), (b:person {name: 'marko'}) MERGE (a)-[e:knows]-(b) RETURN startNode(e).name AS from").to_list() // #{"from": "marko"}: the stored edge marko -> josh
g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'vadas'}), (b:person {name: 'josh'}) MERGE (a)-[e:knows]-(b) RETURN startNode(e).name AS from").to_list() // #{"from": "vadas"}: created left to right Per row, and each row sees the rows before it. MERGE runs once for each row, in order, and a row finds what an earlier row created: a repeated item is created once, so MERGE is idempotent within a query as across queries. The whole pattern is matched or created: MATCH (p:person) MERGE (p)-[:in]->(g:group {name: 'x'}) creates a group for every person without such an edge, because the pattern with the edge does not match for them; to share one group, MERGE the group first and the edge second: g.gql("FOR n IN ['Rome', 'Rome', 'Oslo'] MERGE (c:city {name: n}) RETURN count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT c) AS cities").to_list() // #{"cities": 2, "rows": 3}
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 MERGE (g:group {name: 'over30'}) MERGE (p)-[:in]->(g) RETURN count(DISTINCT g) AS groups").to_list() // #{"groups": 1} ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET. After the pattern, ON CREATE SET <items> changes the elements of a row that the MERGE created, and ON MATCH SET <items> those of a row it found. The items are the items of SET and may read every variable of the row (the pattern's and the earlier ones). Both may be written several times and in any order; they apply in the order written, each in its own case. g.gql("FOR name IN ['marko', 'ann'] MERGE (p:person {name: name}) ON CREATE SET p.visits = 1 ON MATCH SET p.visits = coalesce(p.visits, 0) + 1").iterate();
g.gql("FOR name IN ['marko', 'ann'] MERGE (p:person {name: name}) ON CREATE SET p.visits = 1 ON MATCH SET p.visits = coalesce(p.visits, 0) + 1 RETURN p.name AS name, p.visits AS visits ORDER BY name").to_list() // ann 2, marko 2 g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'marko'}) ON CREATE SET p.new = true ON MATCH SET p.new = false RETURN p.new AS new").to_list() // #{"new": false}
g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'marko'}) ON MATCH SET p.seen = 1 ON MATCH SET p.seen = p.seen + 1 RETURN p.seen AS seen").to_list() // #{"seen": 2} NULL in the pattern. MERGE cannot look for or create a NULL property value: a property of the pattern that is NULL on a row (a missing parameter, an OPTIONAL MATCH that found nothing) fails the query with 22004 when that row runs, and nothing of the query is kept. Keep such rows away with FILTER x IS NOT NULL, or give a default with coalesce(): g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (n:num {v: x})") // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{v: NULL}` (22004)
g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] FILTER x IS NOT NULL MERGE (n:num {v: x}) RETURN count(*) AS n").to_list() // #{"n": 1} A MERGE that only finds changes nothing. It commits no change: a commit hook and the journal see nothing, and the dev server's answer reports no change summary and no commit. An ON MATCH SET that runs is a change, as a SET is. The same in Gremlin: merge_v() finds or creates a vertex, merge_e() an edge between given vertices, and the fold().coalesce(__.unfold(), __.add_v(..)) idiom does it by hand. Their onCreate option map replaces the creation map, while ON CREATE SET changes the created element afterwards. g.merge_v(#{"T.label": "city", name: "Berlin"}).values("name").to_list() // "Berlin"
g.v().has_label("city").has("name", "Berlin").fold().coalesce(__.unfold(), __.add_v("city").property("name", "Berlin")).values("name").to_list() // "Berlin" The same in plain GQL, without the compatibility form: a CALL body that inserts only when nothing exists yet, then a MATCH that reads the result: g.gql("CALL { FILTER NOT EXISTS { MATCH (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } MATCH (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN count(c) AS cities").to_list() // #{"cities": 1}

448.body:
Each clause sees every write of the clauses before it, for all rows; within one clause the rows are processed in order, and each row sees the writes of the rows before it. A query never sees its own writes while it is still finding the rows of an earlier clause: MATCH (n) INSERT (:X) creates exactly one node per node that existed before, and MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) INSERT (a)-[:copy]->(b) copies each existing edge once, never the copies. g.gql("MATCH (n) INSERT (:X)").iterate();
g.v().has_label("X").count().next() // 6 g.gql("FOR i IN range(1, 3) INSERT (:n {i: i}) WITH count(*) AS made MATCH (m:n) RETURN made, count(m) AS seen").to_list() // #{"made": 3, "seen": 3} A value a row carried before a SET keeps the value it had: WITH p.age AS old SET p.age = 0 still returns the old age in old, while p.age reads the new one. g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH p, p.age AS old SET p.age = 0 RETURN old, p.age AS now").to_list() // #{"now": 0, "old": 29} The details, and how this follows from the executor, are on Semantics .

449.body:
A gql() query is one traversal and so one unit ( Transactions ): when any row fails (a data error on the last row, a schema violation, a permission, a resource limit, cancellation), nothing the query wrote stays. Here the second item divides by zero, and the node of the first item is rolled back with it (execute() keeps the error instead of raising it, so the script goes on): let run = g.gql("FOR x IN [1, 0] INSERT (:n {v: 1 / x})").execute(); // fails: division by zero
g.v().has_label("n").count().next() // 0 A SET that fails on one row leaves the rows before it unchanged too: let set = g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.score = 100 / (p.age - 27)").execute(); // fails on vadas (27)
g.v().has("score").count().next() // 0 Commit hooks see the query's ChangeSet and may veto it, a dry run shows its changes without keeping them, and a Store's journal records it like any Gremlin write ( Change capture ).

45.body:
The context for the language model is the hits plus what the graph knows about them, in one query: rows = graph.query(""" g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, 3) .project("text", "doc", "topics") .by("text") .by(__.out("part_of").values("title")) .by(__.out("part_of").out("mentions").values("name").fold()) .to_list()
""", params={"q": q}) context = "\n".join(f"[{r['doc']}; topics: {', '.join(r['topics'])}] {r['text']}" for r in rows)
prompt = f"Answer from this context only.\n\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
# send `prompt` to the language model of your choice To let an AI agent (an MCP client or the playground's AI Chat on the dev server ) run the search itself, store it as a saved query whose parameter is the vector; the agent still needs the question's embedding from a tool of the host: graph.define_query({ "name": "semantic_search", "params": { "q": {"schema": {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "dimension": 384}}, "k": {"schema": {"type": "integer"}, "default": 5}, }, "body": 'fn semantic_search(q, k) { g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, k).values("text") }',
})
graph.call_query("semantic_search", {"q": graphersal.Vector(q), "k": 2}) When the host registers its model as an embedder and the documents were embedded with embed_property(), the schema knows the model, and the parameter can be the question itself: nearest("emb", question, k) with params: {"question": "string"} embeds it with that model, so the agent needs no embedding tool at all. From Python that is graphersal.Embedder("minilm", model.encode, dimension=384, model="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") in Graph(embedders=[..]), then graph.embed_property(label="chunk", source="text", target="emb") ( Python Quick Start: Embedders ). Any model works. OpenAI, Cohere, Ollama or a model of your own: an embedding is just a list of numbers. Keep the schema's dimension equal to the model's, embed documents and questions with the same model, and pick the metric the model is meant for (most text models: cosine).

451.body: The permission check sees the lowered plan before anything runs: an INSERT asks Create on Data(vertex "label") per label of each new node and Create on Data(edge "label") per new edge, exactly as add_v(labels) and add_e(label) do, plus the reads of its MATCH clauses. SET and REMOVE ask Update, as property(), remove_property(), add_label() and drop_label() do: on Data(vertex) for a node (any label, since a node's label set is not fixed by the pattern), on Data(edge "label") for an edge whose pattern names its labels, and on any element when the kind is not known before the run (an item of a FOR list). It asks nothing for the properties: they are part of creating the element. DELETE asks Delete, as drop() does: on Data(vertex) for a node, on Data(edge "label") for an edge whose pattern names its labels, and on any element for a path, a list or a value whose kind is known only at run time; DETACH asks nothing more (as drop() of a vertex, which removes its edges too). MERGE asks what its two halves need, whether a row will find or create: Read for the search (as a MATCH of its pattern), Create per label of every element the pattern can create (as the INSERT of it), and, only when it has ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET items, their Updates (as SET). The step's own Create and Update requests are checked first, then the Reads of its search; a policy that denies Create refuses a MERGE even where every row would only find. merge_v() and merge_e() ask Read on what they search first, then Create and Update on any vertex or edge (no labels, and Update even without on_create / on_match options). (Gremlin's add_v(..).property(..) asks Create and Update, because the check runs before the optimizer folds the property into the creation; a policy that denies only Update allows the INSERT and refuses its Gremlin twin.) A read-only host (AccessPolicy::read_only(), the MCP server's --mcp-read-only, a read-only view of a past state) refuses a GQL write before it runs.

454.body:
An INSERT lowers to the internal steps gql:insert_node and gql:insert_edge, one per element of the pattern, in text order ( Plans and Performance ); a SET clause to one gql:set step and a REMOVE clause to one gql:remove step with its items, which pass the row on unchanged. A DELETE clause lowers to one gql:delete step: it collects the targets of all its rows first (the NODETACH check sees the whole clause), removes the edges, then the nodes, and passes the rows on unchanged. A MERGE lowers to one gql:merge step with two children: the search (the plan of a MATCH of the pattern, starting from a bound node or using a property index where one serves it) and the creation (the gql:insert_node / gql:insert_edge chain of the pattern); .profile() shows both under the step. Because the plan writes, its traversers are never merged into one with a higher bulk: each row creates its own elements and applies its own changes. g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = 1 RETURN p").profile()
g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Rome'}) RETURN c").profile()

456.body: In the Gremlin DSL (the command line, the playground, Python scripts, saved queries) a GQL query is a Rhai string passed to g.gql(..). GQL has quotes and backticks of its own, and Rhai gives some characters a meaning inside strings, so this page shows which string form to use and how to write values, names and comments inside it. Through the MCP tool gql none of this applies: the query is plain text.

457.body: A query on one line goes into a Rhai double-quoted string. Write GQL string literals with single quotes , so nothing needs escaping: g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE s.name = 'lop' RETURN s.lang AS lang").to_list() // #{"lang": "java"} GQL accepts "..." string literals too, but inside a Rhai "..." string each one must be escaped as \": g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE s.name = \"lop\" RETURN s.lang AS lang").to_list() // #{"lang": "java"} A single quote inside a GQL '...' literal is doubled ('it''s'), the GQL rule. Rhai processes backslash escapes in "..." strings first, so a backslash that GQL should see is written \\. g.gql("MATCH (s:software) RETURN 'it''s' AS t LIMIT 1").to_list() // #{"t": "it's"}

46.body: nearest() scores every element it receives, with no index to build or keep up to date, so its time grows with the number of vectors times the dimension. The measured numbers (10 000 vectors of 384 dimensions) show that this is fast enough for most in-memory graphs; a filter before the search scores fewer, and an i8 property takes a quarter of the memory. There is no approximate (ANN) index yet ( Current Limitations ).

462.body:
An agent connected to the dev server's MCP endpoint can call the tool gql with the query as plain text and the parameters as a JSON object, so none of the quoting above applies: { "query": "MATCH (p:person)-[:knows]->(f) WHERE p.name = $name RETURN f.name AS friend ORDER BY friend", "params": {"name": "marko"}, "max_rows": 100
} It runs the same g.gql(..) call with the parameters as values and returns the rows like the query tool, in written column order. Like the query tool it may write (INSERT; the answer says that it changed the graph, with a one-line summary such as +3 vertices, +2 edges), and a server started with --mcp-read-only still offers it but refuses its writes. Prefer it whenever an agent writes GQL: there is no Rhai string to escape and no interpolation to get wrong. To continue a GQL result with Gremlin steps, use the query tool with g.gql(..) in the script.

465.body: These look like Cypher but are GQL too, so they are not aliases: : before a label expression (GQL also has IS), ASC / DESC (also ASCENDING / DESCENDING), string literals in '...' and "...", // and /* */ comments, $name parameters, back-quoted names. The functions abs, floor, ceil, sqrt, exp, log10, left, right, ltrim, rtrim, btrim, trim(s), nullif (Cypher nullIf; names are case-insensitive) and coalesce have the same name in both languages and are GQL functions. Where Neo4j's version differs, GQL's meaning wins: trim(s), ltrim(s) and rtrim(s) remove spaces only (Cypher removes any whitespace), and floor(3) / ceil(3) of an integer stay integers (Neo4j returns floats that compare equal). ceiling(x) is GQL's second spelling of ceil(x).

471.body:
Cypher's MERGE ("find or create") has no ISO GQL counterpart. gql() accepts it as a compatibility form with Neo4j Cypher 25's meaning, and with it its ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET actions: Cypher In gql() Notes MERGE <pattern> supported as a compatibility form one path pattern per clause; per row, every match is a row, or the whole pattern is created; each row sees the rows before it ( Writing with GQL ) ON CREATE SET <items>, ON MATCH SET <items> supported as a compatibility form the items of SET, several actions in any order, applied in the order written MERGE p = <pattern> supported the path found or created MERGE (a)-[:T]-(b) without a direction supported matches either direction, creates from left to right Plain GQL writes the same with a CALL body that inserts only when nothing exists: g.gql("MERGE (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list() // #{"name": "Berlin"}
g.gql("CALL { FILTER NOT EXISTS { MATCH (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'}) } MATCH (c:city {name: 'Berlin'}) RETURN c.name AS name").to_list() // #{"name": "Berlin"} The differences from Neo4j are on Semantics .
471.title: MERGE

473.body: Cypher In gql() id(n) refused: an integer in Neo4j, Graphersal ids are strings; use element_id(n) nodes(p), relationships(p) supported as compatibility functions , not aliases: GQL has no such functions x ^ y supported as a compatibility operator: GQL has no operator for it; it means power(x, y) (always a float, the same errors), binding tighter than * and looser than a unary minus rand(), randomUUID() refused: gql() functions are deterministic time(), time.*(); date.realtime() and the other X.realtime() time() not supported yet (no time-with-offset type: use localtime() or datetime()); X.realtime() refused, like rand() ( Dates and times ) map projections, list and pattern comprehensions supported as compatibility forms , not aliases any() / all() / none() / single(), reduce() supported as compatibility functions , not aliases: GQL has no such functions COUNT { }, COLLECT { } supported as compatibility forms , not aliases CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS refused : a write form; the CALL itself is supported exists(n.p) (Cypher 4) refused : EXISTS takes a pattern; test a property with n.p IS NOT NULL GROUP BY (not Cypher) ISO GQL, accepted after the RETURN items (optional: grouping is implicit); after WITH an error that explains implicit grouping MERGE supported as a compatibility form , with ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET FOREACH not supported yet ( Writing with GQL ); CREATE is an alias of INSERT; SET and REMOVE are supported, += as a compatibility form DELETE, DETACH DELETE the same in GQL, supported ( Writing with GQL ); GQL also writes the default explicitly as NODETACH DELETE SET n[key] = v, SET n:$(expr) (Cypher 25 dynamic keys and labels) not supported; name the key and the label in the query CALL proc(..) YIELD .. supported for saved queries written in GQL: CALL folder.name(..) with YIELD, YIELD * and the standalone forms of Cypher ( Calling saved queries ) CALL db.*(), dbms.*, apoc.*, gds.*, SHOW ... refused: vendor extensions a--1 (minus minus one) a comment starts at -- (GQL wins): RETURN n.age--1 AS x returns the column n.age; write n.age - -1

474.body:
Some constructs gql() refuses for good, not just for now. A refused construct fails before the traversal runs, with GQLSTATUS 0A000, a caret under it and a help line naming what to use instead. (Constructs that are only not supported yet are listed on The Supported Subset .) GROUP BY is neither: it is accepted after the RETURN items, and grouping is implicit anyway; after WITH (no ISO counterpart) it is a syntax error whose help shows the query without it ( Aggregation ). Construct Why Instead undirected edges ~[e]~, <~[e]~, ~[e]~>, ~, <~, ~> Graphersal edges are always directed; there is no undirected edge to match -[e]-, an edge in either direction catalog commands CREATE INDEX, CREATE CONSTRAINT, CREATE GRAPH, CREATE DATABASE not part of a query: indexes, schemas and graphs are the host's g.create_index(..), g.set_schema(..), opening another graph LOAD CSV a vendor extension, not GQL the host's import (GraphSON, GraphML), or the rows as a list parameter: FOR row IN $rows INSERT (..) vendor procedures: the namespaces db, dbms, apoc and gds (CALL db.labels(), CALL apoc.*) vendor extensions, not GQL (an inline CALL { } subquery is supported , and any other CALL folder.name(..) calls a saved query ) the Gremlin steps that do the same, such as g.v().label().dedup(), or a saved GQL query that does it CALL { ... } IN TRANSACTIONS commits the writes of a subquery in batches; a gql() query is one unit, which commits at once or not at all the same CALL without IN TRANSACTIONS SHOW ... a vendor command, not GQL the catalog steps (indexes(), queries(), get_schema(), statistics()) vendor path search *BFS, *WSHORTEST, *ALLSHORTEST vendor extensions, not GQL Gremlin repeat() id(n) Cypher's id() is an integer; Graphersal ids are strings, and returning a different type under the same name would mislead element_id(n), the id as a string exists(n.p), the Cypher 4 property test EXISTS is GQL's subquery predicate and takes a graph pattern; reading it as a property test as well would give one keyword two meanings n.p IS NOT NULL; EXISTS { (n)-[:T]->() } tests a pattern ( EXISTS ) USE graph gql() runs on the graph of its traversal source open the other graph and run there non-deterministic functions rand(), randomUUID() every gql() function is pure, so a LET or WITH name may stand for its expression and the plan stays deterministic; a random value would differ between its uses Gremlin after gql(): sample(n) or coin(p) to pick rows at random vendor and namespaced functions apoc.*, db.*, gds.*, text.*, ... vendor extensions, not GQL; the accepted Cypher functions are a fixed list ( compatibility functions ) a gql() function, or Gremlin steps after gql() g.gql("MATCH (a)~[e]~(b) RETURN a") // refused: undirected edges (`~`) are not supported
g.gql("CALL db.labels() YIELD label RETURN label") // refused: the vendor procedures of db, dbms, apoc and gds are vendor extensions
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } IN TRANSACTIONS RETURN sw") // refused: CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS commits writes in batches
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw ORDER BY sw").to_list() // lop, lop, lop, ripple
g.gql("SHOW INDEXES") // refused: SHOW commands are vendor extensions
g.gql("CREATE INDEX FOR (n:person) ON (n.name)") // refused: CREATE INDEX is a catalog command
g.gql("LOAD CSV FROM 'people.csv' AS row RETURN row") // refused: LOAD CSV is a vendor extension
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN id(n)") // refused: use element_id(n)
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows*BFS]->(b) RETURN b") // refused: *BFS is a vendor path search extension
g.gql("USE g MATCH (n) RETURN n") // refused: USE is not supported
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE exists(n.age) RETURN n.name AS name") // refused: exists(value) is the Cypher 4 property test
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age IS NOT NULL RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").to_list() // josh, marko, peter, vadas
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN rand() AS r") // refused: rand() is a non-deterministic function
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN apoc.text.join(['a', 'b'], ',') AS r") // refused: apoc.text.join() is a vendor function
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name AS name ORDER BY name").sample(1).count().next() // 1
g.gql("MATCH (n) RETURN element_id(n) AS id ORDER BY id LIMIT 2").to_list() // #{"id": "1"}, #{"id": "2"} Writes are supported (INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, and Cypher's MERGE as a compatibility form: Writing with GQL ); Cypher's FOREACH is not supported yet and is listed there. The full message of a refused construct reads: Error: GQL unsupported construct at line 1, column 1: CREATE INDEX is a catalog command, not part of a gql() query (step #1 'gql:error("0A000")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("0A000") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: CREATE INDEX FOR (n:person) ON (n.name) ^^^^^^^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 0A000
Help: create a property index with g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "age"}); every query that can use it then does. gql() does not support this construct; write this part of the query as Gremlin steps.

475.body: A GQL error is a TraverserError::Gql (feature gql) with a kind, a message, the position (line and column inside the query), a caret under the offending text, the expected tokens, a "did you mean" suggestion where one fits, and a GQLSTATUS code, the five-character status code of ISO GQL (derived from SQL's SQLSTATE). Like every Graphersal error it has a Help: line that names the fix.
475.title: Errors

476.body:
A query that does not parse or bind fails before the traversal runs , even when no traverser would ever reach the step, as math() does with an equation. On the empty graph, where nothing matches, the query is still checked: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name +") // error: unexpected end of input Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 33: unexpected end of input (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name + ^ expected: an expression GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: Expected an expression at the marked position. Fix the query at the marked position: a GQL read query is MATCH <pattern> [WHERE <condition>], then any further MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET or FILTER clauses, then RETURN <items>, for example g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name") or g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WITH p, count(s) AS n RETURN p.name, n"). CALL (p) { .. RETURN .. } runs a query for each row, UNION combines the records of two queries and NEXT continues after a RETURN, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p NEXT MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name"). FOR x IN <list> (Cypher UNWIND <list> AS x) gives one row per item of a list, and a query may also start with FOR, LET, WITH, FILTER or RETURN, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['marko', 'josh'] MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age"). The plan of a query that failed this way is the marker step gql:error("<GQLSTATUS>"), which raises the error before anything runs; the query: line, not the plan, shows the position. In a multi-line query the error names the line and shows only that line: g.gql(`MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > RETURN n`) // error: unexpected keyword RETURN at line 3 Error: GQL syntax error at line 3, column 8: unexpected keyword RETURN (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ line 3: RETURN n ^^^^^^ expected: an expression GQLSTATUS: 42001 Misspelt keywords, functions and variables get a suggestion: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETRUN n") // error: unexpected `RETRUN`, did you mean RETURN
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN m.name") // error: the variable `m` is not defined, did you mean n
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > $min RETURN n.name AS name") // error: the parameter `$min` has no value Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 18: unexpected `RETRUN` (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: MATCH (n:person) RETRUN n ^^^^^^ expected: `,`, WHERE, MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET, FILTER, FOR, UNWIND, CALL, RETURN did you mean: RETURN GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: Did you mean RETURN? Expected `,`, WHERE, MATCH, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, LET, FILTER, FOR, UNWIND, CALL, ... at the marked position. ...
476.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Errors » Errors before the run
476.title: Errors before the run

477.body:
A valid query can still fail on a row of the data: a division by zero, an overflow, an operand of the wrong kind. These fail the traversal when the row reaches the expression (kind Data, GQLSTATUS class 22), with the caret under the expression and the step that ran it: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age / 0 AS x") // error: division by zero
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.name + 1 AS x") // error: + joins two strings or adds two numbers, not a string and a number
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN type(n) AS x") // error: type() takes an edge, not a node Error: Step #1 'gql:project("x")' execution failed at #1: v().has_label("person").gql:project("x") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ plan: v(labels: ["person"]).gql:project("x") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 25: division by zero query: MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age / 0 AS x ^^^^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 22012
Help: A row of the data made the marked expression fail. Keep such rows away from it with a WHERE condition or a CASE expression, ... Comparisons never fail: = of values of different kinds is FALSE (<> TRUE), an ordering < of them is NULL, and any comparison with NULL is NULL ( Semantics ). + of a string and a number names the explicit conversions in its help: Help: Convert the number or boolean to text first, with toString(x) or CAST(x AS STRING), and join text with ||, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name || ' is ' || toString(p.age) AS s"); or compute with numbers only, converting text with toInteger(x) or toFloat(x). ...
477.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Errors » Errors while the query runs
477.title: Errors while the query runs

478.body:
A function fails on an argument it cannot take, with a GQLSTATUS that says why and a help line that leads with the fix for that function, then the general advice above: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN CAST(n.name AS INTEGER) AS x") // error: invalid character value for cast (22018)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN substring(n.name, -1) AS x") // error: substring() takes a start of 0 or more (22011)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN TRIM(BOTH 'ab' FROM n.name) AS x") // error: TRIM(.. FROM ..) removes exactly one character (22027)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN ln(n.age - 29) AS x") // error: ln() of a number <= 0 (2201E)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN sqrt(27 - n.age) AS x") // error: sqrt() of a negative number (2201F)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN range(1, n.age, 0) AS x") // error: range() step 0 (22023)
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN toFloat(n.age > 30) AS x") // error: toFloat() takes a number or a string, not a boolean (22G03) Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 30: invalid character value for cast: 'marko' is not an INTEGER (expected a decimal number, surrounding spaces allowed) query: MATCH (n:person) RETURN CAST(n.name AS INTEGER) AS x ^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 22018
Help: CAST is strict: text that is not a value of the target type fails the query. The Cypher conversions are lenient: toInteger(x), toFloat(x) and toBoolean(x) give NULL for such text, and toIntegerOrNull(x), toFloatOrNull(x) and toBooleanOrNull(x) give NULL for a value of any other kind too, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, toInteger(p.name) AS n"). A row of the data made the marked expression fail. ... A function gql() knows but does not support gets a message with the reason and the alternative instead of "unknown function", and a misspelt name a suggestion: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN sin(n.age) AS x") // error: sin() (a trigonometric function) is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN rand() AS x") // refused: rand() is not supported: a non-deterministic function
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN toInt(n.age) AS x") // error: unknown function toInt(), did you mean toInteger() Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 25: sin() (a trigonometric function) is not yet supported in this version (step #1 'gql:error("0A000")' refused the query before the traversal ran) ... GQLSTATUS: 0A000
Help: Gremlin math() after gql(), for example g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN n.age AS a").select("a").math("sin(_)"). This construct comes in a later version of gql(); until then, write the query without it or as Gremlin steps.
478.title: Function errors

479.body:
The temporal functions fail with these codes; the help line shows the accepted forms with a runnable example: Code When 22007 text that is no value of the type (date('nonsense'), date('2015-13-01'), an offset in localtime('12:00+01:00'), an offset that is not the zone's in '..+02:00[Europe/London]'); a map with an unknown key or with two groups of date keys; an unknown time zone 22008 a field out of range (month: 13, day: 30 in February, hour: 25) or a value outside the years -9999 to 9999, also as the result of arithmetic (date('9999-12-31') + duration('P1D')) 22G03 a component the value's type does not have (date(..).hour; the message lists the components it has); a constructor argument of the wrong kind (date(42), localdatetime(date(..))); arithmetic without a meaning (date + date, date * 2); a truncation or difference of a value without the part it needs (date.truncate('day', localtime(..)), duration.inDays() of two local times) 22023 a truncation unit the type does not have (date.truncate('hour', ..)) or an unknown unit 22012 a duration divided by zero 0A000 a part below the microsecond ('12:00:00.0000001', nanosecond: 5), Cypher's zoned time() and ISO zoned_time() (not yet); X.realtime() (refused) g.gql("RETURN date('nonsense') AS d") // error: cannot parse "nonsense" as a date (22007)
g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, mnth: 3}) AS d") // error: the map has an unknown field mnth (22007)
g.gql("RETURN datetime({year: 2015, timezone: 'Mars/Olympus'}) AS d") // error: unknown time zone (22007)
g.gql("RETURN date({year: 2015, month: 13, day: 1}) AS d") // error: the field month cannot be 13 (22008)
g.gql("RETURN date('9999-12-31') + duration('P1D') AS d") // error: the result is outside the supported range (22008)
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01').foo AS x") // error: a date has no component foo; its components are year, quarter, ... (22G03)
g.gql("RETURN date('2015-01-01') * 2 AS x") // error: * with a temporal value takes a duration and a number (22G03)
g.gql("RETURN date.truncate('fortnight', date('2017-10-11')) AS d") // error: unknown unit 'fortnight' (22023)
g.gql("RETURN duration('P1D') / 0 AS d") // error: division by zero (22012)
g.gql("RETURN localtime('12:00:00.0000001') AS t") // error: a part below the microsecond is not yet supported (0A000) Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 13: date(): the field month cannot be 13 query: RETURN date({year: 2015, month: 13, day: 1}) AS d ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 22008
Help: Temporal fields stay within their ranges (month 1 to 12, day within its month, week within its week-numbering year, hour 0 to 23, minute and second 0 to 59, millisecond 0 to 999) and every value within the years -9999 to 9999, as in g.gql("RETURN date({year: 1984, month: 10, day: 11}) AS d, localtime({hour: 23, minute: 59, second: 59, millisecond: 999}) AS t"). A row of the data made the marked expression fail. ...

480.body:
The help of a semantic error explains the rule behind it. A variable that a WITH did not carry on, a value read outside an aggregate that is not a grouping key, and a GROUP BY that leaves out a grouping key each name the fix: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p.name AS name RETURN p.age") // error: the variable `p` is not in scope: the WITH before does not carry it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, count(p.age) + p.age AS x") // error: `p` is read outside an aggregate and is not a grouping key
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, p.age AS a, count(*) GROUP BY n") // error: the RETURN item `a` has no aggregate, so it is a grouping key, and GROUP BY does not list it Help: add `p` to the WITH items, as in WITH ..., p. WITH passes on only its columns: a variable it does not list is out of scope after it (only the WHERE of a WITH without an aggregate still reads it), so list every variable a later clause reads, ...
Help: add `p` to the RETURN items (it then becomes a grouping key), or read it inside an aggregate, as in collect(p). A RETURN or WITH with an aggregate groups the rows by its other items (the grouping keys): ...
Help: add it to GROUP BY (GROUP BY ..., a), or remove GROUP BY: grouping is implicit, the items without an aggregate are the keys. ... A FOR (or UNWIND) defines new names; reusing a name in scope, giving the item and its position one name, or using the position as a node is an error whose help says what FOR defines: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FOR p IN [1] RETURN p") // error: the variable `p` is already defined; FOR defines a new variable
g.gql("FOR x IN [3, 1, 2] WITH OFFSET x RETURN x") // error: `x` names both the item and its position Help: choose another name, as in FOR p2 IN <list>. FOR x IN <list> (Cypher UNWIND <list> AS x) gives one row per item of the list, which it reads on the row before the FOR; the item x and, with WITH ORDINALITY i (from 1) or WITH OFFSET i (from 0), its position i are two new variables with names of their own; ... An unbounded quantifier that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails with the ordinary limit error (RepeatLimitExceeded, ResourceLimitExceeded; no GQLSTATUS), never with fewer rows. Its help is written for GQL: it names the quantified edge, an upper bound to give it and the g.with(..).gql(..) that raises the limit ( Semantics ): g.with("traversal.max_traversers", 3).gql("MATCH (a)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(b) RETURN b.name AS b") // error: traversal.max_traversers exceeded Caused by: Resource limit 'traversal.max_traversers' exceeded (limit 3, reached 6)
Help: The gql() query kept more traversers (rows in the making) alive between two steps than 'traversal.max_traversers' allows (3). Each path a quantified edge (-[:knows|created]->{1,}) matches is a traverser of its own (trail keeps them apart, so they do not merge), ... give it a lower upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}. ... A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), toString() of a list or map, ||) checks the size of its result before it builds it, against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget, like collect_list(). A result that is too large fails with the ordinary limit error (ResourceLimitExceeded, no GQLSTATUS: the option and its lock are the engine's), never with a shortened value; inside gql() its help names the growing functions, a bound for them and the g.with(..).gql(..) that raises the limit: g.gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN range(0, 9223372036854775807) AS r") // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded
g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 100).gql("MATCH (n:person) RETURN split(n.name, '') AS s") // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded Caused by: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded (limit 1073741824, reached 18446744073709551615)
Help: The gql() query built a value larger than 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' allows (1073741824 bytes); ... A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), || and CAST(x AS STRING) of a list or map) and the list of collect_list() are checked before they are built, so the query stops instead of running out of memory; the result is never cut short. Build smaller values: bound range() and replace() by the data, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN range(1, p.age / 10) AS r"), ... or raise the limit for the query, g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 2147483648).gql(..), ...

481.body:
The errors of an EXISTS subquery or a pattern predicate share one help text that explains subqueries: TRUE or FALSE, never NULL; the body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds stay inside it; a pattern predicate binds no new variable. Before it, each names its own fix: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE (p)-[:knows]->(q) RETURN p.name AS name") // error: the pattern predicate introduces the new variable `q`
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, (p)-[:knows]->() AS k") // error: the pattern stands where a value is expected (42001)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN s.name AS s") // error: the variable `s` is not in scope: it is bound inside a subquery
g.gql("MATCH (a:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)-->() WHERE b.age > 1 MATCH (b) } RETURN a") // error: `b` is bound by a later MATCH clause of the subquery Help: write it as EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(q) }, whose MATCH may bind new variables, or leave `q` out of the pattern. A subquery, EXISTS { MATCH <pattern> [WHERE <condition>] }, EXISTS { <pattern> } or a Cypher pattern predicate such as (p)-[:created]->(), is TRUE when its body has a match and FALSE otherwise, never NULL; its body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it. A pattern predicate binds no new variable: name new elements in an EXISTS { MATCH .. }, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE NOT EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WHERE s.lang = 'java' } RETURN p.name"), and bind an element in the MATCH clause of the query to read it after the subquery, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name").
Help: write EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } for whether it has a match, COUNT { (p)-[:knows]->() } for the number of matches, or a pattern comprehension such as [(n)-->(m) | m] for the list of what it matches, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, COUNT { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS friends, [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.name] AS made"). A subquery, ...
Help: bind `s` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or test it inside the subquery. A subquery, ...
Help: move the condition to the WHERE of that later MATCH clause inside the subquery. A subquery, ... A query holds at most 64 subqueries (EXISTS, pattern predicates, pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { }, nested ones included) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies, where a LET or WITH variable holding a subquery counts once for every place that reads it. A CALL { } body counts toward neither; CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies nest at most 16 levels ( UNION, NEXT and CALL ). Either limit is 54001 before the run, and its help names both bounds and the forms that need fewer subqueries: Error: GQL limit exceeded at line 1, column 785: the query holds more than 64 subqueries (EXISTS and pattern predicates), pattern comprehensions included, as are COUNT { } and COLLECT { } ...
Help: join the patterns into fewer subqueries (one EXISTS { MATCH .. } may hold several MATCH clauses and patterns), or add the patterns to the MATCH clause of the query; a pattern comprehension is a subquery too: collect the matches of several patterns with OPTIONAL MATCH and collect_list() instead. The query is larger than gql() accepts: one query holds at most 64 subqueries (EXISTS, pattern predicates, pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { }, nested ones included) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies, where a LET or WITH variable holding a subquery counts once for every place that reads it; a CALL { } body counts toward neither (CALL bodies nest at most 16 levels). One EXISTS may hold several MATCH clauses and patterns, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) MATCH (f)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN p.name"), and one CALL may compute what several COUNT { } and COLLECT { } over the same pattern do, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS n, collect_list(s.name) AS names } RETURN p.name, n, names"). A quantified edge inside a subquery that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails like one outside, and the help says where it stands and why a subquery may loop long: g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { (p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) } RETURN p.name AS n") // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside an EXISTS subquery (or pattern predicate) of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A subquery stops at its first match, so its loop runs this long on a row that has no match, or only a late one. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ... COUNT { } and COLLECT { } follow the same rules (a variable bound inside one is named as bound inside that COUNT { } or COLLECT { }, and the help explains the two forms); a COLLECT { } body must end in a RETURN of exactly one column. Cypher 4's exists(n.p) is refused : g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f.name, f.age } AS l") // error: COLLECT { } needs a body that ends in a RETURN of exactly one column
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) } AS n, f.name AS x") // error: the variable `f` is not in scope: it is bound inside a COUNT { } subquery
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN exists(p.age) AS a") // refused: exists(value), the Cypher 4 property test, is not supported Help: return the one value to collect, as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name } AS names. A subquery, ...
Help: bind `f` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or test it inside the COUNT { } body. COUNT { <body> } is the number of matches of its body (or of the records its RETURN gives), and COLLECT { <body> RETURN <expression> } the list of the values it returns; the body reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it, ...
Help: test a property with n.p IS NOT NULL, here p.age IS NOT NULL; EXISTS tests a graph pattern, as in MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { (p)-[:created]->() } RETURN p.name. ...
481.title: Subqueries

482.body:
A pattern comprehension is a subquery, so its errors follow the rules above with their own help text: the variables it binds stay inside it (read them in its | part), and its | part holds no aggregate (aggregate the list, size([..]), or use OPTIONAL MATCH and an aggregate). A list-comprehension variable must be a new name, and its WHERE and | parts hold no aggregate either. Each help names the form that works: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS l ORDER BY f.name") // error: `f` is bound inside a pattern comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [(p)-->(f) | count(f)] AS l") // error: count() cannot be used inside the | part of a pattern comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [p IN [1, 2] | p * 2] AS l") // error: the comprehension variable `p` shadows the variable `p` in scope
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [1, 2] | count(x)] AS l") // error: count() cannot be used inside the WHERE or | part of a list comprehension
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [1, 2] WHERE x:A|B | x] AS a") // error: unexpected `|` Help: bind `f` in the MATCH clause of the query to use it here, or read it in the | part of the comprehension, as in [(a)-->(f) | f.name]. A pattern comprehension, [(a)-[:knows]->(f) WHERE <condition> | <expression>], is the list of its | part evaluated for every match of its pattern (the empty list when nothing matches); its pattern reads the variables bound before it, and the variables it binds itself stay inside it. ...
Help: aggregate the list the comprehension builds, as in MATCH (p) RETURN size([(p)-->(f) | f.age]) AS n, or aggregate in a WITH after an OPTIONAL MATCH, as in MATCH (p) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-->(f) RETURN p, count(f.age) AS n. ...
Help: give the comprehension its own variable, as in [p2 IN list WHERE p2 > 0 | p2]. ...
Help: aggregate in a WITH first and use its column in the comprehension, as in MATCH (p)-->(f) WITH p, count(f.age) AS n RETURN [x IN [1, 2, 3] WHERE x < n]. ...
Help: a `|` in a comprehension ends its list or its WHERE condition; write a label alternative there in parentheses, as in [x IN l WHERE x:(A|B) | x.name]. ... A map projection of a value that is not an element or a map, and a list comprehension over a value that is not a list, are data errors (22G03) of the row; so is all(), any(), none(), single() or reduce() over a value that is not a list, and the message names the function. Their variables are new names like a comprehension's (42002), and an aggregate inside their condition or | part is 42002 with a WITH example of the same form. A list-comprehension variable read inside an EXISTS or a pattern comprehension of its own WHERE or | part is not supported yet (0A000), the variables of the list predicates and reduce() neither: g.gql("WITH 1 AS m RETURN m {.a} AS x") // error: a map projection reads a node, an edge or a map, not a number
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [x IN [p] WHERE (x)-->() | x.name] AS l") // error: reading the comprehension variable `x` inside a subquery is not yet supported
g.gql("RETURN any(x IN 5 WHERE x > 1) AS a") // error: any() iterates over a list, not a number (22G03)
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN reduce(p = 0, x IN [1] | p + x) AS a") // error: the accumulator `p` of reduce() shadows the variable `p` in scope Help: test `x` outside the subquery, as in [x IN list WHERE x > 0 AND EXISTS { MATCH (n)-->() }]. ...
Help: give reduce() an accumulator of its own, as in reduce(p2 = 0, item IN list | p2 + item). ... The same holds for the variable of all(), any(), none() and single() and for both variables of reduce(), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name, all(a IN [p.age] WHERE a > 30) AS old, reduce(s = 0, a IN [p.age, 1] | s + a) AS total"). A resource limit reached inside a pattern comprehension names it. A quantified edge in its pattern loops until the row's last match is found (unlike EXISTS, which stops at its first), and its list is checked against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget before it is built, like collect_list(): g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS n, [(p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) | x.name] AS r") // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations
g.with("traversal.max_materialized_bytes", 100).gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s.name] AS r") // error: Resource limit 'traversal.max_materialized_bytes' exceeded Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside a pattern comprehension [(a)-->(b) | ..] of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A pattern comprehension collects every match of its pattern for each row, so its loop runs until the row's last match is found. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ...
Help: ... A function whose result can be larger than its arguments (range(), split(), replace(), || and CAST(x AS STRING) of a list or map) and the list of collect_list() are checked before they are built, as is the list of a pattern comprehension [(a)-->(b) | b.name], so the query stops instead of running out of memory; the result is never cut short. ... count the values instead of collecting them, ... or, for the matches of a pattern, g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-->(f) RETURN p.name, count(f) AS n"), ...

482.title: Map projections and comprehensions

483.body:
The errors of a composite query share one help text that explains UNION and NEXT: the operands return the same column names in any order (the result keeps the first operand's order), UNION removes duplicates and UNION ALL keeps them, one chain uses one kind, each operand has its own variables, ORDER BY and LIMIT, and NEXT passes on only the RETURN columns. The column mismatch names both column sets: g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS y") // error: the operands of UNION must return the same column names
g.gql("RETURN 1 AS x UNION RETURN 2 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 3 AS x") // error: UNION ALL is mixed with UNION in one query
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name NEXT RETURN p.age") // error: the variable `p` is not in scope: the RETURN before NEXT does not return it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s") // error: MATCH after RETURN: RETURN ends the query Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 21: the operands of UNION must return the same column names: the first returns `x`, this one returns `y` (`x` is missing) ...
Help: name the columns alike with AS in every operand (their order may differ), as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name. UNION combines the records of queries that return the same column names, in any order (the result keeps the order of the first query): UNION (or UNION DISTINCT) removes duplicate records, UNION ALL keeps them, and one chain of UNIONs uses one kind. Each query of a UNION has its own variables, ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT. NEXT passes the records of the statement before it on by their column names (only those), so it sorts, filters or aggregates a UNION as a whole, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name NEXT RETURN name ORDER BY name LIMIT 3").
Help: write the same kind between every operand, or combine the parts with NEXT, as in RETURN 1 AS x UNION ALL RETURN 1 AS x NEXT RETURN x UNION RETURN 2 AS x. UNION combines ...
Help: add `p` to the RETURN items before NEXT, as in RETURN ..., p NEXT ... UNION combines ...
Help: put every MATCH before the RETURN, or continue with NEXT, which passes the columns of the RETURN on to the next statement, as in MATCH (p:person) RETURN p NEXT MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name, or chain Gremlin steps after gql(). ... The errors of a CALL share a help text on its scope: the body reads only the variables its scope clause names (CALL (*) all, CALL { } none, Cypher's CALL { WITH a .. } those of its first WITH), returns new names, aggregates per row, and drops a row without records unless the CALL is OPTIONAL. Cypher's importing WITH lists plain variables only, as in Neo4j: a first WITH with a WHERE, an alias, an expression, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, OFFSET or LIMIT is no importing WITH, so the body imports nothing and the error says so. A body without RETURN (a unit subquery, which only a write could use) is not supported, and IN TRANSACTIONS is refused : g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(f) RETURN f AS p } RETURN p") // error: the CALL body returns `p`, which is already defined outside it
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p AS q MATCH (q)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw") // error: the variable `p` is not imported into the CALL body: its first WITH is not an importing WITH
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL { WITH p WHERE p.age > 30 MATCH (p)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN sw") // error: the variable `p` is not imported into the CALL body: its first WITH is not an importing WITH
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) } RETURN p") // error: a CALL { } body without RETURN (a unit subquery) only makes sense for writes, and this body writes nothing
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } IN TRANSACTIONS RETURN sw") // refused: CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS commits writes in batches Help: rename the column inside the body, as in RETURN ... AS p2. A CALL subquery, CALL (a, b) { <query ending in RETURN, or in a write (INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, MERGE / FINISH)> }, runs its query once for each incoming row: the body reads only the variables its scope clause names (CALL (*) imports all of them, CALL { } none, and Cypher's CALL { WITH a .. } those of its first WITH), and passes on only the columns of its RETURN, which must be new names; its aggregates, ORDER BY and LIMIT apply to each row's records, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS made } RETURN p.name, made"). A row whose body returns no record is dropped; OPTIONAL CALL keeps it with NULL columns.
Help: import `p` with a variable scope clause, as in CALL (p) { MATCH ... WHERE ... }, or in Cypher with a WITH of plain variables first and the rest of the body after it, as in CALL { WITH p MATCH ... WHERE ... }. A CALL subquery, ...
Help: end the body with RETURN and the columns the query reads after it, for example MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN count(s) AS made } RETURN p.name, made. A CALL subquery, ...
Help: remove IN TRANSACTIONS: the whole query commits at once, and a query that fails changes nothing. A CALL subquery, ... CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies (EXISTS, COUNT or COLLECT with WITH, RETURN, ...) nest at most 16 levels (54001); the help shows how to un-nest them. A resource limit reached inside a CALL body names it: the body runs for each incoming row and keeps every record, so a quantified edge in it loops until the row's last match: g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:knows|created]->{1,}(x) RETURN count(x) AS n } RETURN p.name AS who, n") // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations Error: GQL limit exceeded at line 1, column 113: the query nests CALL { } and subquery bodies deeper than 16 levels ...
Help: un-nest the bodies: a CALL body may follow another in the same query, as in CALL { .. RETURN a } CALL (a) { .. RETURN b }, and NEXT passes the result of one query to the next. The query is larger than gql() accepts. Help: The loop of the quantified edge -[:knows|created]->{1,} inside a CALL { } subquery of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. ... A CALL { } subquery runs its body for each incoming row and keeps every record it returns, so its loop runs until the row's last match is found. Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in -[:knows|created]->{1,5}, ... A limit inside an operand of a UNION or a block after NEXT at the top level keeps the plain text of a top-level clause; inside a subquery the place named is the innermost subquery (CALL, COUNT, COLLECT, EXISTS or a pattern comprehension).
