483.title: UNION, NEXT and CALL

484.body:
The errors of a CALL folder.name(..) of a saved query are found before the run and point at the call; they share one help text that explains the call (folder and name, positional arguments, YIELD, the standalone form, g.queries()), after a fix of their own: GQLSTATUS When 42002 no saved query of that name in that folder (with "did you mean" when it is in another folder); too many arguments, or too few for parameters without a default; a standalone call without parentheses whose parameter has no value; an in-query call without parentheses of a query with parameters; an in-query call of a query with columns without YIELD; YIELD of a column the query does not return, of a name already in scope or twice, YIELD on a query without RETURN; an aggregate in an argument; a saved query that calls itself, directly or through others 42001 YIELD * inside a query (only a standalone call takes it) 22G03 an argument that does not fit its parameter's schema (CALL people.older('x') for an integer) 0A000 a saved query written in Rhai (the help names g.query(..)); an argument that reads the row; a call inside EXISTS { }, COUNT { } or COLLECT { }; the vendor namespaces db, dbms, apoc, gds (refused); a read-only saved query that would write through a call 54001 saved queries that call each other more than 16 levels deep, or more than 1024 calls in one query and the queries it calls g.gql("CALL people.older(26) YIELD name RETURN name") // error: there is no saved query `older` in the folder `people`
g.gql("CALL db.labels()") // refused: procedure calls of the vendor namespaces are vendor extensions With the saved query people.older($min) of Saved Queries , returning name and age: Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 6: there is no saved query `older` in the folder `people` ...
Help: save it first with g.define_query(#{name: "older", folder: "people", language: "gql", body: ".."}); g.queries() lists the saved queries. CALL folder.name(args) runs the saved query `name` of the catalog folder `folder` (the segments before the name, joined by /; CALL name() calls one of the root folder), written in GQL. Its arguments are constants or $parameters, in the order its query first reads its parameters (a trailing one left out takes the parameter's default). YIELD names the columns of its RETURN the query reads after the call (YIELD a AS x renames one; each must be a new name), and a call alone is a whole query returning every column, as in g.define_query(#{name: "adults", folder: "people", language: "gql", body: "MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age >= $min RETURN p.name AS name", params: #{min: "integer"}}); g.gql("CALL people.adults(30) YIELD name RETURN name ORDER BY name"). g.queries() lists the saved queries with their folders and parameters; a saved query written in Rhai runs with g.query(name, #{..}). Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 6: there is no saved query `older` in the root folder: the saved query `older` is in the folder `people` ... did you mean: CALL people.older
Help: Did you mean CALL people.older? CALL folder.name(args) runs the saved query ... Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 22: too many arguments: people.older(min :: integer) takes 1 argument, 2 given ...
Error: GQL data exception at line 1, column 19: the argument for `min` of CALL people.older must be integer: Type mismatch on query 'older.min': expected int64, got string ... GQLSTATUS: 22G03 Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 25: CALL people.older inside a query names the columns it reads with YIELD: the saved query returns `name`, `age` ...
Help: add YIELD, as in CALL people.older(..) YIELD name, age. CALL folder.name(args) runs ... Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 27: `nope` is not a column of the saved query called by CALL people.older; it returns `name`, `age` ...
Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 46: YIELD * is allowed only in a standalone CALL (the whole query) ... Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 38: an argument of CALL people.older that reads the row is not yet supported (the variable s is not defined) ...
Help: pass a constant or a $parameter, or write the saved query's pattern in the query itself. CALL folder.name(args) runs ... Error: GQL construct not supported yet at line 1, column 6: the saved query `rh` is written in Rhai; CALL runs saved queries written in GQL in this version ...
Help: run it from the DSL with g.query("rh", #{..}), or save it again in GQL (language: "gql"). CALL folder.name(args) runs ... Error: GQL semantic error at line 1, column 6: recursive call of the saved query `a`: a calls b calls a (the arguments of a CALL are constants, so the recursion would never end) ... Error: GQL limit exceeded at line 1, column 6: saved queries call each other more than 16 levels deep (CALL q0 at the end of q16 -> q15 -> ... -> q1) ... GQLSTATUS: 54001
Help: Saved queries called with CALL nest at most 16 levels deep, and one query and the saved queries it calls hold at most 1024 calls in all. Call an inner saved query directly, as in g.gql("CALL people.adults(30) YIELD name RETURN name"), or write a part of the chain in the query itself; g.get_query(name) shows a saved query's body. Error: GQL unsupported construct at line 1, column 1: CALL: procedure calls are vendor extensions, not part of GQL ...
Help: write what the procedure does as Gremlin steps, for example g.v().label().dedup() instead of CALL db.labels(), or save it as a query in GQL and call that one, CALL folder.name(args), which runs a saved query of the graph's catalog. ... An error inside the called query keeps its own text and caret (under the saved query's text) and gains the line in saved query: "name".

485.body:
The forms a quantified path pattern does not take yet are refused before the run with 0A000; each help names the rewrite. A body variable is a new name (42002), and outside a quantified body it is a list, so a property of it is an error whose help offers the body's WHERE or a list comprehension: g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-[:knows]->{1,2}(y)){1,3} (b) RETURN b") // error: a quantified edge inside a parenthesized path pattern is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-->(y) WHERE y.age > a.age){1,3} (b) RETURN b") // error: a condition inside a parenthesized path pattern that reads a variable declared outside it is not yet supported
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((a)-->(y)){1,2} (b) RETURN b") // error: `a` is already bound; a variable of a quantified path pattern must be a new name
g.gql("MATCH (a) ((x)-->(y)){1,3} (b) RETURN x.name") // error: `x` is a group variable of the quantified path pattern Help: write the edge out as often as needed inside the parentheses, as in ((x)-->()-->(y)){1,3}, or quantify the edge outside them, as in MATCH (a)-[:knows]->{1,3}(b) RETURN b. ...
Help: compare the body's variables with each other, with values or with parameters inside it, as in ((x)-[e]->(y) WHERE e.weight > $w){1,3}, and test the outer variable in the WHERE of the MATCH clause. ...
Help: give the element inside its own variable: the node before a parenthesized path pattern is the first node of its first iteration and the node after it the last node of its last iteration, as in (a) ((x)-->(y)){1,3} (b). ...
Help: test each element inside the parenthesized path pattern, with WHERE x.name ... before its closing parenthesis, or read the list, as in [v IN x | v.name]. ... An unbounded quantified path pattern that reaches repeat.max_loops or traversal.max_traversers fails like a quantified edge (RepeatLimitExceeded, ResourceLimitExceeded, no GQLSTATUS), never with fewer rows, and its help names the pattern as the plan walks it : read back from the lowered repeat() body, so it shows each node's labels but not its variable (a node without a label is ()), each edge with its labels in the direction of the walk (the plan may walk the pattern from its far end), and a body of one edge with nothing on its nodes as the quantified edge it equals (-[:knows]->{1,}): g.with("repeat.max_loops", 1).gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) ((x:person)-[:knows]->(m)-[:created]->(y))+ (b) RETURN b.name AS b") // error: repeat() exceeded the loop limit of 1 iterations Help: The loop of the quantified path pattern ((:person)-[:knows]->()-[:created]->()){1,} of the gql() query ran 1 iterations, the limit of repeat.max_loops. A quantifier without an upper bound ({m,}, *, + or Cypher [*]) repeats the pattern until every path has used all the edges it can reach (trail), ... Give the quantifier an upper bound, as in ((:person)-[:knows]->()-[:created]->()){1,5}, ... Or raise the limit for the query, g.with("repeat.max_loops", 2).gql(..), ... A MATCH clause holds at most 64 edge patterns; an edge in a quantified body counts once, however often the body repeats, so the help of that limit names a quantified path pattern as one of the fixes: Help: split the pattern into several MATCH clauses that share a variable, for example MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(c) MATCH (c)-->(d)-->(e) RETURN e (edge uniqueness then holds within each clause only), repeat a chain as a quantified path pattern, whose body edges count once however often it repeats, for example MATCH (a) (()-->()){65} (z) RETURN z, or walk a long path with Gremlin repeat(), for example g.v().repeat(__.out()).times(100). The query is larger than gql() accepts.
485.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Errors » Quantified path patterns
485.title: Quantified path patterns

486.body:
An INSERT pattern that cannot create what it says fails before the run; its help shows the accepted form and ends with one shared paragraph on INSERT: g.gql("INSERT (a:x)-[:r]-(b:y)") // error: INSERT needs a direction; write -[e:T]-> or <-[e:T]-
g.gql("INSERT (:a)-[:r|s]->(:b)") // error: an edge in INSERT has exactly one label
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p:admin)") // error: the variable `p` is already bound
g.gql("INSERT (:x {a: 1, a: 2})") // error: the key `a` appears twice in this map
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (:x {n: count(p)})") // error: the aggregate function count() cannot be used in INSERT
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { INSERT (:a) } RETURN p") // error: INSERT inside EXISTS { }: a subquery expression or a comprehension cannot write Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 13: INSERT needs a direction; write -[e:T]-> or <-[e:T]- (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: INSERT (a:x)-[:r]-(b:y) ^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: give the new edge its direction, from the node before it (-[:r]->) or to it (<-[:r]-); for example g.gql("INSERT (a:person {name: 'ann'})-[:knows]->(b:person:admin)"). INSERT (Cypher CREATE) creates its pattern once for each row: a new node with the labels written, joined by & or :, and a property map; a new edge with a direction and exactly one label; and a variable bound before, written alone as (p), connects the existing node, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit&food {name: 'apple'}) RETURN f.name"). A query may end with the INSERT (it then returns no rows), and FOR gives it one row per item, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'bob'] INSERT (:person {name: n})"). To create a pattern only where it is missing, MERGE finds it or creates it, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'marko'] MERGE (:person {name: n})"). While the query runs, a row whose endpoint is NULL (22004) or no node (22G03), or whose property value is a node, an edge or a path (22G03), fails the query, and it changes nothing: g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (p:person {name: 'nobody'}) INSERT (p)-[:knows]->(:person)") // error: the source node `p` of the inserted `:knows` edge is NULL
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) INSERT (:x {v: p})") // error: the value of property `v` is a node Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 51: the source node `p` of the inserted `:knows` edge is NULL query: …person {name: 'nobody'}) INSERT (p)-[:knows]->(:person) ^^^ GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: keep only the rows where it is bound before the INSERT: FILTER p IS NOT NULL. A row of the data gave the marked endpoint of the new edge no node: an edge connects two nodes, so a variable that OPTIONAL MATCH may leave NULL is filtered first, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) FILTER s IS NOT NULL INSERT (p)-[:made]->(s)"), and a value that is no node is turned into one by a MATCH, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['lop'] MATCH (s:software {name: n}) INSERT (:review {stars: 5})-[:about]->(s)"). A schema violation of an INSERT is the schema's error, with a help line written for GQL: a missing required property names the INSERT map and coalesce(), a type mismatch the conversion function (toInteger(), ...) with a $parameter example ( Writing with GQL ). A bound node written with labels or properties (MATCH (p:person) INSERT (p:admin)) gets the SET that changes it, built from the query, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p:admin"), beside the Gremlin steps. The write clause that is not supported yet (FOREACH) is 0A000 with a help line naming the GQL form: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FOREACH (x IN [1] | SET p.k = x)") // error: FOREACH is not yet supported in this version Help: write FOR x IN <list> followed by the write clause, for example FOR name IN ['ann', 'bob'] INSERT (:person {name: name}). DELETE takes a list itself, as in MATCH p = (:person)-[:knows]->() DETACH DELETE nodes(p). This construct comes in a later version of gql(); until then, write the query without it or as Gremlin steps.
486.title: INSERT

487.body:
A SET / REMOVE item of the wrong form fails before the run: a label item joined by |, ! or % (42001), a label item on a variable known to be an edge, an aggregate in a value, or a target that is undefined, a LET / WITH value, a path, a group variable or a FOR position (42002); a deeper target such as p.a.b or head(l).k is not supported yet (0A000). Each help names the accepted form and ends with one shared paragraph on SET / REMOVE: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p:A|B") // error: `|` (a label alternative) cannot stand in SET
g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]->(b) SET e:met") // error: `e` is an edge: an edge has exactly one label
g.gql("MATCH (p) SET p.k = count(*)") // error: the aggregate function count() cannot be used in SET
g.gql("MATCH (p) SET p.a.b = 1") // error: `p.a.b` as a SET target is not yet supported in this version Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 24: `|` (a label alternative) cannot stand in SET: a label item names the labels, joined by `:` or `&` (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: MATCH (p:person) SET p:A|B ^^^ GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: write the labels, as in SET p:A:B. SET changes the nodes and edges of each row, item by item from left to right: n.k = <value> sets a property (a NULL value removes it), n = {map} replaces every property, n += {map} merges the map into them, and n:A:B adds labels to a node (an edge has exactly one label); REMOVE n.k removes a property and REMOVE n:A a label, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = p.age + 1, p:employee REMOVE p.nick RETURN p.age"). A variable that OPTIONAL MATCH leaves NULL is skipped, and a query may end with the SET or REMOVE (it then returns no rows), as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software) SET s += {open: true}").
Help: change the type of the edge with the Gremlin step set_label(), as in g.gql("MATCH (a)-[e:knows]->(b) RETURN e").select("e").set_label("met"). In a MATCH clause a node variable names one node ... While the query runs, a NULL right side of n = .. or n += .. (22004), a right side that is no map, node or edge, a node, edge or path as a property value, a target that holds no element, and a label item on a value that turns out to be an edge (22G03) fail the query, and it changes nothing. The help rewrites the failing query where it can: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = NULL") // error: the right side of SET p = .. is NULL, not a map
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.best = p") // error: the value of property `best` is a node
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = 1") // error: the right side of SET p = .. is a single value
g.gql("FOR x IN [1] SET x.k = 1") // error: SET changes a node or an edge, but `x` holds a value of type 'int64' Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 26: the right side of SET p = .. is NULL, not a map query: MATCH (p:person) SET p = NULL ^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: SET p = {} removes every property; to keep them when the map is NULL, give it the element's own properties as a default with coalesce($p, properties(p)), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p = coalesce(NULL, properties(p))"). A row of the data gave the marked SET or REMOVE item a value it cannot write; keep such rows away from it with FILTER or WHERE, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) FILTER p.age IS NOT NULL SET p.next = p.age + 1"). SET changes the nodes and edges of each row, ...
Help: store a value of it instead, such as its id, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) SET p.best = element_id(p)"), or its properties with properties(..). A row of the data gave the marked SET or REMOVE item a value it cannot write; ... A schema violation of a SET / REMOVE gets a help line written for GQL too: a type mismatch names the conversion function in a SET of the label and key, a removed required property (REMOVE, a NULL value, SET n = {map} without the key) the map that keeps it and +=, and a label whose required property the node lacks the SET that writes the key before the label.
487.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Errors » SET and REMOVE
487.title: SET and REMOVE

488.body:
A DELETE target that cannot hold an element fails before the run: a label test such as n:person or n IS person (42001: it is a boolean, and DELETE removes whole elements), a literal, a computed value, a map or a FOR position (42002). DROP n, the Gremlin step written as a clause, is a syntax error naming DETACH DELETE, and REMOVE n without an item names it too. Each help rewrites the failing query and ends with one shared paragraph on DELETE: g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n:person") // error: `n:person` is a label test (a boolean), not an element
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) DELETE 1 + 1") // error: `1 + 1` is a computed value, not a node, an edge, a path or a list of them
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) DROP p") // error: GQL has no DROP clause: DELETE removes nodes and edges Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 41: `n:person` is a label test (a boolean), not an element; DELETE removes whole nodes and edges (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n:person ^^^^^^^^ GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: delete the element itself with DELETE n, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) DELETE n"), or remove the label and keep the element with REMOVE n:person, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'vadas'}) REMOVE n:person"). DELETE removes, for each row, the nodes and edges its targets give: a node or edge variable, a path (all its nodes and edges) or a list of them; a NULL target is skipped, and an element given twice is removed once. A node that still has edges is removed only together with them: DETACH DELETE removes its edges too, as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'lop'}) DETACH DELETE s"). The rest of the query can no longer read what it deleted, so read what it needs first, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'vadas'}) WITH p, p.name AS name DETACH DELETE p RETURN name"); a query may end with the DELETE (it then returns no rows).
Help: name the element to remove by its variable, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person) DETACH DELETE n"). DELETE removes, for each row, ...
Help: write DETACH DELETE (the GQL form of the Gremlin step drop()), as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) DETACH DELETE p"). DELETE removes, for each row, ... While the query runs, a plain (or NODETACH) DELETE of a node that still has an edge the same clause does not delete fails with G1001; the help names DETACH DELETE in the failing query and the form that deletes the edges in the same clause. A target that turns out to hold no element (a WITH value, a property) is 22G03. Either failure changes nothing: g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DELETE n") // error: `n` is a node that still has edges
g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WITH 1 AS x DELETE x") // error: DELETE removes nodes, edges and paths, but `1` gives a number on this row Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 41: `n` is a node that still has edges, and DELETE removes only nodes without edges (besides the edges deleted in the same clause) query: MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DELETE n ^ GQLSTATUS: G1001
Help: remove the node together with its edges with DETACH DELETE, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE n"), or delete its edges in the same clause, as in g.gql("MATCH (s:software {name: 'ripple'})<-[r]-() DELETE r, s").
Help: give DELETE a node, an edge, a path or a list of them, and keep the rows where the target holds something else away from it with FILTER or WHERE, as in g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE n"). DELETE removes, for each row, ... After a DELETE, a later part of the query that reads a deleted element (a property, labels(), element_id(), a SET, REMOVE or INSERT on it) or returns it fails, and the query changes nothing. The error is the storage's (ElementRemoved), with a help line written for GQL: read what the query needs before the DELETE, for example with properties(n). count(n), n IS NULL and type(r) of a deleted edge still work, and a pattern from a deleted node matches nothing: g.gql("MATCH (n:software) DETACH DELETE n RETURN n.name") // error: the node was deleted earlier in this query
g.gql("MATCH ()-[r:created]->() DELETE r RETURN r.weight") // error: the edge was deleted earlier in this query Caused by: The vertex was removed earlier in this query; its id, label and value are no longer available
Help: The node was deleted earlier in this query (by DELETE or DETACH DELETE, or together with a node a DETACH DELETE removed), but a later part of the query still reads it: a deleted node has no properties, labels or id any more and cannot be returned or changed, and a pattern from it matches nothing; only count(n) and n IS NULL still work. Read what you need before the DELETE and keep that instead, for example g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH n, properties(n) AS p DETACH DELETE n RETURN p"), or run the DELETE as a separate query after reading.
Help: The edge was deleted earlier in this query (...); only count(r), r IS NULL and type(r) still work. Read what you need before the DELETE and keep that instead, for example g.gql("MATCH (:person)-[r:knows]->() WITH r, properties(r) AS p DELETE r RETURN p"), or for a node g.gql("MATCH (n:person {name: 'marko'}) WITH n, properties(n) AS p DETACH DELETE n RETURN p"), or run the DELETE as a separate query after reading.
488.title: DELETE

489.body:
A MERGE pattern that cannot be matched or created as written fails before the run: a second pattern after ,, an edge without its one label or with a label expression, a quantifier (42001); a node bound before written with labels or properties, a bound edge variable, and a pattern that is only a node bound before (MATCH (a) MERGE (a): nothing to find or create) (42002). Each help rewrites the failing query where it can and ends with one shared paragraph on MERGE: g.gql("MERGE (a:x), (b:y)") // error: MERGE takes exactly one pattern
g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a)") // error: MERGE (a) with `a` bound earlier has nothing to find or create
g.gql("MATCH (a:person) MERGE (a:admin)-[:r]->(:b)") // error: the variable `a` is already bound
g.gql("MERGE (a:x)-[:r|s]->(b)") // error: an edge in MERGE has exactly one label Error: GQL syntax error at line 1, column 12: MERGE takes exactly one pattern: a second pattern after `,` cannot stand here (step #1 'gql:error("42001")' refused the query before the traversal ran) at #1: v().gql:error("42001") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ query: MERGE (a:x), (b:y) ^ GQLSTATUS: 42001
Help: write one MERGE for each pattern, as in g.gql("MERGE (a:x) MERGE (b:y)"), or connect the patterns with an edge into one. MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: every match is a row, and when nothing matches the whole pattern is created, reusing the nodes bound before. Its one pattern has nodes with the labels written, joined by & or :, and a property map, edges with exactly one label (an edge without a direction matches either direction and is created from left to right), and a node bound before written alone, as (p); ON CREATE SET and ON MATCH SET items change what was created or matched, as in g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: 'ann'}) ON CREATE SET p.new = true ON MATCH SET p.new = false RETURN p.new"). Each row sees what the rows before it created, so FOR creates a repeated item once, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['ann', 'ann'] MERGE (:person {name: n})").
Help: to find or create a connection, give the pattern an edge, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a)-[:T]->(:Label)"); to find or create another node, give it its own name, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) MERGE (a2:Label)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: write (a) to connect the node, or give a new node its own name, as in MERGE (a)-[:T]->(a2:Label {k: 1}); to change the bound node itself use SET on it, as in g.gql("MATCH (a:person) SET a:admin"), or the Gremlin steps add_label() and property() on it, as in g.gql("MATCH (a) RETURN a").select("a").add_label("admin"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: give the new edge one label, as in -[:r]->; for example g.gql("MERGE (a:person {name: 'ann'})-[:knows]->(b:person:admin)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ... While the query runs, a property value of the pattern that is NULL (22004: MERGE can neither match nor create {k: NULL}, checked for each row before the match), a node bound before that is NULL (22004) or no node (22G03), and a node, edge or path as a property value (22G03) fail the query, and it changes nothing, also what earlier rows created. The help names the FILTER before the MERGE or the coalesce() default in the failing query: g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: x})") // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{k: NULL}`
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) MERGE (p)-[:made]->(s)") // error: the destination node `s` of the merged `:made` edge is NULL
g.gql("MERGE (p:person {name: NULL})") // error: MERGE cannot match or create `{name: NULL}` Caused by: GQL data exception at line 1, column 34: MERGE cannot match or create `{k: NULL}`: a property value is NULL query: FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: x}) ^ GQLSTATUS: 22004
Help: keep only the rows where it has a value with FILTER x IS NOT NULL before the MERGE, or give it a default with coalesce(), as in g.gql("FOR x IN [1, NULL] MERGE (:n {k: coalesce(x, 0)})"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: a property value that is NULL or a graph element, or a node bound before that is NULL or no node. A variable that OPTIONAL MATCH may leave NULL is filtered first, and a value that is no node is turned into one by a MATCH, as in g.gql("FOR n IN ['lop'] MATCH (s:software {name: n}) MERGE (:review {stars: 5})-[:about]->(s)"). MERGE looks for its whole pattern for each row: ...
Help: keep only the rows where it is bound before the MERGE: FILTER s IS NOT NULL, as in g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) FILTER s IS NOT NULL MERGE (p)-[:made]->(s)"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: ...
Help: MERGE matches and creates only property values that are not NULL: leave `name` out of the pattern, and find the elements that lack it with a MATCH, as in g.gql("MATCH (n) FILTER n.name IS NULL RETURN n"). A row of the data gave the marked part of the MERGE pattern a value it can neither match nor create: ... A schema violation of a MERGE gets a help line written for GQL too. One raised by the create names the MERGE pattern and keeps its node variable: a type mismatch the conversion function, as in g.gql("MERGE (p:person {w: toFloat($v)})", #{v: "1.5"}), and a missing required property the pattern's property map, because the ON CREATE SET items run after the create and cannot give it (or a "default" in the schema, to match on other keys only). One raised by an ON CREATE SET / ON MATCH SET item gets the SET fix in MERGE form, as in g.gql("MERGE (n:person) ON MATCH SET n.w = toFloat($v)", #{v: "1.5"}).
489.title: MERGE

491.title: In Rust

492.body:
gql() has no executor of its own. A query is parsed, its variables bound, a planner picks where each pattern starts and in which order it expands, and the result is lowered into an ordinary traversal plan: Gremlin steps (v(), has_label(), has(), out(), as(), where(), skip(), limit(), ...) plus a few internal steps. That plan then goes through the same optimizer , path analysis, property indexes, limits, cancellation, permissions and storages as a hand-written traversal. .profile() shows it. g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name AS name").profile() Step Call In Out
==================================================================================
v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
has("age", P.gt(30)) 1 4 2
gql:project("name") 1 2 2
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown (The profiles on this page leave out the time columns.) The query became v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(30)) plus a projection, and the optimizer folded the label into the scan, exactly as it does for the Gremlin form.
492.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Plans and Performance
492.title: Plans and Performance

493.body: Step Does gql:project("a", "b", ...) builds the row map of RETURN (or of a WITH that builds rows) in written order, keeping NULL columns gql:aggregate([keys], [aggregates], [columns]) groups the rows by the key values and builds one row map per group (a barrier) gql:distinct() DISTINCT on the row maps, with GQL's equality (1 = 1.0) gql:bind("p") continues the pattern from the element in a WITH column gql:trail("#1", ...) the trail check of a quantified edge or of an edge in the body of a quantified path pattern: the edge is none of the edges already bound under these labels gql:filter("<condition>") a WHERE condition, or the part of it that cannot become has(), with GQL's three-valued logic gql:order("<keys>") ORDER BY with GQL's NULL placement and type order; stable gql:not_self_loop() keeps a self-loop from matching twice in an either-direction edge gql:for("x IN <list>") FOR / UNWIND: one row per item of the list (unfold() with GQL's NULL rule); with an ordinal the row is the record of item and position gql:lookup("(n:label)", "<equality>") starts a pattern at the vertices an equality with a value of the row finds, by id ([id]) or through a property index ([index: vertex label.key]) gql:value("<expression>") the last step of a pattern comprehension's child: the value of its | part for one match, which the host step collects into the list gql:insert_node(["label", ...], "{props}") INSERT of one node: creates it per row, with all its properties in one storage call, and makes it the current element ( Writes ) gql:insert_edge("label", "from", "to", "{props}") INSERT of one edge between the nodes of the row named from and to ((#n) for an unnamed node of the pattern) gql:set("<items>"), gql:remove("<items>") one SET / REMOVE clause: applies its items per row to the elements the row's variables hold and passes the row on unchanged gql:delete("[DETACH] DELETE <targets>") one DELETE clause: collects the targets of every row, checks the NODETACH rule for the whole clause, removes the edges, then the nodes, and passes the rows on unchanged gql:merge("<pattern>", <search>, <creation>[, "ON CREATE SET ..", "ON MATCH SET .."]) one MERGE clause: per row, runs the search child (a MATCH of the pattern from the row) and emits a row per match, or runs the creation child (the insert chain) once; then its ON items gql:error("<GQLSTATUS>") the marker of a query that failed to parse or bind; raises the error before the run gql:filter, gql:project, gql:value, gql:order, gql:aggregate and gql:for may hold the bodies of the EXISTS, COUNT { } and COLLECT { } subqueries and pattern comprehensions their expressions contain as child traversals, shown as \> lines under the step ( EXISTS and pattern predicates , comprehensions , COUNT and COLLECT ). UNION and CALL need no step of their own: they are Gremlin's union(), flat_map() and optional() ( UNION, NEXT and CALL ). They exist only in plans of gql(); they are not DSL steps. Everything else in a GQL plan is an ordinary step.
493.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » The internal steps
493.title: The internal steps

494.body:
A WHERE condition is split at its top-level ANDs. A part of the form var.key <op> value, where the value is a literal or a $parameter, is pushed into has() right at the scan or the edge it reads, where the optimizer and the property indexes see it; the rest runs in gql:filter. Pushed: = (as P.eq), <, <=, >, >=, IN (with NULL items removed), STARTS WITH, ENDS WITH, CONTAINS with a string, IS NOT NULL. Never pushed: <>, IS NULL, OR, NOT, conditions over two variables, NULL or list operands: there the semantics of has() and GQL's three-valued logic differ. g.gql("MATCH (n:person) WHERE n.age > 30 AND n.name STARTS WITH 'j' RETURN n.name AS n").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (n) WHERE n.age <> 29 RETURN n.name AS n").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
has("name", TextP.starting_with("j")) 1 4 1
has("age", P.gt(30)) 1 1 1
gql:project("n") 1 1 1 v() 1 0 6
gql:filter("n.age <> 29") 1 6 3
gql:project("n") 1 3 3
494.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » What becomes has()
494.title: What becomes has()

495.body:
When a property index exists, the planner starts at the node with an indexed equality (or IN), then one with a label and a property condition, then one with a label, then the first node; and the property index rule of the optimizer serves the scan. A parameter works as well as a literal: { g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "name"}); g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: $n})-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS s ORDER BY s", #{n: "josh"}).to_list() } // #{"s": "lop"}, #{"s": "ripple"} v(labels: ["person"]) [index: vertex person.name] 1 0 1
has("name", P.eq("josh")) 1 1 1
out("created") 1 1 2
gql:project("s") 1 2 2
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown, property_index The planner reads only what every storage offers (statistics() and the index catalog), so a host's own storage gets the same plans.
495.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Index use
495.title: Index use

496.body:
An edge that is not named, filtered or read becomes a plain out("T") / in("T"), the cheapest form. A named, filtered or trail-checked edge becomes out_e("T") ... in_v(), with its filters on the edge in between. An either-direction edge is a union() of both directions with the self-loop guard: g.gql("MATCH (a:person)-[e:created]->(s) WHERE e.weight > 0.5 RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s ORDER BY a").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]-(b) RETURN b.name AS b").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
as("a") [path: labels(a)] 1 4 4
out_e("created") [path: labels(a)] 1 4 4
has("weight", P.gt(0.5)) [path: labels(a)] 1 4 1
in_v() [path: labels(a)] 1 1 1
gql:project("a", "s") 1 1 1
gql:order("a") 1 1 1 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
union(__.out("knows"), __.in_e("knows").gql:not_self_loop().out_v()) 1 4 4
gql:project("b") 1 4 4
496.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Edges: out() when nothing reads the edge
496.title: Edges: out() when nothing reads the edge

497.body: A variable gets a path label (as("a")) only when something reads it while the traversal has moved past it: a RETURN column of an earlier node, a join, a trail check, a condition over two variables. MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name records no path at all. The [path: ...] note in the profile shows what is recorded ( Path Requirement Analysis ). Return only what you need: each returned earlier variable is one more label per traverser.
497.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » as() only where needed
497.title: as() only where needed

498.body:
Between two hops the lowering places a lazy_barrier(), a merge point: traversers that reached the same vertex with the same recorded labels merge into one with a higher bulk, so the next hop runs once for all of them ( Bulk and Barriers ). The rows stay the same; the work shrinks. Here four authors (josh twice) become three traversers: g.gql("MATCH (s:software)<-[:created]-(p)<-[:knows]-(m) RETURN m.name AS m").profile() Step Call In Out Bulk
=======================================================================================
v(labels: ["software"]) 1 0 2 2
in("created") 1 2 4 4
lazy_barrier() 1 4 3 4
in("knows") 1 3 1 2
gql:project("m") 1 1 1 2 Merging needs equal labels, so it pays off where the middle node is not returned. Returning p labels it, and traversers at the same vertex still merge only with the same p. Trail checks and merging. The trail rule (an edge is bound once per MATCH) is checked with where(P.neq("#1")) against the earlier edge, which must therefore be labelled. When two edges of one MATCH can have the same label, the first is labelled and the traversers stay apart until the check has run. The planner skips the check when the label sets cannot overlap (-[:knows]-> then -[:created]->), so name edge labels in multi-hop patterns where you can: g.gql("MATCH (a)-[:created]->(s)<-[:created]-(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b").profile() v() 1 0 6
as("a") [path: labels(a)] 1 6 6
out_e("created") [path: labels(a)] 1 6 4
as("#1") [path: labels(#1,a)] 1 4 4
in_v() [path: labels(#1,a)] 1 4 4
lazy_barrier() [path: labels(#1,a)] 1 4 4
in_e("created") [path: labels(#1,a)] 1 4 10
where(P.neq("#1")) [path: labels(a)] 1 10 6
out_v() [path: labels(a)] 1 6 6
gql:project("a", "b") 1 6 6
498.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Merge points
498.title: Merge points

499.body:
Patterns that share no variable (MATCH (a:person), (s:software)) are a Cartesian product, built with a second v() in the middle of the traversal. The optimizer does not fold labels or use indexes for a v() there yet, so the second scan runs in full once per row of the first: g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (s:software) RETURN a.name AS a, s.name AS s").profile() v(labels: ["software"]) 1 0 2
as("s") [path: labels(s)] 1 2 2
v() [path: labels(s)] 1 2 12
has_label("person") [path: labels(s)] 1 12 8
gql:project("a", "s") 1 8 8 A pattern after the first with an equality an id or index serves is the exception: it starts with a gql:lookup instead of the second v(). Otherwise, connect patterns through a shared variable where the question allows it; the planner prefers connected patterns and starts the product at the smaller side. The same holds for a pattern after a WITH or inside an OPTIONAL MATCH that shares no variable with what came before, and for a leading OPTIONAL MATCH (its scan runs inside optional()).
499.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Disconnected patterns are not optimized yet
499.title: Disconnected patterns are not optimized yet

5.body: The command-line tool graphersal (the one-shot query runner, the REPL, the dev server and the graphersal store commands) comes as a prebuilt binary for Linux, macOS and Windows, or builds from source with Cargo. The engine is also a Python package and a Rust crate. To only try it, nothing has to be installed: the playground runs in the browser.
5.title: Installation

50.body: Graphersal comes with the several key features. Feature Description io Reads and writes graph files: GraphSON 3.0 (TinkerPop's format; values keep their types, dates and other types Graphersal cannot hold are skipped with a report) and GraphML. GraphML values are written as their plain text (a UUID as its canonical string, arrays and objects as JSON text); logical types (uuid, array, object) are restored on import only from the schema stored in the target graph, so set the schema first. GraphML never carries the schema; it travels as its own JSON. serde Converts between plain JSON and Graphersal values (a UUID is written as its canonical string), and reads/writes schema files. script Graphersal also supports a Domain Specific Language (DSL) for scripting based on the Rhai library. The math() step does not need it: its equations run on Graphersal's own expression engine in every build (see Math Expressions ). gql GQL queries (experimental): GraphTraversalSource::gql / gql_with run ISO GQL queries (MATCH ... WHERE ... RETURN ..., INSERT, SET, REMOVE, DELETE, Cypher's MERGE, Cypher spellings as aliases) as ordinary traversals; with script also g.gql(..) in the DSL. No dependencies. persist Graphersal's own lossless binary format: packed snapshots (.gsnap), a write-ahead journal with recovery, and the Store (one directory or one .gstore file = one graph, durable commits, point in time, fork, rollback, backups, repair). See Persistence . persist-zstd zstd-compressed snapshot chunks on top of persist (pure Rust). persist-zip ZIP backup archives of a Store on top of persist. model2vec The embedder vector::Model2Vec: a Model2Vec static embedding model loaded from a local directory (never the network), through model2vec-rs and tokenizers (pure Rust). Native targets only; the graphersal CLI has it on by default.
50.title: Supported Features

500.body:
LET, FILTER and a WITH that only passes values on add no steps: the planner treats their names as the expressions they stand for and their conditions like WHERE, so a condition on a LET value can still become has() where it reads a property directly, and the plan is that of the same query written without them: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) LET d = p.age / 10 FILTER d = 3 AND p.name STARTS WITH 'j' RETURN p.name AS name").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
has("name", TextP.starting_with("j")) 1 4 1
gql:filter("d = 3") 1 1 1
gql:project("name") 1 1 1 A WITH with DISTINCT, an aggregate, ORDER BY, OFFSET or LIMIT builds its rows with the same steps as a RETURN. When a later clause reads them, the row is labelled once (#w1) and gql:bind moves to the element of a column to continue the pattern; the barrier starts fresh paths, so nothing recorded before it is carried on: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WITH p ORDER BY p.age DESC LIMIT 2 MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, s.name AS sw").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
as("p") [path: labels(p)] 1 4 4
gql:project("p") [path: labels(p)] 1 4 4
gql:order("p.age DESC") 1 4 4
limit(2) 1 4 2
as("#w1") [path: labels(#w1)] 1 2 2
gql:bind("p") [path: labels(#w1)] 1 2 2
out("created") [path: labels(#w1)] 1 2 3
gql:project("name", "sw") 1 3 3
500.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » LET, FILTER and WITH
500.title: LET, FILTER and WITH

501.body:
FOR (and UNWIND) becomes one gql:for step; the item is the current object of each row, and as("x") labels it only when a later step reads it after the row moved on. A query that does not start with MATCH starts from one empty row, inject(0): g.gql("FOR x IN [10, 20] WITH ORDINALITY i RETURN x, i").profile() inject(0) 1 0 1
gql:for("x IN [10, 20] WITH ORDINALITY i") 1 1 2
gql:project("x", "i") 1 2 2 A MATCH after FOR runs once per row. Without help that is a scan per item, so a list of 1000 names reads the whole label 1000 times: g.gql("FOR n IN $names MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age AS age", #{names: ["vadas", "marko", "nobody"]}).profile() inject(0) 1 0 1
gql:for("n IN $names") 1 1 3
as("n") [path: labels(n)] 1 3 3
v() [path: labels(n)] 1 3 18
has_label("person") [path: labels(n)] 1 18 12
gql:filter("name: n") [path: labels(n)] 1 12 2
gql:project("n", "age") 1 2 2 When an equality between the pattern's vertex and a value of the row can be answered directly, the planner starts the pattern with gql:lookup instead: by element id always (element_id(n) = id, either operand order), by a property ({name: n}, n.name = x) when a property index on that key exists for every label of the node. Each row then reads only the vertices the value finds: g.gql("FOR id IN $ids MATCH (n) WHERE element_id(n) = id RETURN id, n.name AS name", #{ids: ["1", "3", "42"]}).profile() inject(0) 1 0 1
gql:for("id IN $ids") 1 1 3
as("id") [path: labels(id)] 1 3 3
gql:lookup("(n)", "element_id(n) = id") [id] [path: labels(id)] 1 3 2
gql:project("id", "name") 1 2 2 { g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "name"}); g.gql("FOR n IN $names MATCH (p:person {name: n}) RETURN n, p.age AS age", #{names: ["vadas", "marko", "nobody"]}).profile() } inject(0) 1 0 1
gql:for("n IN $names") 1 1 3
as("n") [path: labels(n)] 1 3 3
gql:lookup("(p:person)", "name: n") [index: vertex person.name] [path: labels(n)] 1 3 2
has_label("person") [path: labels(n)] 1 2 2
gql:project("n", "age") 1 2 2 The lookup checks every vertex it finds with GQL's =, so it returns exactly the rows of the scan ( Semantics ); a NULL value finds nothing, and a value an index cannot serve (a list, NaN, a non-string id, a storage that reports no index) falls back to scanning the label. The same lookup starts any pattern that is not the first one: a second, disconnected pattern with an indexed equality (MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}), (b:person) WHERE b.age = a.age + 3 with an index on person.age), or a MATCH after a WITH. The first pattern of a query is never a lookup: it is a scan the optimizer serves with the index as usual. Edges are not looked up (an equality on element_id(e) stays a filter).
501.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » FOR and the correlated lookup
501.title: FOR and the correlated lookup

502.body:
An aggregating RETURN (or WITH) becomes one gql:aggregate in place of gql:project. It does not use Gremlin's group() / count() / fold(), whose rules for missing values and empty input differ from GQL's ( Semantics ). It counts a merged traverser by its bulk, so merge points before it save work without changing a count: g.gql("MATCH (s:software)<-[:created]-(p) RETURN s.name AS sw, count(p) AS authors ORDER BY sw").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN DISTINCT p.age > 30 AS old").profile() v(labels: ["software"]) 1 0 2
as("s") [path: labels(s)] 1 2 2
in("created") [path: labels(s)] 1 2 4
gql:aggregate(["s.name"], ["count(p)"], ["sw", "authors"]) 1 4 2
gql:order("sw") 1 2 2 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("old") 1 4 4
gql:distinct() 1 4 2
502.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Aggregation
502.title: Aggregation

503.body:
An OPTIONAL MATCH is Gremlin's optional() around the lowered part, its WHERE inside. Where the part does not match, the row continues unchanged and the labels set inside are absent, which reads as NULL. A leading OPTIONAL MATCH starts from one row, inject(0): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN p.name AS name, count(s) AS n").profile()
g.gql("OPTIONAL MATCH (n:robot) RETURN n").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) [path: labels(s)] 1 0 4
as("p") [path: labels(p,s)] 1 4 4
optional(__.out("created").as("s")) [path: labels(p,s)] 1 4 5 \> out("created") [path: labels(p)] 4 4 4 \> as("s") [path: labels(p,s)] 4 4 4
gql:aggregate(["p.name"], ["count(s)"], ["name", "n"]) 1 5 4 inject(0) [path: labels(n)] 1 0 1
optional(__.v(labels: ["robot"]).as("n")) [path: labels(n)] 1 1 1 \> v(labels: ["robot"]) 1 1 0 \> as("n") [path: labels(n)] 1 0 0
gql:project("n") 1 1 1 After an optional part every later read goes through a label, since the current element differs between the rows that matched and those that did not.
503.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » OPTIONAL MATCH
503.title: OPTIONAL MATCH

504.body:
A quantified edge is a repeat() of the single edge, with emit() and times() for its bounds: {1,2} is repeat(..).emit().times(2), {0,n} emit().repeat(..).times(n), {n} repeat(..).times(n), {m,n} with m > 1 emit(__.loops().is(P.gte(m))), an unbounded one has no times(). Inside the loop each edge is labelled and checked with gql:trail against the edges of the match so far (trail): g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows|created]->{1,2}(b) RETURN b.name AS b").profile() v() [path: labels(#1)] 1 0 6
has("name", P.eq("marko")) [path: labels(#1)] 1 6 1
repeat(__.out_e("knows", "created").gql:trail("#1").as("#1").in_v()).times(2).emit() 1 1 5
[loops: 2, max_depth: 2, avg_loops: 1.4] \> out_e("knows", "created") [path: labels(#1)] 2 4 5 \> gql:trail("#1") [path: labels(#1)] 2 5 5 \> as("#1") [path: labels(#1)] 2 5 5 \> in_v() [path: labels(#1)] 2 5 5
gql:project("b") 1 5 5 The labels keep the traversers of different matches apart, so there is no merge point after a quantified edge: a quantified pattern costs more than the plain repeat() that ignores trail. The plan never records full paths ([path: labels(..)], never full).
504.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Quantified edges
504.title: Quantified edges

505.body:
A quantified path pattern is a repeat() of its whole body, with the same emit() / times() modulators as a quantified edge. Inside the loop each body edge is labelled and checked with gql:trail against every edge of the match so far that could be the same edge (the earlier iterations of each body edge, the other body edges, the edges of the clause outside), and each body variable the query reads is labelled with as(): the list of a group variable is read back from those labels, one per iteration. The plan records labels only, never full paths: g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'marko'}) ((x)-[e:knows]->(m)-[f:created]->(y)){1,2} (b) RETURN b.name AS b, [n IN m | n.name] AS via").profile() {p1} The two gql:trail steps check one label each here: a knows edge can never be a created edge. A body condition on one element runs where it is matched, as a has() or gql:filter; one that reads several body elements runs as a gql:filter at the end of the body, in every iteration. ? is emit().repeat(B).times(1) and a body without a quantifier is inlined, its steps run once in the plan as if the parentheses were not there: g.gql("MATCH (a {name: 'josh'}) ((x)-[:created]->(s))? (q) RETURN s.name AS s, q.name AS q").profile()
g.gql("MATCH ((x:person)-[:created]->(s) WHERE s.name = 'ripple') RETURN x.name AS who").profile() {p2} {p3} The planner may walk a quantified path pattern from its far end when that end is the cheaper start (a label, an indexed property); the body then runs in reverse, and the group lists are still given in the order the text reads.
505.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Quantified path patterns
505.title: Quantified path patterns

506.body:
A path variable is assembled from labels, not from Gremlin's path() (which would record the full path at every step): every element of the named pattern is labelled, and for a quantified edge also the vertices inside the loop (#gv..): g.gql("MATCH p = (a {name: 'marko'})-[:knows]->{1,2}(b) RETURN p").profile() v() [path: labels(#2,#gv2)] 1 0 6
has("name", P.eq("marko")) [path: labels(#2,#gv2)] 1 6 1
as("a") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 1 1 1
repeat(__.out_e("knows").gql:trail("#2").as("#2").in_v().as("#gv2")).times(2).emit() [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 1 1 2
[loops: 2, max_depth: 2, avg_loops: 1.0] \> out_e("knows") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 2 3 2 \> gql:trail("#2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 2 2 2 \> as("#2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 2 2 2 \> in_v() [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 2 2 2 \> as("#gv2") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a)] 2 2 2
as("b") [path: labels(#2,#gv2,a,b)] 1 2 2
gql:project("p") 1 2 2 A path variable that nothing reads labels nothing.
506.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Path variables
506.title: Path variables

507.body:
A subquery is lowered in one of two ways. The fast path. A [NOT] EXISTS (or pattern predicate) that is a condition of its own in a WHERE or FILTER (alone, or joined to the others by AND) becomes Gremlin's filter(__.<body>) or not(__.<body>), the step Gremlin's where(__..) / not(__..) would run. The body starts where the row stands: a body that starts at the element the row is on needs no step and no label, so the "who has no ..." question is exactly its Gremlin twin: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE NOT (p)-[:created]->() RETURN p.name AS name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (a:person), (b:person) WHERE (a)-[:knows]->(b) RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (s:software) WHERE EXISTS { (p:person) WHERE p.age > 33 } RETURN s.name AS s").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
not(__.out("created")) 1 4 1 \> out("created") 4 4 4
gql:project("name") 1 1 1 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
as("a") [path: labels(a)] 1 4 4
v() [path: labels(a)] 1 4 24
has_label("person") [path: labels(a)] 1 24 16
filter(__.in("knows").where(P.eq("a"))) [path: labels(a)] 1 16 2 \> in("knows") [path: labels(a)] 16 16 8 \> where(P.eq("a")) 8 8 2
gql:project("a", "b") 1 2 2 v(labels: ["software"]) 1 0 2
filter(__.v(labels: ["person"]).has("age", P.gt(33))) 1 2 2 \> v(labels: ["person"]) 2 2 8 \> has("age", P.gt(33)) 2 8 2
gql:project("s") 1 2 2 A body that reads a second imported variable joins it with where(P.eq("a")) (or starts from it with select(), or with gql:bind from a WITH column); a body that imports nothing starts with its own scan, which the optimizer folds and pushes down as anywhere else. The optimizer treats the child like any Gremlin child: between two hops it may add a lazy_barrier(), as it does for where(__.out("knows").out("created")). The expression hook. Anywhere else (under OR, XOR, CASE, in a RETURN or WITH column, an ORDER BY key, an aggregate, a FOR list) the gql:* step that evaluates the expression holds the body as a child and runs it when the evaluation of a row needs the answer: the Call and In columns of the child show how many rows ran it. Here only the two rows that p.age > 30 did not already decide ran in("knows"): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 OR (p)<-[:knows]-() RETURN p.name AS name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, EXISTS { (p)-[:knows]->() } AS knows").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:filter("p.age > 30 OR (p)<-[:knows]-()") 1 4 3 \> in("knows") 2 2 1
gql:project("name") 1 3 3 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("name", "knows") 1 4 4 \> out("knows") 4 4 2 Both forms run the same body, so they give the same rows. On an element, the subquery steps come last ( Semantics ): after the pushed has() and the plain gql:filter, and after the element's as(), so a body that reads the element through its label (a second body clause starting at it) finds it: g.gql("MATCH (a:person) WHERE CASE WHEN EXISTS { MATCH (a)<-[:knows]-() MATCH (a)--() } THEN true ELSE false END RETURN a.name AS name ORDER BY name").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
as("a") [path: labels(a)] 1 4 4
gql:filter("CASE WHEN EXISTS { MATCH (a)<-[:knows]-() MATCH (a)--() } THEN t…" (82 chars)) 1 4 2 \> in("knows") [path: labels(a)] 4 4 2 \> select("a") 2 2 2 \> union(__.out(), __.in_e().gql:not_self_loop().out_v()) 2 2 4
...
gql:project("name") 1 2 2
gql:order("name") 1 2 2 The global optimizer rule filter_reorder may still move a fast-path child before a gql:filter by its cost estimate (WHERE NOT (p)-->() AND p.name <> 'x' runs not(__.out()) before gql:filter("p.name <> 'x'")), as it would in a Gremlin plan; the rows are the same.
507.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » EXISTS and pattern predicates
507.title: EXISTS and pattern predicates

508.body:
A map projection and a list comprehension add no step: the gql:* step that evaluates the expression builds the map or the list from the row's values, with no allocation per item beyond the result. g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, .age} AS m, [x IN [p.age, 30] WHERE x > 28] AS l").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("m", "l") 1 4 4 A pattern comprehension is a subquery that collects: like an EXISTS in an expression, its body is a child of the step evaluating it, and the child ends in gql:value(..), the value of the | part per match. The host runs it once per row that reaches it and builds the list from the child's results (here 4 rows ran out("knows"), which found 2 friends), the plan of its Gremlin twin project(..).by(__.out("knows").values("name").fold()): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, [(p)-[:knows]->(f) | f.name] AS friends").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p {.name, projects: [(p)-[:created]->(s) | s {.name, n: size([(s)<-[:created]-(c) | c])}]} AS m").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("name", "friends") 1 4 4 \> out("knows") 4 4 2 \> gql:value("f.name") 4 2 2 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("m") 1 4 4 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> gql:value("s {.name, n: size([(s)<-[:created]-(c) | c])}") 4 4 4 \> in("created") 4 4 10 \> gql:value("c") 4 10 10 A comprehension nested in the | part is a child of the inner gql:value, so it runs once per match of the outer pattern: nested comprehensions from the same element multiply the work, as nested Gremlin fold() children do ( Semantics ). The collected list is checked against the limits before it is built ( Limits ).
508.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Map projections and comprehensions
508.title: Map projections and comprehensions

509.body:
COUNT { } and COLLECT { } are hosted like an EXISTS in an expression: the step evaluating the expression holds the body as its child and runs it once per row that reaches it. A COUNT child ends in count(), which counts the body's traversers with their bulk, and a COLLECT child in gql:value(..), the RETURN item, which the host collects in arrival order (after the body's own gql:order). A COUNT body whose RETURN only projects keeps its gql:project, which count() never reads, so its items are not evaluated ( Semantics ): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS who, COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } AS n").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS who, COLLECT { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name ORDER BY s.name } AS sw").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } > 1 RETURN p.name AS who").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("who", "n") 1 4 4 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> count() 4 4 4 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:project("who", "sw") 1 4 4 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> gql:project("s.name") 4 4 4 \> gql:order("s.name") 4 4 4 \> gql:value("s.name") 4 4 4 v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
gql:filter("COUNT { (p)-[:created]->() } > 1") 1 4 1 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> count() 4 4 4
gql:project("who") 1 1 1 A whole-query body (WITH, an aggregate, RETURN) is lowered like a top-level query onto the child, so an EXISTS with one keeps the fast path when it stands alone in a WHERE; the child ends in the body's own steps, and filter() asks only whether one traverser comes out: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) WITH count(s) AS c WHERE c > 1 RETURN c } RETURN p.name AS who").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
filter(__.out("created").gql:aggregate([], ["count(s)"], ["c"]).gql:filter("c > 1").gql:project("c")) 1 4 1 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> gql:aggregate([], ["count(s)"], ["c"]) 4 4 4 \> gql:filter("c > 1") 4 4 1 \> gql:project("c") 4 1 1
gql:project("who") 1 1 1 A body that starts from an import with an equality the id or a property index serves starts with gql:lookup, as a later pattern of the query does ( FOR and the correlated lookup ); this holds for EXISTS, COUNT, COLLECT, pattern comprehensions and CALL bodies alike.
509.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » COUNT and COLLECT
509.title: COUNT and COLLECT

510.body:
UNION is Gremlin's union() as the start step: each operand is lowered onto its own child exactly as a query of its own, so its scan keeps the label, the pushed has() and an index, and UNION (not ALL) adds gql:distinct() after it. Each operand's ORDER BY and LIMIT stay inside its child: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) WHERE p.age > 30 RETURN p.name AS name UNION MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name").profile() union(__.v(labels: ["person"]).has("age", P.gt(30)).gql:project("name"), __.v(labels: ["software"]).gql:project("name")) 1 1 4 \> v(labels: ["person"]) 1 1 4 \> has("age", P.gt(30)) 1 4 2 \> gql:project("name") 1 2 2 \> v(labels: ["software"]) 1 1 2 \> gql:project("name") 1 2 2
gql:distinct() 1 4 4 NEXT adds no step. After a plain query it is the WITH of the same items, so it gives the same plan (here the FILTER after NEXT became the has() of the scan); after a UNION the next statement continues from the union's row maps: g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.age AS age NEXT FILTER age > 30 RETURN name").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.name AS name UNION ALL MATCH (s:software) RETURN s.name AS name NEXT RETURN name ORDER BY name LIMIT 3").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
has("age", P.gt(30)) 1 4 2
gql:project("name") 1 2 2 union(__.v(labels: ["person"]).gql:project("name"), __.v(labels: ["software"]).gql:project("name")) 1 1 6 \> v(labels: ["person"]) 1 1 4 \> gql:project("name") 1 4 4 \> v(labels: ["software"]) 1 1 2 \> gql:project("name") 1 2 2
gql:project("name") 1 6 6
gql:order("name") 1 6 6
limit(3) 1 6 3 CALL is flat_map(__.<body>): the body is lowered onto the child from the row's current element, so a body that continues from an import needs no step to reach it, and its gql:order and limit() run per call (Call 4: once per person). OPTIONAL CALL wraps it in optional(..) and labels the body's row (as("#c<k>")) so a row without results reads NULL columns. After a CALL, the outer variables are read through their labels (as("p")): g.gql("MATCH (p:person) CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[e:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS top ORDER BY e.weight DESC LIMIT 1 } RETURN p.name AS who, top").profile()
g.gql("MATCH (p:person) OPTIONAL CALL (p) { MATCH (p)-[:created]->(s) RETURN s.name AS sw } RETURN p.name AS who, sw").profile() v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
as("p") [path: labels(p)] 1 4 4
flat_map(__.out_e("created").as("e").in_v().gql:project("top").gql:order("e.weight DESC").limit(1)) [path: labels(p)] 1 4 3 \> out_e("created") 4 4 4 \> as("e") [path: labels(e)] 4 4 4 \> in_v() [path: labels(e)] 4 4 4 \> gql:project("top") [path: labels(e)] 4 4 4 \> gql:order("e.weight DESC") 4 4 4 \> limit(1) 4 4 3
gql:project("who", "top") 1 3 3 v(labels: ["person"]) [path: labels(#c2)] 1 0 4
as("p") [path: labels(#c2,p)] 1 4 4
optional(__.flat_map(__.out("created").gql:project("sw")).as("#c2")) [path: labels(#c2,p)] 1 4 5 \> flat_map(__.out("created").gql:project("sw")) [path: labels(p)] 4 4 4 \> out("created") 4 4 4 \> gql:project("sw") 4 4 4 \> as("#c2") [path: labels(#c2,p)] 4 4 4
gql:project("who", "sw") 1 5 5 flat_map() builds the results of one call before the first moves on, so an outer LIMIT does not shorten a call that has started ( Semantics ); a body that imports nothing still runs once per row. A UNION or NEXT inside a body is a union() or the next steps inside the flat_map child, run per row.
510.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » UNION, NEXT and CALL
510.title: UNION, NEXT and CALL

511.body:
An INSERT becomes one gql:insert_node per new node and then one gql:insert_edge per new edge, in text order; a query that ends in a write ends with discard(), which drops the rows. A leading INSERT starts from one empty row, inject(0): g.gql("INSERT (:city {name: 'Berlin'})").profile() Step Call In Out
==================================================================================
inject(0) 1 0 1
gql:insert_node(["city"], "{name: 'Berlin'}") 1 1 1
discard() 1 1 0 After a MATCH, the variables the insert reads are labelled with as(): g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) INSERT (p)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'})").profile() Step Call In Out
=====================================================================================
v(labels: ["person"]) 1 0 4
has("name", P.eq("marko")) 1 4 1
as("p") [path: labels(p)] 1 1 1
gql:insert_node(["fruit"], "{name: 'apple'}") [path: labels(p)] 1 1 1
gql:insert_edge("likes", "p", "f") 1 1 1
discard() 1 1 0
Optimizer rules applied: source_filter_pushdown A SET or REMOVE clause becomes one gql:set / gql:remove step with its items as written; the variables it changes are labelled with as() before it, like those an insert reads: g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) SET p.age = p.age + 1, p:admin").profile() A DELETE clause becomes one gql:delete step with the clause as written. It is a barrier: it takes every row before it removes anything, so the NODETACH check sees the whole clause: g.gql("MATCH (p:person {name: 'marko'}) DETACH DELETE p").profile() A MERGE clause becomes one gql:merge step holding two children, shown as \> lines: the search, planned like a MATCH of the pattern that starts from a bound node of the row (or from a lookup by id or a property index), and the creation, the insert chain of the pattern; both end in the same gql:project of the pattern's variables, so a found and a created row look alike: g.gql("MATCH (a:person {name: 'marko'}) MERGE (a)-[:likes]->(f:fruit {name: 'apple'})").profile() A plan that writes never merges traversers, so the lowering places no merge points in it; a lazy_barrier() the optimizer adds between two hops passes every traverser on unmerged (In = Out). The write steps run only after the steps before them consumed their whole input, which is what makes the visibility rule of Semantics hold. A CALL body that ends in a write is optional(__.<body>.discard()): it runs per row and keeps the row.
511.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Writes
511.title: Writes

512.body: A GQL query is a traversal, so everything that bounds a traversal bounds it too: resource limits and query limits , cancellation, the memory budget, and the permission check, which sees the reads and writes of the lowered plan (an INSERT asks Create per new label, like add_v() and add_e(), a SET or REMOVE Update like property(); Writing with GQL ): reading a denied label through gql() is refused as the equivalent Gremlin is (also a label reached only through a quantified edge, the body of a quantified path pattern or an optional part, or only inside an EXISTS, COUNT or COLLECT body, a pattern comprehension, a CALL body or a later UNION operand, whichever way it is lowered: a subquery's child is checked like a Gremlin child, even when no row reaches it). An unbounded quantifier (on an edge or a path pattern) is bounded by repeat.max_loops and traversal.max_traversers ( Semantics ), also inside a subquery. The list of a pattern comprehension expands the bulk of its child's results under bulk.max_expansion and is checked against traversal.max_materialized_bytes and the memory budget before it is built, like collect_list(). The parser bounds nesting (128 levels, 54001) so no query can exhaust the stack, CALL bodies and whole-query subquery bodies nest at most 16 levels, and a query holds at most 64 subqueries (pattern comprehensions, COUNT { } and COLLECT { } included; CALL bodies are not counted) and runs at most 1024 subquery bodies ( Errors ).
512.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » Plans and Performance » Limits, cancellation, permissions
512.title: Limits, cancellation, permissions

513.body: This page lists which parts of ISO/IEC 39075 (GQL) gql() supports, in the style of the conformance appendices that GQL implementations publish. It is maintained by hand together with the code; when a construct lands, its row moves here in the same change. GQL names its optional features with identifiers such as G036 (graph pattern features), GQ.. (query features), GE.. (expressions), GF.. (functions), GA.. (additional behaviour), GB.. (lexical), GL.. (literals), GH.. (other). This page cites only those identifiers and short descriptive names of our own; it does not reproduce the standard. An identifier marked (provisional) could not be checked against the standard text yet and may be corrected. How far the Cypher compatibility forms agree with Neo4j's behaviour is measured against the openCypher TCK: TCK Compliance . Status: supported , partial (what is missing is named), not yet (planned), no (refused for good; see Refused Constructs ).
513.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » GQL Conformance » GQL Conformance
513.title: GQL Conformance

514.body: The mandatory core of a GQL query, by construct. Construct Status Notes MATCH with node and edge patterns, comma-separated patterns, several MATCH clauses supported trail (DIFFERENT EDGES) match mode per clause WHERE after MATCH, inline WHERE and property maps in element patterns supported RETURN, RETURN *, RETURN DISTINCT, AS supported RETURN is mandatory unless the last clause writes; FINISH ends a query without a result ORDER BY ... ASC / DESC supported NULL last ascending, first descending label expressions &, |, !, ( ) supported property reference x.key supported comparison, AND / OR / NOT, IS [NOT] NULL supported three-valued logic arithmetic + - * / %, string concatenation || supported simple and searched CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF supported UPPER, LOWER, CHAR_LENGTH / CHARACTER_LENGTH, LEFT, RIGHT, TRIM(s) supported TRIM removes spaces by default; NORMALIZE not yet BYTE_LENGTH / OCTET_LENGTH of a character string supported the number of UTF-8 bytes; Graphersal has no byte strings list trim TRIM(list, n) supported drops the last n items parameters $name supported values only, never text aggregate functions COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COLLECT_LIST, with DISTINCT supported implicit grouping by the items without an aggregate; Cypher collect alias binary set functions PERCENTILE_CONT, PERCENTILE_DISC supported value first, then the percentile (0.0 to 1.0, 22003 outside); Cypher percentileCont / percentileDisc aliases (stage 3f) OPTIONAL MATCH supported also as the first clause EXISTS predicate: EXISTS { MATCH ... }, EXISTS { <pattern> }, EXISTS ( ... ) (provisional: whether the standard makes it core or an optional feature, and its identifier, are still to be checked) supported anywhere an expression stands, nested too; TRUE or FALSE, never NULL; the body is a pattern, MATCH clauses, or a whole query ending in RETURN ( EXISTS ); Cypher pattern predicates as aliases Cypher WITH supported not GQL; accepted with Cypher's meaning ( Cypher Aliases ) record constructor {k: expr, ...} / RECORD {k: expr, ...} and list value constructor [a, b] supported RECORD is contextual: a variable named record stays usable, back-quoted before a projection that starts with key: or is empty ( Expressions ) Cypher map projections p {.k, .*, x, k: expr}, list comprehensions [x IN l WHERE c | e], pattern comprehensions [(a)-->(b) WHERE c | e] supported not GQL; 516.body: Where the standard leaves a choice to the implementation, gql() makes this one (Neo4j's, where it has one): Topic Choice NULL in ORDER BY last ascending, first descending order of values of different types map, vertex, edge, list, date/time, UUID, string, boolean, number, vector, NULL row order without ORDER BY unspecified item order of a pattern comprehension unspecified: the order the matches are found, which depends on the plan item order of COLLECT { } the order of the body's rows: its ORDER BY when it has one, unspecified otherwise UNION operands with the same column names in another order accepted, matched by name; the result has the first operand's column order (provisional) order of the rows of a UNION unspecified, also when the operands are sorted: sort after NEXT a CALL body that imports nothing still run once per incoming row; its rows are not cached the RETURN items of a projecting COUNT { } body not evaluated: the rows are counted, an expression that would fail raises no error (a deviation, Semantics ) a comprehension variable named like another variable of the query an error (42002) for a name in scope or one a LET / WITH value in scope still reads (stricter than Neo4j only there); a name no longer in scope may be used again ( Semantics ) DISTINCT, grouping keys, DISTINCT in aggregates GQL equality: 1 and 1.0 are one value, NULLs form one group aggregates of no rows (no grouping keys) one row: count 0, sum 0, collect_list [], avg / min / max NULL (Neo4j's values, which the openCypher TCK confirms; the ISO text is still to be checked) min / max over values of different kinds the ORDER BY order, never an error sum of integers an integer; overflow is an error (22003) unbounded quantifiers no own limit: trail ends them; repeat.max_loops and traversal.max_traversers are errors, never a shortened result (quantified edges and quantified path patterns alike) outer nodes next to a quantified path pattern merged with the body's first node of the first iteration and last node of the last iteration (Neo4j Cypher 25's reading) order of a group variable's list the iterations in the order the text reads, also when the plan walks the pattern from its far end WITH ... LIMIT ... WHERE the WHERE filters after ORDER BY / OFFSET / LIMIT (Cypher's order; provisional) name of an unaliased column the expression as written (Neo4j's names, such as count(*), which the openCypher TCK confirms; the ISO text is still to be checked) element ids strings, the same as Gremlin's id(); vertex and edge ids are separate spaces integer division truncates toward zero; % takes the sign of the dividend temporal precision microseconds; a value with a non-zero part below the microsecond is 0A000, never cut default time zone UTC: a datetime without an offset or zone, and the clocks without a zone the current date and time one instant per query, taken when it starts; X.realtime() is refused ORDER BY of durations by length, a month counted as 30 days (< on two durations is NULL) CAST(temporal AS STRING) the engine's ISO 8601 text ('12:00:00'); Cypher's toString() writes Neo4j's ('12:00') integer overflow an error (22003), never a wrap text and numbers no implicit conversion: 'a' + 1 is an error (22G03); convert with CAST(x AS STRING) CAST of a float to INTEGER, of text with surrounding spaces truncated toward zero; the spaces are skipped (provisional) CAST to STRING of a float, a boolean, a list or a map Java's float text ('1.0', '1.0E7'), 'true' / 'false', Neo4j's list and map text (provisional) CAST(x AS BOOLEAN) of a number; of 'unknown' 22G03; NULL (provisional) default character of TRIM, BTRIM, LTRIM, RTRIM the space U+0020 only (provisional) BTRIM / LTRIM / RTRIM with characters any character of the set is removed (Neo4j's semantics; provisional) functions and NULL a NULL argument gives NULL, before the kinds are checked strings in functions positions and lengths count characters (Unicode scalar values) GQLSTATUS codes 42001 for syntax errors; the others provisional ( Errors ) order of the writes of one INSERT per row: its nodes in text order, then its edges in text order property values of INSERT NULL is not stored; maps and lists of any kinds are stored as given (a difference from Neo4j )

517.body: Where ISO GQL and Neo4j disagree and the openCypher TCK measures the Neo4j behaviour, gql() follows Neo4j in these places (user decision, stage 3f): Topic ISO GQL gql() = / <> / IN / simple CASE between values of different kinds not comparable = FALSE, <> TRUE (1 = '1', [1] = 1, 1 IN ['1']); the orderings < .. >= stay NULL ( Semantics ) < <= > >= on two lists not comparable lexicographic, three-valued a float divided by zero 22012 IEEE 754: Infinity, -Infinity or NaN; an integer divided by zero stays 22012 NaN in a comparison (no NaN arises: every division by zero is 22012) never equal (NaN = NaN FALSE), every ordering against a number FALSE The deliberate differences from Neo4j are listed on Semantics .

517.title: Differences from the standard

518.body: Graphersal's GQL is measured against the openCypher TCK (Technology Compatibility Kit): Gherkin scenarios that each set up a graph, run one query and state the exact expected result, side effects or error. They exercise the Cypher compatibility forms that gql() accepts (CREATE, MATCH ... RETURN, WITH, UNWIND, ...) with Neo4j's semantics, so the kit works as a ready-made differential test. It serves three purposes: Compliance measure: what passes, what does not, and why. Regression gate: a test case that passed must keep passing; cargo test fails otherwise. Backlog generator: the report ranks the missing constructs and lists every wrong behaviour. Graphersal's GQL is not a Cypher implementation; the TCK measures how far its compatibility forms agree with the behaviour the kit specifies.
518.breadcrumbs: GQL Queries » TCK Compliance » TCK Compliance
518.title: TCK Compliance

519.body: Pinned version: openCypher TCK release 2024.3 (commit 677cbafabb8c3c5eed458fd3b1ec0daec8d67d23), vendored unmodified under crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/ (features/, the named graphs in graphs/, its licence and notice). The directory's README.md records the upgrade procedure. A test case is a scenario, or one Examples row of a scenario outline. Runner: the integration test target crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher_tck.rs (feature gql), with its harness in crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/harness/. Every case runs on a fresh graph through the Rust GQL API: the setup queries (having executed, the named graphs) run through gql()'s own writes, the query runs with its parameters, then its rows, its side effects (a state diff) and its error are compared. Every query runs under resource limits and a wall-clock guard. Gate: crates/graphersal/tests/opencypher/baseline.toml lists every in-scope case that does not pass yet, with its class and a one-line reason.
