772.title: More like this

773.body:
vector_mean() is a reducing barrier (like mean()): the component-wise mean of the incoming vectors, as an f32 vector. An incoming list of vectors (fold()) counts each of its vectors, null is skipped, quantized vectors count with their values, an empty stream gives no result, and vectors of different dimensions fail. local(__.unfold().vector_mean()) averages each list on its own. The mean of what a user liked is a taste vector to search with: g.add_v("user").property("name", "u7").as("u") .add_v("article").property("title", "Graphs").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).as("a") .add_v("article").property("title", "Trees").property("emb", vector([0.8, 0.4])).as("b") .add_v("article").property("title", "Cooking").property("emb", vector([0.0, 1.0])) .add_v("article").property("title", "Forests").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.3])) .add_e("liked").from("u").to("a").add_e("liked").from("u").to("b").add_e("read").from("u").to("a") .add_e("read").from("u").to("b") .iterate();
g.v().has("name", "u7").out("liked").values("emb").fold().vector_mean().as("taste") .v().has_label("article") .where(__.in("read").has("name", "u7").count().is(0)) .nearest("emb", __.select("taste"), 1) .values("title").next() // "Forests"
773.title: Recommendations with vector_mean()

774.body: The search is an exact scan: its time grows with the number of scored elements times the dimension, and it needs no index, so it costs nothing to keep up to date and answers the same at every commit, mark and snapshot. Measured with the bench nearest_10k_x_384 (cargo bench -p graphersal --bench graph --features io,script,display,serde -- nearest_10k_x_384): 10 000 vertices with a random 384-dimensional embedding, v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", q, 10), on an Apple M3: Stored element Metric Median Per vector f32 cosine 1.3 ms 130 ns f16 cosine 2.3 ms 230 ns i8 cosine 1.8 ms 180 ns bit hamming 0.21 ms 21 ns So about 13 ms per 100 000 f32 vectors of 384 components: enough for most in-memory graphs, and a filter before the search (above) scores fewer. There is no approximate (ANN) index yet (see Current Limitations ). These figures come from a source build, not from the musl-linked prebuilt Linux binary ( Performance of the prebuilt Linux binaries ).
774.title: Performance

775.body: A quantized property takes less memory and gives approximately the same answers. Measured by the test quantized_search_recall_against_f32 on 2 000 random 128-dimensional vectors (20 queries, recall@10 against the f32 search with cosine); random vectors are the hardest case, real embeddings usually keep more: Stored as Bytes per 384 components recall@10 f32 1 536 1.00 (exact) f16 768 1.00 i8 384 (+ 4 for the scale) 0.99 bit (hamming) 48 0.30 bit top 100, re-ranked by f32 48 + 1 536 0.74 Bit vectors are a coarse, very fast prefilter: keep both properties and re-rank the prefilter's hits exactly, nearest("emb_bit", q.quantize("bit"), 100, #{metric: "hamming"}) followed by nearest("emb", q, 10).
775.title: Quantization: memory against accuracy

776.body:
An embedder turns text into vectors. The step embed() embeds the incoming string, embed(key) the string property key (a name or a jpath(..)) of the incoming element, and the function embed(text) makes a query vector before any traversal runs. Each takes an option map naming the embedder, #{embedder: "name"}; without it the host's default runs. g.embedders() lists what is registered: g.embedders()[0].name // "hash-ngram/1"
embed("graph").dimension // 256
g.v().has_label("person").embed("name").count().next() // 4
g.v().embed("name", #{embedder: "hash-ngram/1"}).count().next() // 6
g.v().values("age").embed().next() // error: embed() takes a string, not int64
g.v().embed("name", #{embedder: "nope"}).next() // error: there is no embedder "nope" Rules of the step: an element without the property is dropped (like values(key)); a value that is not a string fails: nothing is converted implicitly, write as_string() first; an empty text, or one with no word at all, fails (has(key, P.neq("")) leaves them out); the step hands the embedder batches (up to the embedder's max_batch traversers per call), each traverser once whatever its bulk, and keeps the order; .profile() names the embedder that ran: embed("name", embedder: "hash-ngram/1"); writing the vectors (property("emb", __.embed("text"))) happens inside the traversal's unit under the graph's write lock, which suits a fast local embedder such as the built-in one; a property declared {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "dimension": 384} refuses a vector of another dimension or element kind, as for any write ( Vectors in a schema ). A fuzzy name search on the modern graph: g.v().has_label("person").property("name_emb", __.embed("name")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("person").nearest("name_emb", embed("Markus"), 2).values("name").to_list() // ["marko", "vadas"] What g.embedders() returns for each embedder: Key name the registry name, what #{embedder: ..} takes model the stable identity of what computes the vectors (hash-ngram/1, acme/minilm@3f2a9c41b7de), independent of the host's name for it and of any file path: two embedders of one model give comparable vectors dimension, element the shape of every vector it returns metric the metric it recommends for comparing them max_batch the most texts per call deterministic whether the same text always gives the same bits local whether the texts stay in the process default whether it runs without an embedder option Running an embedder asks Execute on the resource Embedder("name"), for every embedder including the built-in one ( Permissions ); AccessPolicy::read_only() allows it, and a saved query may embed. A computed vector is stored as a plain value: replay, recovery, change sets and loads never call an embedder, so an embedder that is not deterministic is safe to use.
776.title: Embeddings

777.title: Embedding a property: embed_property()

778.body: Vectors of different models cannot be compared: a cosine between a hash-ngram/1 vector and one of a semantic model means nothing. The schema therefore records, per label and property, which model produced the vectors: the keyword embedder of a vector declaration holds the embedder's model identity (model in g.embedders(), never a registry name or a file path): {"type": "array", "format": "vector", "element": "f32", "dimension": 256, "metric": "cosine", "embedder": "hash-ngram/1"} embed_property needs an attached schema (mode open or closed) and keeps it right; it never creates or attaches one itself (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.open) attaches the structure a graph has): to undeclared for the label: the job declares it (type, format: vector, element, dimension, metric from the embedder, embedder its model), in the unit of the first page, so the declaration and the first vectors commit together (and travel together through the journal, a rollback, a fork); declared as a vector of the embedder's dimension (or of any dimension) without embedder: the job adds embedder; declared with the same model: nothing to change; declared with another model : refused ("the schema declares "doc"."emb" as vectors of the model ..."): embed into another property, or change the schema deliberately and embed again with only_missing: false; declared as something else (not a vector, or another dimension): refused with the schema's own type mismatch, before the embedder runs; declared with another element kind (i8, f16, bit) than the embedder returns: fine, each vector is quantized to the declared element on write, exactly as a schema write of a vector of another element is, so an f32 model can fill an i8 property (a quarter of the memory) directly. Different labels and properties may use different models: doc.emb from one, doc.title_emb or person.emb from another. A plain write of a vector (property("emb", vector)) still checks only the element kind and the dimension: the provenance is kept by embed_property and used by the text queries, not checked on every write.

A traversal without a final step is displayed (a table in the command line and the playground). In code, a terminal step returns the data: to_list() all results, next() the first one, iterate() runs it for its side effects only. let names = g.v().has_label("person").values("name").to_list(); // a list
let marko = g.v().has("name", "marko").next(); // one vertex

780.body: hash-ngram/1 needs no model file and no dependency and gives the same bits on every target (the CLI, Python, the dev server, the browser playground). It lowercases the text, splits it into words (runs of letters and digits), and hashes each word and its character 3-, 4- and 5-grams (of the word framed as <word>) into 256 signed buckets, then scales the result to length 1 (f32 components, metric cosine). It measures lexical similarity: typos, word forms and shared stems come out close, in any script ("Graph" and "grahp", "Москва" and "Москве"), meaning does not ("car" and "automobile" are unrelated). Uses: fuzzy lookup, entity matching, deduplication, and a baseline before a semantic model. The algorithm is frozen: the output of hash-ngram/1 never changes (a different algorithm would be a new name, hash-ngram/2), and tests pin its bits. Two caveats: there is no Unicode normalization (a precomposed "é" and "e" followed by a combining accent are different words), and lowercasing and the letter/digit classes follow the Unicode version of the Rust toolchain the binary was built with. Its time grows with the length of the text. Measured with the bench embed_hash_ngram_1000 (cargo bench -p graphersal --bench graph --features io,script,display,serde -- embed_hash_ngram_1000, 1000 texts per call, Apple M-series, source build): about 0.84 µs per short title (5 words) and about 18.5 µs per paragraph of about 1 KB, so embedding a property of 100 000 short texts takes well under a second.
780.title: The built-in hash-ngram/1

783.body: Format A vector Graphersal's binary format (snapshots, the Store, the journal) its own value tag: the element kind, the dimension, for i8 the scale, then the packed components ( format spec 3 ) Serialized ChangeSet exact, tagged: {"@type": "graphersal:Vector", "@value": {"element": "f32", "data": [..]}} ( Transactions ) JSON results, to_json() the list of its values (an i8 or bit vector dequantized) GraphSON export a g:List of g:Float, which TinkerGraph loads GraphSON import a list stays a list; it becomes a vector where the target schema declares one (mode open/closed); the exact graphersal:Vector tag is read too ( GraphSON ) GraphML the JSON text of the list; a vector again where the target graph's schema declares one (any mode) Exporting an i8 or bit vector as its values loses nothing that matters: a declared i8 property quantizes them back to the same codes. memory_usage() counts a vector's components exactly (plus a small header), and the memory budget of a query estimates them the same way.
783.title: Storage and exchange

784.body:
A vector property is a graphersal.Vector in Python, built from a list of numbers or from any one-dimensional float32/float64 buffer such as a numpy array (the extension does not depend on numpy): import numpy as np
from graphersal import Graph, Vector g = Graph()
emb = np.array([0.12, -0.5, 0.33], dtype=np.float32) # model.encode(text) in practice
g.execute('g.add_v("doc").property("emb", e).iterate()', params={"e": Vector(emb)})
v = g.query('g.v().values("emb").next()') # graphersal.Vector
v.element, v.dimension, v.tolist() # ('f32', 3, [0.12, -0.5, 0.33])
Vector(emb, element="i8") # quantized, 1 byte per component q = np.array([0.1, -0.4, 0.3], dtype=np.float32) # the question's embedding
g.query('g.v().nearest("emb", q, 10).to_list()', params={"q": q}) A one-dimensional float32/float64 numpy array passed as a parameter arrives as an f32 vector, like Vector(array). See the Python binding's README for the details. Python registers its own embedders: graphersal.Embedder(name, fn, dimension=..) wraps any Python model (fn(texts) returns the rows, or one 2-D numpy array), graphersal.Model2Vec(name, path, model="minishlab/potion-base-8M") loads a Model2Vec model from a directory you downloaded (the same model identity as the command line's download), and Graph(embedders=[..]), graph.register_embedder, graph.embed_property(label=.., source=.., target=..) and text queries work as described above ( Python Quick Start: Embedders ).

786.body: Graphersal has five date and time types. They are values of their own, like numbers and UUIDs : a property holds a date, not a string that looks like one, and a query compares, sorts and computes with it. The model follows PostgreSQL and the SQL standard; the part TinkerPop defines (datetime(), asDate(), dateAdd(), dateDiff(), DT.second to DT.day) behaves exactly as TinkerPop 3.8 specifies it ( TinkerPop compatibility ).
786.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates and Times
786.title: Dates and Times

787.body:
Graphersal (type_of, GType) What it is Literal PostgreSQL SQL standard Python TinkerPop / java.time datetime (GType.DATETIME) an instant with the UTC offset it was written with datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00") timestamptz (keeps no offset) TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE aware datetime.datetime datetime, OffsetDateTime localdatetime (GType.LOCALDATETIME) a wall-clock date and time, no zone localdatetime("2023-08-02T09:30") timestamp TIMESTAMP naive datetime.datetime LocalDateTime date (GType.DATE) a calendar day date("2023-08-02") date DATE datetime.date LocalDate time (GType.TIME) a time of day, no zone time("09:30:15.5") time TIME naive datetime.time LocalTime duration (GType.DURATION) months, days and microseconds, each with its own sign duration("P1Y2M3DT4H") interval INTERVAL datetime.timedelta, or graphersal.Interval with months Duration, Period type_of(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")) // "datetime"
date("2024-02-29").day // 29
duration("P1Y2M3DT4H").months // 14
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30Z")).is(P.typeOf(GType.DATETIME)).count().next() // 1 Resolution: one microsecond for every type, as in PostgreSQL and Python. TinkerPop's millisecond views (as_number() of a datetime, date_diff()) round down to milliseconds. Range: the years -9999 to 9999 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (date("-0044-03-15") is year 44 BC counted astronomically, year 0 = 1 BC). A value outside the range, or a result that would leave it, is an error, never a wrapped value. Offsets: a datetime keeps its offset (±18:00, whole seconds) and shows it, unlike PostgreSQL's timestamptz, which keeps only the instant. A time zone is never stored in a value: operations take one ( Time Zones ). A duration is not normalized: P1M, P30D and PT720H are three different values. A month has no fixed length and a day is not always 24 hours in a time zone, so the three fields stay apart, as in PostgreSQL's interval. No guessing: a string stays a string whatever it looks like. A date comes from a constructor, a conversion step ( Conversions ), a schema that declares the property ( Schema ), a typed value in a file ( Storage and Exchange ) or a Python datetime ( From Python ).
787.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » The five types
787.title: The five types

788.body:
In a script each type is a value of its own Rhai type with getters and operators: Type Getters datetime year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond (on its own wall clock), offset (seconds), epoch_millis localdatetime year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond date year, month, day time hour, minute, second, microsecond duration months, days, micros let d = datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:15.25+02:00"); [d.hour, d.offset, d.microsecond] // [9, 7200, 250000]
datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") + duration("P1M") // datetime("2023-09-02T12:00:00Z")
date("2023-08-02") - date("2023-01-01") // duration("P213D")
time("10:00") - time("09:30") // duration("PT30M")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00").as_string() // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00" + and - with a duration work as date_add() does; the difference of two values of one type is a duration (two datetimes or localdatetimes give days of 24 hours and a time part, two dates days, two times the elapsed time). as_string() is the canonical text, to_string() the DSL literal. A value printed or shown as a script value is its literal (date("2023-08-02")); tables, JSON and the playground show the canonical text.
788.title: Script values

789.body: Comparing and Sorting : equality by instant, field-wise durations, the order of types. Text Formats : the canonical output, what is read, strict and lenient input. Time Zones : the bundled IANA database, offsets, daylight saving. Arithmetic : date_add(), date_diff(), age(). Truncation and Parts : date_trunc(), date_part(). Conversions : as_date(), as_duration(), as_number(), as_string(). now() and today() : the evaluation's start time and how a host pins it. Dates in a Schema : the date formats, bounds and coercion. Storage and Exchange : the binary format, GraphSON, GraphML, change sets. From Python : the datetime mapping. TinkerPop Compatibility : what is TinkerPop and what is an extension. Dates in GQL : the openCypher temporal functions of gql() (date(), x.year, date.truncate(), duration.between()) beside the steps of this part. The steps have generated reference pages: as_date , as_duration , date_add , date_diff , age , date_trunc , date_part , at_zone and as_local ; the constructors, now(), today() and DT are on Functions, Tokens and Values .

790.body: Every comparison of dates goes through one set of rules: == in a script, the predicates (P.eq, P.gt, P.between, P.within, ...), dedup(), group() and group_count() keys, order(), min()/max() and the schema bounds .
790.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » Comparing and Sorting
790.title: Comparing and Sorting

791.body:
Two datetimes are equal when they are the same instant, whatever their offsets (12:00Z equals 14:00+02:00). This is PostgreSQL's equality and TinkerPop's ("dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"). The offset is kept and shown, but never compared: datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") == datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00") // true
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z"), datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).dedup().count().next() // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).is(P.gt(datetime("2023-08-02T11:00Z"))).count().next() // 1 Of two values with the same instant and different offsets the first one met is kept (dedup(), a group() key); their order in a sort is unspecified. To compare the wall clocks instead, convert first: as_local() gives the wall-clock localdatetime ( Time Zones ).
791.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » datetime: by its instant
791.title: datetime: by its instant

792.body:
Two durations are equal when their months, days and microseconds are equal: P1M is not P30D, and P1D is not PT24H (a day in a time zone may have 23 or 25 hours). Sorting compares their length as PostgreSQL does for an interval, counting a month as 30 days and a day as 24 hours; equal lengths are ordered by months, then days, then microseconds: duration("P1M") == duration("P30D") // false
g.inject(duration("P1M"), duration("P30D"), duration("PT719H")).order().to_list() // [PT719H, P30D, P1M]
792.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length
792.title: duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length

793.body:
A date, a localdatetime and a time compare by their calendar or clock value. g.inject(time("10:00")).is(P.between(time("09:00"), time("17:00"))).count().next() // 1
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.within(date("2023-08-02"), date("2023-08-03"))).count().next() // 1
793.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » The other types: by calendar and clock
793.title: The other types: by calendar and clock

794.body:
Values of different types are never equal, and an ordering predicate between them does not match (no error): a date is not a datetime, and a date is never equal to a string, as a UUID is not. Convert one side first ( Conversions ). g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.eq("2023-08-02")).count().next() // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next() // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_date().is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next() // 1 order() of a mixed stream puts the dates after the numbers and before the strings (TinkerPop's orderability places its date type there), in the order date, localdatetime, datetime, time, duration: g.inject("x", 1, duration("P1D"), time("01:00"), datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z"), date("2023-08-02")).order().to_list()

796.body: Dates are read and written as ISO 8601 text (RFC 3339 for a datetime, with the RFC 9557 zone suffix). No locale formats, no two-digit years, no guessing: a text is read as a date only where a date is asked for (a constructor, a conversion step, a declared schema format, a typed value in a file).
796.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Text Formats
796.title: Text Formats

797.body:
Every value has one text, the one tables, JSON, GraphML, GraphSON and as_string() write. It is the text java.time writes, so other tools read it back: Type Canonical text date 2023-08-02; a year before 1 or after 9999 with its sign: -0044-03-15 time 09:30:00; a fraction only when it is not zero, as milliseconds or microseconds: 09:30:00.500, 09:30:00.123456 localdatetime 2023-08-02T09:30:00 (the date, T, the time) datetime 2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00; Z for a zero offset; an offset with seconds as +00:19:32 duration P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S: years and months from the months, days, then the time part; a zero part is left out, a zero duration is PT0S; a sign before P when every part is negative (-P1M2D), else a sign per part (P1M-2D) time("09:30:00.1").as_string() // "09:30:00.100"
datetime("2023-08-02 09:30+00:00").as_string() // "2023-08-02T09:30:00Z"
duration("PT90M").as_string() // "PT1H30M"
duration("P2W").as_string() // "P14D" A duration keeps its three fields as they are: PT36H stays PT36H (not P1DT12H), and weeks are read as 7 days. Years and months are one field, months: P1Y2M is 14 months.
797.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Canonical output
797.title: Canonical output

798.body:
Type Accepted text date YYYY-MM-DD; a year before 1 with its sign (-0044-03-15) time HH:MM, HH:MM:SS, HH:MM:SS.f with 1 to 9 fraction digits (digits below the microsecond are cut off) localdatetime a date, optionally followed by T (or t, or a space) and a time; a date alone is midnight datetime a local date-time, then an offset (Z, +02:00, +0200, +02, +00:19:32) and/or a zone in brackets ([Europe/Berlin]) duration [+-]P[nY][nM][nW][nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f]S]], a sign per number allowed (P1M-2D), letters in either case datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+0200") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30[Europe/Berlin]") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456789Z") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456Z")
date("10000-01-01") // error: expected a four-digit year
duration("1 day") // error: not an ISO 8601 duration A datetime with only a zone is resolved in it (a wall-clock time the zone skips moves forward, one it repeats takes the earlier offset, see Time Zones ); with an offset and a zone the offset must be the zone's at that instant.
798.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » What is read
798.title: What is read

799.body:
TinkerPop reads a date-time text without an offset as UTC (asDate("2023-08-02") is midnight UTC). Graphersal does that only where a query asks for a conversion: lenient (no offset = UTC, a date alone = midnight UTC): the datetime() / DateTime() constructor and the conversion steps as_date() and as_date(GType.DATETIME); strict (an offset or a zone is required): every place a text is stored as a datetime, namely a property declared "format": "date-time" in the schema , the formatMinimum/formatMaximum bounds, a typed gx:OffsetDateTime in GraphSON or a change set, a saved query argument declared as a date-time, and the playground's property editor. datetime("2023-08-02T09:30") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00Z")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date().next() // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00Z") A stored instant without its offset would be a guess about where it was written; the strict rule turns that guess into an error that names the expected form. The other types have no offset, so they read the same everywhere.
799.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset
799.title: Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset

80.body: Every step has a snake_case name and its Gremlin camelCase twin, so a query copied from TinkerPop documentation runs as it is (with double quotes for strings): g.V().hasLabel("person").outE("created").has("weight", P.gte(0.5)).inV().values("name")

800.body: A time zone is never stored in a value. A datetime carries a fixed UTC offset (the one it was written with); an operation that needs a zone takes it as an argument and gives back a datetime with the zone's offset at that instant. This is the PostgreSQL model (AT TIME ZONE, a session zone for the calendar arithmetic), with the zone passed explicitly instead of a session setting.
800.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Time Zones
800.title: Time Zones

801.body: A zone argument is one of: an IANA zone name : "Europe/Berlin", "America/New_York", "UTC"; a fixed offset : "+02:00", "-0530", "Z". The IANA rules come from the time zone database bundled with Graphersal (the jiff-tzdb crate). Every machine, and the browser playground, gives the same answer to the same query, and a replayed journal computes what it computed when it was written; the database changes only with a Graphersal release, not with an operating system update. An unknown name is an error, found before any value is read: g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("Mars/Olympus").next() // error: unknown time zone The steps that take a zone: at_zone(zone) , as_local(zone) , date_add(.., zone) , date_diff(.., zone) , age(.., zone) , date_trunc(.., zone) , date_part(.., zone) , and today(zone). Only a datetime (and the localdatetime of at_zone) takes one; the other types have no instant, and a zone argument for them is an error.
801.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Zone arguments
801.title: Zone arguments

802.body:
at_zone(zone) on a datetime: the same instant, written with the zone's offset at it (PostgreSQL AT TIME ZONE, java.time atZoneSameInstant). at_zone(zone) on a localdatetime: the wall-clock time read in the zone, the datetime of that instant (java.time atZone). as_local() / as_local(zone): the wall-clock localdatetime a datetime shows on its own offset or in the zone (toLocalDateTime). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("America/New_York").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T08:00:00-04:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-08-02T12:00")).at_zone("+02:00").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).as_local("Asia/Tokyo").next() // localdatetime("2023-08-02T21:00:00")
802.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Moving between a datetime and its wall clock
802.title: Moving between a datetime and its wall clock

803.body:
Where a zone moves its clocks, a wall-clock time can be missing (a spring-forward gap ) or happen twice (a fall-back fold ). Graphersal resolves both as PostgreSQL and java.time do (the "compatible" rule), never with an error: a time in a gap moves forward by the length of the gap: 02:30 on 2023-03-26 in Berlin becomes 03:30+02:00; a time in a fold takes the earlier offset: 02:30 on 2023-10-29 in Berlin is 02:30+02:00, the first of the two. g.inject(localdatetime("2023-03-26T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T03:30:00+02:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-10-29T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-10-29T02:30:00+02:00") The same rule applies to a text with only a zone (datetime("2023-03-26T02:30[Europe/Berlin]")) and to every result a zone computes on the wall clock.
803.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Daylight saving: gaps and folds
803.title: Daylight saving: gaps and folds

804.body:
Without a zone a datetime is computed on its own fixed offset: date_add(DT.day, 1) adds 24 hours, as TinkerPop specifies. With a zone, calendar units work on the zone's wall clock, so a day stays a calendar day across a daylight saving change (23 or 25 hours long), while hours stay hours: g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1).next() // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+01:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1, "Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 24, "Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T13:00:00+02:00") The same holds for date_diff() in days and larger units, age(), date_trunc() and date_part(): they read the wall clock of the zone. Without a zone, date_diff() and age() read both operands on the wall clock of the second operand's offset: g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day).next() // 0 (23 hours)
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day, "Europe/Berlin").next() // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_trunc(DT.day, "America/New_York").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00-04:00") GQL has no zone argument: a zone name in its text (datetime('..[Europe/Berlin]')) or in a map (timezone: 'Europe/Berlin') resolves to the zone's offset when the value is built, and its arithmetic then stays at that offset, unlike Neo4j, which keeps the name ( Dates in GQL , Semantics ).
804.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Calendar arithmetic in a zone
804.title: Calendar arithmetic in a zone

805.body: Three steps compute with dates: date_add() moves a value, date_diff() measures the distance between two values as a number, age() as a duration. All of them are checked: a result outside the years -9999 to 9999 is an error, never a wrapped value. In a script the operators + and - do the same ( script values ). In GQL, + with a duration and duration.between() follow Neo4j's rules instead ( Dates in GQL ).
805.title: Arithmetic

806.body: DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day are TinkerPop's (the bare names second, minute, hour and day work too, as in the TinkerPop scenarios). Graphersal adds the smaller and the calendar units, with PostgreSQL's field names: Unit Kind Adding it DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour a fixed length moves the instant (or the clock) by that many microseconds DT.day, DT.week calendar days moves the wall-clock date; in a zone the time of day is kept across a daylight saving change DT.month, DT.quarter, DT.year, DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millennium calendar months (1, 3, 12, 120, 1200, 12000) moves the month and clamps the day to the end of the target month DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch and DT.offset are parts, not units: only date_part() takes them.
806.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Arithmetic » Units: the DT token
806.title: Units: the DT token

807.body:
date_add(DT.unit, n) adds n units (a negative n subtracts); date_add(duration) adds a duration. Both take an optional zone as the last argument ( Time Zones ). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.hour, 36).next() // datetime("2023-08-04T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).date_add(day, 3).next() // date("2023-08-05")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.millisecond, 1500).next() // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:01.500Z") Month ends. Adding months keeps the day of the month where it exists and otherwise takes the last day of the target month, as PostgreSQL and java.time do. Each step clamps on its own, so two single months can end earlier than two months at once: g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).next() // date("2024-02-29")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 2).next() // date("2024-03-31")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).date_add(DT.month, 1).next() // date("2024-03-29") A duration is added in PostgreSQL's order: its months first (clamped), then its days, then its time part. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(duration("P1M1DT1H")).next() // datetime("2023-09-03T13:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(duration("P1Y1D")).next() // date("2025-03-01") What each type accepts: Type DT units A duration datetime all units; a fixed length moves the instant and keeps the offset (TinkerPop: a day is 24 hours at a fixed offset), with a zone the result takes the zone's offset any localdatetime all units, on the wall clock any date day and larger without a time part time hour and smaller; the clock wraps around midnight (PostgreSQL time + interval) without months or days duration all units: adds to the matching field any (field by field) g.inject(time("23:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next() // time("01:00:00")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next() // error: adding the unit hour is not defined for a date
807.title: date_add()

808.body:
date_diff(other) is TinkerPop's dateDiff(): the incoming value minus other in milliseconds , an int64, each operand's epoch milliseconds rounded down. other is a value or a child traversal whose first result is the operand; () (null) stands for the epoch. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z")).next() // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(__.constant(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"))).next() // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("1970-01-01T00:00:01Z")).date_diff(()).next() // 1000 Graphersal extends it to the other types (both operands of one type: a date counts from midnight, a time within the day; () is 1970-01-01 or midnight) and adds date_diff(other, DT.unit[, zone]): the difference in whole units , truncated toward zero. Units below a day count the elapsed time. Days and weeks count wall-clock days (a datetime on the wall clock of other's offset, or of the zone). Months and larger count as java.time's ChronoUnit.between: a month is complete when the day of the month (and the time) is reached again, so January 31 to February 28 is 0 months. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"), DT.hour).next() // 36
g.inject(time("10:00")).date_diff(time("09:00"), DT.minute).next() // 60
g.inject(date("2024-02-28")).date_diff(date("2024-01-31"), DT.month).next() // 0
g.inject(date("2024-03-31")).date_diff(date("2024-02-29"), DT.month).next() // 1
808.title: date_diff()

809.body:
age(other[, zone]) is PostgreSQL's age: the difference as a duration of whole years and months, days and a time part, all with the same sign. It is counted down from the incoming value to other with PostgreSQL's borrowing rules, so swapping the operands negates the result. Both operands have the same type; () is an error. g.inject(date("2001-04-10")).age(date("1957-06-13")).next() // duration("P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(date("1957-06-13")).age(date("2001-04-10")).next() // duration("-P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(datetime("2024-02-29T00:00Z")).age(datetime("2023-01-31T12:00Z")).next() // duration("P1Y28DT12H") To get a plain number of days, years or hours, use date_diff(other, DT.unit); to get a duration of elapsed time without calendar units, subtract the two values in a script (a - b).
809.title: age()

81.body: Graphersal and TinkerPop : what is the same and what is not; Writing Queries : the DSL in detail, by topic; Step Reference : the steps one by one.
81.title: Next

810.body: date_trunc(DT.unit) is PostgreSQL's date_trunc, and date_part(DT.unit) is its extract. Both are Graphersal extensions; TinkerPop has neither. GQL's X.truncate() and x.year do the same with Neo4j's names, but truncate millennia and centuries as Neo4j does ( Dates in GQL ). A datetime is read on its own wall clock, or on the wall clock of a zone given as the last argument ( Time Zones ).
810.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » Truncation and Parts
810.title: Truncation and Parts

811.body:
The fields below the unit become their first value: the start of the hour, the day, the month. A truncated datetime keeps its offset (or, with a zone, takes the zone's offset at the new instant). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.hour).next() // datetime("2023-08-17T15:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.week).next() // datetime("2023-08-14T00:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.day, "UTC").next() // datetime("2023-08-17T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_trunc(DT.quarter).next() // date("2023-07-01")
g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M")).date_trunc(DT.day).next() // duration("P1Y2M3D") Unit Truncates to microsecond ... hour the start of that unit of the clock day midnight week Monday, midnight (ISO 8601 weeks) month, quarter, year the first day of the month, of the quarter (January, April, July, October), of the year decade the first day of a year divisible by 10 (2020-01-01) century, millennium the first day of a year ending in 01/001: centuries and millennia start at year 1, as PostgreSQL counts them (2001-01-01 starts the 21st century) A date takes day and larger, a time hour and smaller, a duration keeps the fields at and above the unit (month and larger keep whole multiples of the unit's months and drop the days and the time part).
811.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » date_trunc()
811.title: date_trunc()

812.body:
One field as a number: an int64, except DT.epoch, a float64 of seconds. Part Value DT.year, DT.month (1-12), DT.day (1-31), DT.hour, DT.minute, DT.second (0-59) the field DT.millisecond (0-999), DT.microsecond (0-999999) the fraction of the second; unlike PostgreSQL, not the seconds with the fraction DT.quarter (1-4) the quarter DT.week (1-53) the ISO 8601 week number DT.iso_year the ISO 8601 week-numbering year (2023-01-01 is in week 52 of 2022) DT.day_of_week 0 = Sunday to 6 = Saturday (PostgreSQL dow) DT.iso_day_of_week 1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday (PostgreSQL isodow) DT.day_of_year (1-366) the day of the year DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millennium as PostgreSQL counts them (the 21st century is 2001-2100) DT.epoch seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (a localdatetime read as UTC); for a duration its length with a year of 365.25 days and a month of 30 days DT.offset the UTC offset of a datetime in seconds g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.day_of_week).next() // 4
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.week).next() // 52
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.iso_year).next() // 2022
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.epoch).next() // 1692280032.5
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.offset).next() // 7200
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T02:00Z")).date_part(DT.day, "America/New_York").next() // 1 A date has no clock parts (hour and smaller), a time only those (and epoch, the seconds since midnight). A duration gives PostgreSQL's interval fields: year and month from its months (14 months are 1 year and 2 months), day its days, hour and smaller from its time part; it has no week, day-of parts, iso_year or offset: g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.5S")).date_part(DT.month).next() // 2
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.hour).next() // error: the part hour is not defined for a date
812.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » date_part()
812.title: date_part()

813.body: A value becomes a date only through an explicit step; nothing is converted by guessing (a string that looks like a date stays a string).
813.title: Conversions

814.body:
as_date() converts to a datetime exactly as TinkerPop's asDate() does: Incoming Result a datetime unchanged a string read leniently as ISO 8601 / RFC 3339: without an offset it is UTC, a date alone is midnight UTC ( Text Formats ) an int64 milliseconds since the epoch, in UTC a date, a localdatetime the datetime at UTC (Graphersal: TinkerPop has no such types) anything else (a float64, (), a list, a map, a time, a duration, an element) an error starting with "Can't parse", as in TinkerPop g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00", 1690000000000, date("2023-08-02")).as_date().to_list() // [2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00, 2023-07-22T04:26:40Z, 2023-08-02T00:00:00Z]
g.inject(1.5).as_date().next() // error: Can't parse float64 1.5 as a datetime
814.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()
814.title: as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()

815.body:
as_date(GType.DATETIME | DATE | LOCALDATETIME | TIME) converts to that type (a Graphersal extension, spelled like as_number(GType.LONG)): Incoming → DATETIME DATE LOCALDATETIME TIME string lenient, as as_date() strict: a date text strict: a local date-time text strict: a time text datetime unchanged its wall-clock date (at its own offset) its wall clock its wall-clock time localdatetime at UTC its date unchanged its time date midnight UTC unchanged midnight an error time an error an error an error unchanged int64 epoch milliseconds, UTC an error an error an error GType.DURATION is not a target here: use as_duration(). To read a datetime's wall clock in another zone, use as_local(zone) first ( Time Zones ). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_local("UTC").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-03")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // error: unexpected text after the value
815.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » as_date(GType.X): to another date type
815.title: as_date(GType.X): to another date type

816.body: as_duration() reads an ISO 8601 duration text; a duration passes unchanged, anything else fails with "Can't parse". g.inject("PT90M").as_duration().next() // duration("PT1H30M")
816.title: as_duration()

817.body:
as_number() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds (TinkerPop), rounded down; the other date types are not numbers (use date_part(DT.epoch) or date_diff()). as_string() of any date is its canonical text; in a script, x.as_string() does the same. cast(GType.DATETIME) (and the other date tokens) parses a string or, for DATETIME, reads an int64 as epoch milliseconds, like as_date(GType.X). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z")).as_number().next() // 1690934400000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00")).as_string().next() // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_number().next() // error: Cast exception
817.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » To numbers and text
817.title: To numbers and text

818.body: A property written as a string stays a string. To store dates, declare the property in the schema ("format": "date-time"): in open and closed mode a string written to it is converted on write. Or convert in the query: property("at", __.constant(text).as_date()), or write a date value (property("on", date("2023-08-02"))).
818.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » Storing text as a date
818.title: Storing text as a date

819.body:
now() is the current time as a datetime in UTC; today() is its date, and today(zone) the date in a zone (an IANA name or an offset). type_of(now()) // "datetime"
now() == now() // true
type_of(today("Europe/Berlin")) // "date"
g.add_v("event").property("at", now()).values("at").count().next() // 1
819.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » now() and today()
819.title: now() and today()

82.body: Apache TinkerPop™ defines the property graph model and the Gremlin language that many graph databases implement. Graphersal is an independent implementation in Rust: it does not use TinkerPop's Java code, and it is not a Gremlin Server, so a TinkerPop driver does not connect to it. What it shares with TinkerPop is the language and its meaning.
82.breadcrumbs: Graphersal and TinkerPop » Graphersal and TinkerPop
82.title: Graphersal and TinkerPop

820.body:
Like PostgreSQL's now() (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), now() is the time the script evaluation started , the same value for every call in it: a script that stamps a thousand elements stamps them all with one instant, and now() == now() holds. In the playground a whole script is one unit, so now() is the start of that unit. A saved query called from a script sees its caller's now(). now() and today() are script functions, evaluated before the traversal runs: the traversal gets the resulting value as a constant (inject(now()), property("at", now()), has("at", P.lt(now()))). The journal of a Store and a change set record that value, never the call, so a replay or a recovery writes the same instant, not the time of the replay. today() is the date of now() in UTC, PostgreSQL's current_date in a UTC session. For the date in another zone pass the zone, or convert the instant yourself: today("UTC") == today() // true
g.inject(now()).as_local("America/Los_Angeles").as_date(GType.DATE).next() == today("America/Los_Angeles") // true
820.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » The start of the evaluation
820.title: The start of the evaluation

821.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » Pinning the clock (hosts)
821.title: Pinning the clock (hosts)

822.body: A schema declares a date property as a JSON Schema string with a format, and bounds it with the format* keywords. The full reference (every keyword, the errors and why, inference and diffs) is on the Schemas page; this page is the overview. format Type Example value date-time datetime 2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00 local-date-time localdatetime 2024-05-01T09:30:00 (a Graphersal name: JSON Schema has none) date date 2024-05-01 time time 09:30:00 (local; JSON Schema's own time requires an offset) duration duration P1Y2M3DT4H JSON Schema validators treat format as an annotation and ignore one they do not know, so a schema with these formats stays usable with other tools; Pydantic writes date-time, date, time and duration for datetime, date, time and timedelta fields.
822.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Dates in a Schema
822.title: Dates in a Schema

823.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Coercion on write
823.title: Coercion on write

824.body:
formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum (the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal, which ajv-formats implements) bound a date property. Their value is the text of a value of the node's type, and a value is compared as the type compares : a datetime by its instant, a duration by its length. minimum and maximum stay number keywords. { "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }
824.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Bounds
824.title: Bounds

825.body: infer_schema() reports a stored date with its format ({"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), and a position that holds strings and dates as an anyOf, so freezing the structure you have (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)) keeps the dates dates. The playground's schema editor offers the five formats as types and their bounds as constraints.
825.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Inference
825.title: Inference

826.body: A date keeps its type wherever it goes: in memory, in a snapshot or a Store, in a change set and in a GraphSON file. GraphML has no date type and needs the schema.
826.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Storage and Exchange
826.title: Storage and Exchange

827.body: A date is stored inline in the property value, 16 bytes at most, without a heap allocation: a date is a day number, a time and a localdatetime microseconds, a datetime microseconds since the epoch plus its offset in seconds, a duration its months, days and microseconds. Equality and ordering compare these numbers ( Comparing and Sorting ).
827.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » In memory
827.title: In memory

828.body: The binary format (packed snapshots .gsnap, Store segments, the write-ahead log) has a value tag per type, 9 to 13, defined in the format specification : the exact payload, the range of each type, and the rule that a datetime keeps its offset while equality uses the instant. These tags came with file format version 2 : a build that knows them writes version 2 and reads versions 1 and 2, so a .gsnap written by 0.1.x still loads, while an older build refuses a version 2 file instead of misreading it. See Format Versions and Upgrade for a Store written by 0.1.x.
828.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Snapshots, journals and the Store
828.title: Snapshots, journals and the Store

829.body: A serialized ChangeSet (feature serde) writes a date as a per-value type tag in TinkerPop's GraphSON style, so a replay restores the type without a schema: Type Tag datetime {"@type": "gx:OffsetDateTime", "@value": "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00"} date, localdatetime, time gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime, gx:LocalTime duration of microseconds only gx:Duration (PT26H) duration of months and days only gx:Period (P1Y2M3D) any other duration graphersal:Interval (P1MT2H) Reading is strict: the text must be a value of the tag's type, and a gx:OffsetDateTime must carry its offset.
829.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Change sets
829.title: Change sets

83.body: The rule is simple: a step that Graphersal implements behaves as the TinkerPop specification says, unless a difference is documented. The specification is TinkerPop's own test suite, a set of Gherkin scenarios (TinkerPop 3.8.2) that runs with every cargo test of Graphersal. A scenario that passes once is protected from regressing, and the number of supported steps whose results are wrong is kept at zero. The current numbers are on TinkerPop Compliance . Not every step exists yet. An unimplemented step is an error that names it, never a silently different result; the gaps are listed in Current Limitations .
83.breadcrumbs: Graphersal and TinkerPop » Same meaning, checked by TinkerPop's own tests
83.title: Same meaning, checked by TinkerPop's own tests

830.body: GraphSON 3.0 reads and writes the java.time types: g:Date/g:Timestamp (epoch milliseconds) become a datetime in UTC, gx:OffsetDateTime, gx:Instant and gx:ZonedDateTime a datetime with the offset of the text (the zone id of a gx:ZonedDateTime is dropped and reported), gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime and gx:LocalTime the local types, gx:Duration and gx:Period a duration. The export writes the tags of the change set table above, which TinkerGraph's g.io(file).read() loads, with one exception: a duration with both months or days and a time part has no java.time type, so it is written as graphersal:Interval, which only Graphersal reads (a deliberate deviation ). Digits below a microsecond are cut and reported, and the java.time types Graphersal cannot hold (gx:Year, gx:YearMonth, gx:MonthDay, gx:OffsetTime, gx:ZoneOffset) are skipped and reported. The full mapping is on the GraphSON page. A date-like string without a type tag (GraphSON 1.0, types=false) stays a string; declare the property in the schema to store it as a date.

833.body:
The Python binding converts the five types to and from the standard datetime module, both as results and as params=, to the microsecond (the resolution of both sides): Graphersal Python datetime aware datetime.datetime with tzinfo=datetime.timezone(timedelta(seconds=offset)) localdatetime naive datetime.datetime date datetime.date time naive datetime.time duration without months datetime.timedelta duration with months graphersal.Interval(months, days, micros) import datetime as dt
import graphersal graph = graphersal.Graph()
at = dt.datetime(2023, 8, 2, 9, 30, tzinfo=dt.timezone(dt.timedelta(hours=2)))
graph.query("g.inject(x).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()", params={"x": at})
# datetime.datetime(2023, 8, 3, 9, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(seconds=7200)))
graph.query('duration("P1Y2M")')
# Interval('P1Y2M') An aware datetime with any tzinfo (a zoneinfo.ZoneInfo too) is passed with the UTC offset it has at that instant; the zone name is not kept. An offset with a fraction of a second is refused. An aware datetime.time is refused: a time of day has no instant without a date. A timedelta becomes whole days and the rest, both with the sign of the whole (timedelta(hours=-1) is -PT1H). graphersal.Interval is immutable, equal when its three fields are equal (Interval("P1M") != Interval(0, 30), as in the engine), has months, days, micros and to_iso(), and is built from the fields or from ISO 8601 text (Interval("P1Y2M3DT4H")). Python's datetime holds the years 1 to 9999; a date before year 1 cannot be returned as one (read it with as_string()). The binding's README has the details and more examples.

834.body: TinkerPop 3.8 has one date type, datetime (a Java OffsetDateTime), the literal datetime(..), the steps asDate(), dateAdd() and dateDiff(), the units DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day, and the tokens GType.DATETIME and GType.DURATION (a Java Duration, which no TinkerPop step produces). Graphersal implements all of it as TinkerPop specifies, with no deviation: datetime("..") (also spelled DateTime("..")) reads ISO 8601 text, a text without an offset as UTC; asDate() converts text and epoch milliseconds, and fails with "Can't parse" for the same inputs as TinkerPop; dateAdd(DT.unit, n) keeps the offset and moves the instant, a day being 24 hours; dateDiff(other) is the difference in milliseconds, null being the epoch; asNumber() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds; equality and ordering use the instant ("Dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"), and dates sort after numbers and before strings. Every date scenario of the vendored TinkerPop 3.8.2 suite passes (DateTime, AsDate, DateAdd, DateDiff, the date cases of TypeOf and AsNumber), except two Orderability scenarios that also hold a set literal ({"x", "y", "z"}), for which Graphersal has no value type ( TinkerPop Compliance ).

835.body: Everything else on the pages of this part is a Graphersal extension, modelled on PostgreSQL: the types date, localdatetime and time (GType.DATE, LOCALDATETIME, TIME; typeOf names LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime), and duration as a value with months, days and microseconds (PostgreSQL's interval, broader than Java's Duration), with their constructors; the units DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.week to DT.millennium and the parts DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch, DT.offset; date_add(duration), zone arguments, date_diff(other, DT.unit), age(), date_trunc(), date_part(), at_zone(), as_local(), as_duration(), as_date(GType.X); now(), today(), the getters and operators of script values; the schema formats and bounds, GraphSON's java.time types beyond g:Date, and the Python mapping . The extensions add behaviour where TinkerPop defines none; none of them changes what a TinkerPop step returns. The one deliberate difference in the exchange formats is GraphSON's graphersal:Interval for a duration that no java.time type can hold ( Storage and Exchange ); all deviations are listed on TinkerPop Deviations .

84.body: A few behaviours differ on purpose, each for a reason that is written down. The most visible ones: Every traversal is a transaction. A failing traversal leaves nothing behind ( Transactions ). Ids are strings , so they sort as text ( Predicates ). One integer and one float type (int64, float64) instead of Java's number tower. A removed element stays removed : reading it through an old reference finds nothing, and writing to it is an error ( Dropping Elements ). No match(), io() or graph-computer algorithms ; files are read and written by the API and the command line instead. Every difference, with its page, is in TinkerPop Deviations .

843.body: A graph can store a schema: which vertex and edge labels exist, which properties they carry, of which types and within which constraints, and how edges may connect labels. The schema is plain data in one format, the same in Rust, the script DSL, Python and the playground: our envelope outside, standard JSON Schema 2020-12 inside (a strict subset), so a model_json_schema() from Pydantic can be pasted as a label's schema. The rule behind enforcement: the storage owns consistency. Every operation that changes the graph passes the schema inside one storage call, never in a step, and every traversal is one unit of work: it is applied completely or not at all.
843.title: Schemas

844.title: A first schema

845.body:
A common way to start: build the graph without a schema, experiment until the shape is right, then freeze that shape so every later write has to follow it: g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) // or SchemaMode.open / SchemaMode.none set_schema(schema, mode) stores schema with its mode replaced by mode (an inferred schema has mode none, which enforces nothing). The mode is a SchemaMode token (SchemaMode.closed, SchemaMode::closed) or one of the strings "none", "open", "closed"; validate_schema(schema, mode) is the dry run. SchemaMode is a reserved name in the script scope. Binding Freeze DSL g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (also setSchema(.., "closed")) Rust let s = g.infer_schema()?.with_mode(SchemaMode::Closed); g_mut.set_schema(s)? Python graph.set_schema(graph.infer_schema(), mode="closed") Playground Schema panel: Freeze as open / Freeze as closed (shown while the graph stores no enforcing schema) What each mode freezes: open: the labels and properties that exist get their types and required lists; new labels and new properties stay allowed (unchecked). closed: additionally, no other label, no other property (at any depth) and no edge between other labels than the ones that exist. It always succeeds on the data the schema was inferred from , in both modes: inference declares every kind seen at every position and requires only the keys every element has (see Inference ). The one exception is closed with elements without a label : an unlabeled vertex or edge has no label to declare, and a closed schema admits only declared labels. Then the call fails, changes nothing, and the report names them: Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (2 kinds of violations on 2 elements of 6 checked) 1) 1 edge without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "7"] 2) 1 vertex without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "3"] Freeze such a graph in open mode (it admits unlabeled elements unchecked), or give those elements a label first with the label steps ( add_label, drop_label, set_label ) and freeze again: g.v("3").add_label("thing").to_list(); // a vertex from the report
g.e().not(__.has_label()).set_label("link").to_list(); // every unlabeled edge
g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (g.v().not(__.has_label()).add_label("thing") labels every unlabeled vertex; Rust: the same steps, or GraphStorage::add_vertex_label/set_edge_label.) (The generated large sample graph has unlabeled edges: it freezes open, not closed.) Later changes go through patch_schema (add a property, relax a rule) like any other schema.
845.breadcrumbs: Schemas » Freeze the structure you have
845.title: Freeze the structure you have

847.body: Key Type Meaning $schema string, optional The format: https://graphersal.dev/schema/v1 (any other value is an error). meta object, optional Free-form data the library stores, round-trips and never interprets (a version, a status, server data). Changing it is a schema change. mode "none" | "open" | "closed", default "none" What is enforced, see Modes . vertices object Vertex label → {"schema": <label schema>}. edges object Edge label → {"connections": [{"from": .., "to": ..}], "schema": <label schema>}. A label schema is a JSON Schema object node describing the element's property map: {"type": "object", "properties": {..}, "required": [..], "additionalProperties": ..} plus annotations. It may carry $defs (for $ref), $schema and $id (accepted and not stored). A label without schema declares no properties. A connection's from/to is a vertex label or * (any label). Unknown keys are errors everywhere , the envelope included: {"mdoe": "closed"} is rejected with its location (Invalid schema at /mdoe: unknown key 'mdoe'), never silently ignored. The canonical form (what get_schema, to_json and every binding return) always writes $schema, mode, vertices and edges, keywords in a fixed order, integers as integers. The empty schema (mode none, no meta, no labels) is no schema: set_schema({}) removes the stored schema. The format is described by the meta-schema graphersal-schema-v1.json (graphersal::schema::META_SCHEMA_JSON).
847.title: Envelope

848.body: JSON Schema Engine type Note "integer" int64 A value outside i64 cannot be stored at all; 3.0 is not an integer. "number" float64 An int64 written to it is coerced when exactly representable; a stored int64 does not conform. "string" string "string" + "format": "uuid" uuid A canonical UUID string is coerced on write; a stored string does not conform. "string" + "format": "date-time" datetime An instant with its UTC offset (2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00). "string" + "format": "date" date A calendar day (2024-05-01). "string" + "format": "local-date-time" localdatetime A date and time without a zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00). A Graphersal format name: JSON Schema has none. "string" + "format": "time" time A time of day without an offset (09:30:00). JSON Schema's own time requires an offset; Graphersal's is local. "string" + "format": "duration" duration ISO 8601 (P1Y2M3DT4H): months, days and microseconds. "boolean", "null" boolean, null "array" + items array<T> items is a full schema (constraints and nullability apply to the items); without items any item. "array" + "format": "vector" (+ element, dimension, metric) vector<f32, 768> A vector of the declared element (f32 default, f16, i8, bit) and dimension (optional). A list of numbers is coerced on write, a vector of another element quantized; a stored list does not conform. items is not allowed next to it; metric is an annotation; embedder (a label's top-level property only) records the model identity of the embedder that produced the vectors ("hash-ngram/1"), which embed_property() fills in and checks and the text queries of nearest()/similarity() read; a plain write does not check it. Book page Vectors . "object" + properties object With required and additionalProperties. ["integer", "null"] union<int64|null> A type array: any of the listed types. anyOf: [..] union<..> At least one member accepts the value (Pydantic's Optional[X] is anyOf: [X, {"type": "null"}]). {} (no type) any Admits every value. Diagnostics, Display and GType keep the engine's names (int64, float64, uuid, datetime, localdatetime, ...). Dates and times. In open and closed mode a property declared with a temporal format coerces a string on write: any text the type's parser accepts (ISO 8601 / RFC 3339; the canonical form and the usual variants such as 2024-05-01 09:30Z or 09:30) becomes the temporal value, and text it refuses is a coercion failure that names the expected form. A date-time text must carry its UTC offset or a time zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00Z, 2024-05-01T09:30[Europe/Berlin]): 2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC, and the same holds for a formatMinimum/formatMaximum bound and a typed gx:OffsetDateTime (only the explicit conversion step as_date() keeps TinkerPop's "no offset is UTC"). This is the explicit declaration at work, like the uuid coercion, never a guess from content: an undeclared date-like string stays a string. A stored string does not conform to a temporal format (reads never coerce), and one temporal type never conforms to another (a date is not a datetime). JSON Schema's format is an annotation for other validators, which ignore a format they do not know, so a schema with local-date-time stays usable with them. The part Dates and Times describes the types themselves; its page Dates in a Schema has examples.
848.title: Types

849.body:
Kind Keywords Structure type, format (uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration on a string; vector on an array), element, dimension, metric, embedder (with format: "vector"; embedder on a top-level property only), items, properties, required, additionalProperties (true/false), anyOf Constraints minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum (numbers), formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum, formatExclusiveMaximum (dates and times), minLength, maxLength, pattern (strings), minItems, maxItems (arrays), enum, const (any value) Annotations (no effect on validation) title, description, $comment, examples, deprecated Create-time defaults ( Defaults on create ) default (also an annotation below the top level), defaultFunction (uuidv4, uuidv7, now, today) References $ref: "#/$defs/Name" with $defs at the label schema's root; inlined when the schema is loaded A constraint applies to the values of its own kind and ignores the others (JSON Schema semantics): in {"type": ["integer", "string"], "minimum": 10, "minLength": 3} the bound checks the integers and the length the strings. Next to a declared type, a keyword of another kind is an error (minLength on an integer is a mistake, not a no-op). enum/const compare JSON values (1 equals 1.0, a uuid and a date or time compare as their canonical text, so a datetime matches only the text with its own offset). formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum bound a date or time: the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal (ajv-formats implements them; other validators ignore unknown keywords). Their value is the text of a value of the node's temporal format, and they are valid only next to one (minimum stays a number keyword): { "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" } A value is compared with its type's ordering: a datetime by its instant (2020-01-01T01:00:00+01:00 equals the minimum above), a duration by its length (a month counts 30 days, a day 24 hours, as PostgreSQL orders intervals), the others by their calendar or clock value. Local references are inlined : a loaded schema has no $ref/$defs, and a reference cycle is an error (recursive schemas are not supported). Only annotations, default and defaultFunction may sit next to a $ref; they override the definition's.
849.title: Keywords

85.body: TinkerPop's reference language is Gremlin embedded in Groovy or Java. Graphersal's text form is Gremlin embedded in Rhai , a small scripting language for Rust. A Groovy line usually pastes as it is; the differences are small: Gremlin Groovy Graphersal 'single quotes' "double quotes" order().by('age', desc) order().by("age", Order.desc) (token classes are written out) out() inside where(...), repeat(...) __.out() (anonymous traversals always start with __.) [name: 'ann'] (a map) #{name: "ann"} def x = ... let x = ...; The full copy-paste table is in Repeated Labels: select with Pop . Every step also has a snake_case name (has_label, out_e) next to its camelCase one (hasLabel, outE), and the Rust API uses the snake_case names.
85.breadcrumbs: Graphersal and TinkerPop » The query text
85.title: The query text

850.body: Input Why it is rejected An unknown key or keyword, anywhere A typo must never weaken a schema silently. format other than uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration (email, uri, ...) Accepting an unknown format as a plain string now would let a later version silently change what an existing schema accepts. Remove the format (the value is a string). formatMinimum (and the other format bounds) without a temporal format, or with text that is not of the format's type A bound needs the type it compares in; the hint shows an example of the type's text. additionalProperties: {schema} (a map of T, Pydantic dict[str, T]) No map type yet. Use {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}. oneOf, allOf, not, if/then/else Not implemented; anyOf covers oneOf when the members cannot both match. prefixItems, contains, tuples (items: [..]) An array has one item schema. uniqueItems, multipleOf Not yet (additive later). patternProperties, propertyNames, minProperties, dependent*, unevaluated* Keys are declared with properties, required, additionalProperties. readOnly, writeOnly, content* Not among the accepted annotations. A remote or non-$defs $ref, a reference cycle References are inlined at load. nullable, variants, min, min_length, int64, ... (spellings of other schema dialects, such as OpenAPI's nullable) The hint names the JSON Schema spelling. Every error is SchemaError::InvalidSchema { path, reason, hint }, path a JSON Pointer into the input (/vertices/person/schema/properties/age/minimum), and its help names the fix.

851.title: Defaults on create

852.body: required (on the object) and nullability (the type) are independent, as in JSON Schema: null not admitted ("type": "string") null admitted ("type": ["string", "null"]) in required must be present, non-null must be present, may be null not in required may be absent, never null may be absent or null A missing required key is MissingRequiredProperty; a null where the type does not admit it is a TypeMismatch (expected string, got null). null stays a real stored value (property("k", ()) stores it, it never removes a property: use remove_property, see Removing Properties ). Inside a JSON value {"a": null} differs from {}. Required properties must be supplied when an element is created. The optimizer rule add_property_fold folds addV(..)/addE(..) and the property(k, v) steps that follow into one creation, so g.addV("Person").property("name", "Ann").property("age", 30) creates a valid element in one call. With the rule disabled, or for a property() that cannot be folded, the empty creation is rejected before anything is written. Removing a required property is rejected in open and closed mode.
852.title: Required and nullable

853.body: none open closed Coercion on write (canonical string to uuid, date and time text to its declared type, int64 to float64) no declared properties declared properties Types, constraints, required of declared labels (any depth) no yes yes Undeclared labels allowed allowed, unchecked rejected (also unlabeled elements) Default additionalProperties of an object node - true false Defaults on create (default, defaultFunction) no yes yes Edge topology (connections) no no yes mode governs undeclared labels and topology, and it is the default additionalProperties of every node typed object that does not state its own. An explicit value wins, both ways: a free-form object in a closed graph is {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}, a strict object in an open graph says false. A node without type: "object" (an anyOf wrapper) puts no constraint on keys; its members do. Multi-label vertices (see Multi-Label Vertices ): every label checks the properties it declares and its own required list; a top-level property that no label declares is allowed when ANY label admits additional properties (the same "any label" rule as topology). Coercion uses the first label, in label order, that declares the key. closed rejects a vertex without a label or with an undeclared label. Adding or removing a label re-validates the vertex under the new label set and commits only on success. Edge labels are single, but can be changed (set_label(..), GraphStorage::set_edge_label). The change checks the edge as stored under the new label (closed: a declared label and a declared connection; open and closed: the new label's required keys and declared types) and changes nothing on a violation. Stored values are not coerced by a label change (reads never coerce); later writes coerce by the new label's declarations. none describes without enforcing; the GraphML import still restores the declared logical types from it (uuid, the date and time types, array, object; see UUID Values ). A date or time is written to GraphML as its canonical text under a string key and read back as a temporal value where the target schema declares its format (text that is not of the type fails the import with InvalidAttributeValue); without a declaration it stays a string.
853.title: Modes and additionalProperties

854.body: An edge label declares its allowed connections ({"from": "Person", "to": "Company"}, * matches every label). Because labels are a set, an edge is accepted if ANY label of the source and ANY label of the target matches a declared connection. An edge label without connections allows every pair. A label change that would make an incident edge violate the connections is rejected as a whole.
854.title: Edge topology (closed)

855.body: The content of an object, array or anyOf value is validated at any depth: declared nested keys are type- and constraint-checked, required nested keys must be present, undeclared nested keys follow the object's additionalProperties. Errors name the canonical path ($.address.zip, $.items[1].n). A nested write (property(jpath("address.zip"), v)) coerces the leaf to the type declared at that location. See Path Keys (jpath) .
855.title: Nested values

856.title: Constraints

857.body:
Seven methods, the same everywhere. They are plain calls on the graph source, not traversal steps (like g.statistics()); each runs in the current unit (a transaction, a whole-script unit) or as a unit of its own. Method Returns Authorization get_schema() the stored schema, or none (never inferred) Read on Schema set_schema(schema), set_schema(schema, mode) - (replaces the stored schema; mode replaces the schema's mode) Update on Schema patch_schema(patch) the new schema (JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7396, onto the stored one) Update on Schema validate_schema(schema), validate_schema(schema, mode) {violations, diff, compatible}: a dry run against the data Read on Schema validate_schema_patch(patch) the same for a patch Read on Schema infer_schema() the schema the data satisfies Read on Schema diff_schema(schema) {changes, compatible} from the stored schema Read on Schema Input Output Rust (GraphTraversalSource) GraphSchema (GraphSchema::from_json(text), from_value, or the builders), SchemaPatch (graphersal::schema) GraphSchema, SchemaValidation, SchemaDiff (to_value() gives the data shape) DSL (both spellings: get_schema/getSchema, ...) a map or JSON text a map Python (Graph.get_schema(), ...) a dict or JSON str (keyword policy=) a dict Playground engine (wasm getSchema, ...) JSON text JSON A map built in the DSL keeps its keys in alphabetical order (Rhai maps are sorted), so the property order of a schema that went through a map is alphabetical; JSON text and Python dicts keep it. The traversal step g.v()...infer_schema() infers over a stream, with the same inference. In a DSL map literal, quote the keys that are not plain identifiers: $ref, $defs, $schema and $id start with $. default (a word Rhai reserves) is accepted as a plain key in the Graphersal DSL, quoted or not: g.patch_schema(#{vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{ age: #{type: ["integer", "null"], default: 7}
}}}}}) JSON text needs no quoting rules of its own: g.set_schema(text) takes the schema as written. A schema change is a database change : it advances the commit sequence number, makes the run mutated, is recorded as Mutation::SetSchema { before, after } (the canonical JSON) in the same change set as the data, rolls back with its unit, and is reported in the result's changes: {data, schema} (Execution::changes(), the DSL's r.changes, the playground's response). Validation is immediate: the existing data is checked when the schema is set, not at commit.
857.title: The schema methods

858.body: set_schema and patch_schema validate all existing data first , in one pass over the vertices and edges, when the mode is open or closed. If anything violates the schema, the graph and its current schema stay unchanged and the call fails with one aggregated error that lists every kind of violation, grouped by rule with a count and a few sample ids: Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (5 kinds of violations on 22 elements of 22 checked) 1) Person.age is declared mandatory but is missing on 12 vertices [ids: "p0", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4" and 7 more] 2) vertex label Alien is not declared (Closed): 5 vertices [ids: "x0", "x1", "x2", "x3", "x4"] 3) Company.name is declared mandatory but is missing on 3 vertices [ids: "c0", "c1", "c2"] 4) Person.age has the wrong type on 1 vertex (declared int64, found string) [ids: "t"] 5) Robot.model is not declared (Closed) on 1 vertex [ids: "r"] A group is (kind, label, field or path): missing required keys, undeclared labels or properties, type mismatches, constraint violations, edge topology violations (closed) and nested path violations (Person $.address.zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 1 vertex). Every violation inside a value is listed, not only the first: all keys, all array items, at any depth, each under its own path ($.address.zip wrong type, $.address.street missing and $.address.city undeclared are three groups). Array indices are collapsed into [*]: a rule broken by any item of an array is ONE group ($.addresses[0].zip and $.addresses[2].zip missing are the group $.addresses[*].zip), which shows the first concrete path it met (Person $.addresses[*].zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 5 vertices (first at $.addresses[1].zip) [ids: ...]). Per node only the first failing constraint is named. An element counts once per group, however many of its items break the rule. A single write still fails on the first violation it meets. Groups are ordered by count (largest first), then kind, element, label and field, so the same data gives the same report. Each group shows its count and up to 5 sample ids (cut to 40 characters, escaped); at most 20 groups are printed, the structured report keeps up to 1000, further violations are only counted. Stored data is checked exactly as it is: nothing is coerced and nothing is written. validate_schema returns the same report as data: violations: {mode, elements_checked, violating_elements, total_violations, omitted_violations, groups: [{kind, element, label, field, example_field, detail, count, sample_ids, omitted_ids}]} (example_field is the first concrete path of a [*] field, null otherwise), with kind one of unknown_label, missing_required, type_mismatch, constraint_violation, undeclared_property, invalid_topology. How to proceed: fix or migrate the offending data, relax the schema (make a key optional, admit null, declare the label or property), apply it with mode none, or start from infer_schema(), which is valid for the data it came from.
